*Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, Upper Volume, composed by the Śramaṇa Huīhuī of Xīmíng Monastery in Jīngzhào. Regarding the *Abhidharmapiṭaka*:
it is the grand framework of all treatises and the essential pivot of all sūtras; its six feet and eight aggregates can be understood through investigation.

Through the nine divisions and three categories, one attains understanding; the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang retranslated the True Doctrine and further refined it with the assistance of his disciple, Dharma Master Guang, who personally transmitted the sublime phrasing and secretly received the principles of establishment and refutation.

Consequently, the commentaries and exegeses produced became numerous and complex; as the Jing and Wei rivers flow together, jade and stone become intermingled. How shall those of later generations find their way?

As for Master Baoshu returning [to this work], his realization was nearly equal to that of one born with innate wisdom (*jñāna*), and his talent was fit for occasional emergence; yet, even after further refinement, nothing could surpass it.
This commentary on the hymn relies largely upon the Guangzhai interpretation, and its merit of simplicity and ease shall be suspended like the sun and moon.

However, regarding the principles of selection and rejection, there may be points of divergence. The reason for composing this abridgment now lies precisely here: to briefly extract and rectify the new commentary by Master Baoshu.
The principles are subtle and the words are paired; I have synthesized the two schools to mend their deficiencies. Although I am not gifted, my aspiration is to offer praise.

Furthermore, I observe that those who have recently composed commentaries on the *Vyākhyāyukti* are numerous, yet they extensively cite the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* as their primary exegesis. Their texts are voluminous while their meanings are meager, making them difficult to rely upon.
To abandon the root text and seek instead in those [later works] is sufficient to cause self-confusion; it loses the intent of the original commentary and leads later generations astray.

Regarding this study, my current transcription of the text does not yet fully capture the comprehensive talents and vast meanings [of the original]; I hope you will kindly provide a thorough explanation.

As for the sequence of the six gates: first, it clarifies the origins of the treatise and demonstrates Vasubandhu’s intention in composing it as a condition for severing delusions and generating wisdom;
then, it shows that within the one hundred years following [the Buddha’s passing] and before the three hundred years, there were twenty schools of the Hinayana.
Since the treatise has already clarified which school of the Hīnayāna it belongs to, the second section clarifies the fundamental tenets of the treatise.

Because the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna each possess their own Tripiṭaka and do not mutually trust one another, the third section clarifies which of the Tripiṭakas this treatise is subsumed under within the Tripiṭaka of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Thus, more than eight hundred years have passed since the teaching was translated [into Chinese].
First, the period of antiquity; second, the clarification of the time of translation of the treatise; third, the explanation of the title; fourth, the naming of the Abhidharmakośa;
fifth, the division of the text and the explanation of its meaning.

Regarding the first, the original causes and conditions, there are four parts: (1) the oral transmission of five masters (referring to the period within one hundred years after the passing of seven days); (2) the division into two schools.

I. The School (one hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing], within three hundred years); II. The Intent of the Third Council (with the events of the beginning of the fourth century); III. The Causes for the Attainment of This Treatise (events from nine hundred years ago); IV.

Based on this, regarding the four stages of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) leading to Buddhahood: according to the *Buddha-darśana-sūtra*, he was born and attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the fourth month;
according to the intent of the *Āgama-sūtras*, he was born and attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the second month.

Daoliang explained that because the dates for the observance of the *varṣā* (the rainy season retreat) differ from those in the West, the Western regions take the month of *jianzi* (the eleventh lunar month) as the beginning of the year, whereas this country formerly also took *jianzi* as the beginning of the year but now takes *jiantin* (the first lunar month) as the beginning of the year. If calculated according to the *jianzi* system, it is the eighth day of the fourth month;
if calculated according to the *jiantin* system, it is the eighth day of the second month. This discrepancy arises because the translators cited the date according to the Western calendar.
Regarding the uncertainty of the lunar months, there are two occasions for the eighth day of the second month and the eighth day of the fourth month.
According to the *Sudarsana-vibhasa* and the *Karunapundarika-sutra*, he attained enlightenment at thirty-five years of age, remained in the world for forty years, and entered nirvana at eighty.
The verse by Bodhiruci states: "He acted as an infant for eight years, as a youth for seven years, and studied the five [sciences] for four years."

In his tenth year of enlightenment, he experienced the five desires; in his eightieth year, he entered *nirvāṇa*, relinquishing one-fifth of his life-span—according to one tradition in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, he relinquished one-third of his life-span—as explained extensively below. The signs at the time of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* are described in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*.
When the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa* in the city of Kuśinagara, Kāśyapa was not present at the assembly; he learned of it afterward.

When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, before the Three Piṭakas were to be compiled, they first painted the eight phases of the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment in a single hall and placed medicinal dregs there.
Subsequently, King Ajātaśatru was led on a tour; finally, upon seeing the place where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, he fainted and died.
Only after he had revived did he proceed with King Ajātaśatru to the site of the parinirvāṇa, where Kāśyapa paid homage to the Tathāgata’s coffin.

Manifesting his feet to signify that he was entrusting the Dharma to Kāśyapa, and furthermore, according to the *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that while the Buddhas remain in the world for one kalpa or more than one kalpa, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Do not speak thus.
You should know that the True Dharma of the future has been entrusted to Mahākāśyapa; I give it to you as a place of refuge, even unto the various [beings] of the six heavens of desire."
The devas paid homage at the feet of Kāśyapa, who fully established the Buddha-dharma;

within the stone chamber, he presided over the council of one thousand *aśaikṣas*, forming the Sthavira school, while outside the stone chamber, the multitude of ordinary and noble beings formed the Mahāsāṃghika school.

Seven days after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the names of these two schools already existed, for it was due to the five elders, including Kāśyapa, upholding the single flavor of the Dharma without division.
King Ajātaśatru had previously made a request, saying, "When you enter parinirvāṇa, I pray that you allow me to see you.
Kāśyapa, weary of the world, entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda and took leave of the king before entering parinirvāṇa. The king dreamed that the ridgepole of his palace broke;
upon waking, he informed the gatekeeper, who immediately went to the Bamboo Grove to ask Ānanda where Kāśyapa was. Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru and Ānanda together proceeded to Kukkuṭapāda Mountain.
Having completed various offerings on the mountain and wishing to cremate [the body] with fragrant wood, Ānanda informed Kāśyapa in detail of his previous vows and so forth.
When Kāśyapa entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda, he fulfilled three vows: first, upon entering the mountain, the three peaks closed over him;
second, when King Ajātaśatru and Ānanda came to the mountain, the peaks immediately opened; third, he left this body until the descent of Maitreya, after which he would enter parinirvāṇa.

Later, Ānanda saw a bhikṣu misrecite the Dhammapada verses: "If one lives for a hundred years and does not see the drying up of the waters of old age, it is better to live for a single day and behold them.

Ānanda corrected the second line to read, "not knowing the law of arising and ceasing," and the fourth line to read, "and thereby attaining full understanding. Afterward, he observed the world as before, reciting according to the correct version.
No one was able to correct him, so he immediately took his leave of the king. The king saw in a dream that the handle of a parasol had broken. Ānanda traveled north to the Ganges River;
having invited [the people] from the south, north, above, below, and the four cardinal directions, he transformed the middle of the Ganges into golden ground.
At that time, five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains came to seek refuge with Ānanda, requesting ordination; among them were two individuals. One...
His name was Maudgalyāyana (formerly transcribed as Matian-dijia; here translated as "Golden Land"), so called because he converted a body of water into golden land and thereby attained liberation.
Another name was Śaṇakavāsin (here translated as "Womb-Raiment"). Only after entrusting [the Dharma] to these two men did he enter parinirvāṇa.
Within the borders of North India, there was originally a dragon pond regarding which the Tathāgata had prophesied: "Within one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be..."

Madhyāntika widely propagated my Dharma. When Madhyāntika saw the Buddha’s prediction concerning that very country, a Buddha entered meditative absorption there, and his radiance was exceptionally wondrous.
A nāga king emerged and asked, "Virtuous one, what do you require? [Madhyāntika] then extended his body until it filled the entire pond;
he left only a square and round area of one hundred *li* in the northwest corner for the nāga pond, and made all the rest into a monastery.
It is here that the Buddha-dharma shall be practiced. Venerable Ānanda, having entrusted the Dharma to Śāṇakavāsin, addressed him, saying:
"In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through the country of Mathurā, he charged me, saying:
'In this country there will be an elder named Kuṭadanta; his third son shall have power within the Buddha-dharma. That third son is named Upakuṭa."
Through many skillful means, he exhorted and transformed others so that they attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*), entrusting the Dharma to this Kuṭadanta.
Later, Kuṭadanta converted a husband and wife, both of whom simultaneously attained the fruit of Arhatship. For every person converted, he would break off a tally stick four inches long;

when the stone chamber was filled with these tallies, the chamber—measuring sixty feet square—was so crowded with those who had been saved that the people of the world called him the "Buddha Without Physical Marks. Subsequently, he was harassed by a celestial Māra.
Even to the point that he caused the body of the Tathāgata to appear; Kuṭadanta did not realize it and prostrated himself.
His five hundred disciples were under the influence of Śoṇa, with whom they had no karmic connection, thinking, "Only our teacher can deliver us. They then directed their whole hearts toward Śoṇa.
By means of his supernormal power, Śoṇa came from the kingdom of Kaśmīra and sat upon Kuṭadanta’s seat. Thereupon, the five hundred men immediately announced [the news].
The Master said, "If it were not for my teacher, who would dare sit upon my bed?

When Śāṇakavāsin pointed toward the sky, five hundred streams of fragrant milk appeared in mid-air—all signs of meditative concentration. [The Master] explained the name and significance of each one, whereupon he attained the fruit of the Path.
The Commentary states: "A slight deviation from the great meaning" refers to Ānanda seeing a bhikṣu misrecite the *Dharmapada*.

Kuṭadanta was the fifth master who did not succeed the three sages—namely Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and Śāṇakavāsin—because Madhyāntika converted the border regions and, furthermore, because he transmitted the Dharma simultaneously with Śāṇakavāsin; thus, it is said there were "three."
Sage. Mahā means "Great. Deva means "Heavenly Being. To the southeast of the Kingdom of Magadha, there was the country of Mathurā.
A merchant leader had a son named Mahādeva. After the merchant leader had gone on a long journey, his son became intimate with his mother; subsequently, the father returned home.

Fearing that his evil deeds would become manifest—having murdered his father with his mother and having taken his mother to the city of Pāṭaliputra, which still belonged to the kingdom of Magadha—he encountered an Arhat there who was receiving offerings from his own country.
Fearing that his disgraceful acts might be spread abroad, he again used a stratagem to kill this Arhat.
Later, when his mother became unfaithful, he killed her as well. Having thus committed three heinous crimes (ānantarya), his mind became filled with terror, and he entered the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
Upon meeting a monk reciting a verse from the sutras, he said: "If a person commits a grave offense, practicing virtue will surely extinguish it;

that [virtue] can illuminate the world like the sun emerging from the clouds. His heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately sought ordination. The monk, not yet having examined his spiritual capacity (*indriya*), ordained him.
Not long after, he mastered the twelve divisions of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). He entered and exited the royal palace, and there was no one who did not turn toward him in devotion.
Consequently, there were five matters on account of which he did not inform his disciples that he was an Arhat. The first was as follows:
due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), he had a dream in which he emitted semen and asked his disciple to wash it.

He said, "I have heard that for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted. The disciple then replied, "There are two kinds of outflows: first, the outflow of afflictions (*kleśa-āsrava*), which you have already exhausted as one beyond training..."
For those who are non-dual, impurity still persists even in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Desiring to gladden his disciples, he falsely contrived a prophetic declaration (*vyākaraṇa*) that the disciples had attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The disciples said: "Master, you have declared that we have attained the second or third fruit; we ourselves should know this through our own realization. How could it be so?"
He was entirely unaware of this himself; his answer that he was "ignorant" refers to two types of ignorance: first, defiled ignorance, which you have now severed;
second, non-defiled ignorance, which you have not yet severed.
A third time he addressed the Teacher, saying: "I have heard that the Noble One has already severed doubt; yet I still harbor a doubt regarding the reality of the truths.

He replied: "There are two kinds of doubt: first, doubt of the nature of affliction, which you have already severed; second, doubt concerning what is possible and what is impossible, which remains even for those beyond training (aśaikṣas)."
The four clouds of disciples read the scriptures and [realized that] Arhats possess the eye of wisdom and are able to personally realize and know their own liberation.
They then declared: "There are Arhats who cannot know it themselves, but must rely on others—such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
If they do not know it themselves when it has not yet been predicted for them, how much less could they know it through others?"
At night, the five great gods contemplated how they were being led astray from the holy teaching and were oppressed by anxiety; unconsciously, they cried out, "Alas, what suffering!
A disciple immediately asked about this, and he replied: "I call the Noble Path 'suffering'. He then compiled these five matters and composed a verse:
"Led astray by others, ignorant, and wavering, Others cause one to enter the path; Because it arises due to sound, This is called [the Name]."
In the True Buddhist temple, during the *poṣadha* ceremony, when Mahādeva ascended the seat to recite the precepts, he first recited five matters to inform the others.
The assembly then revised the fourth clause, stating: "This is not the teaching of the Buddha.

According to the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*, at that time the fourfold assembly was in discord for one night: one group was like a noble elephant (*nāga-hastin*), possessing majesty and power beyond resistance; the other was like a mere monkey (*markaṭa*).

The power of King Nalijana and his ministers overcomes the holy assembly of the sea, which belongs to the class of Mahādeva. The two types of "border" (pratyanta) assemblies have minds that wander outside of principle;
they are called "border" because they lack virtues worthy of praise, and "base" (pāpa) because they are the followers of Mahādeva.

The three types of "learned" (bahuśruta) assemblies have profoundly mastered the subtle and profound and are extensively familiar with the Tripiṭaka. The four types of "virtuous" (mahāpuṇya) assemblies possess wisdom that accords with principle.
Their supernormal powers were unsurpassed, and they were indeed the Noble Assembly. Consequently, these four assemblies deliberated together regarding the five matters concerning Mahādeva;

their disputes became so tumultuous that they did not cease until dawn. The officials and commoners of the city went to the monastery to mediate with the assembly, but none of their reconciliatory efforts succeeded.
At that time, King Aśoka went in person to mediate with the assembly; each adhered to their own verses, asserting their own views as correct and others' as wrong. The King said: "I..."

"Now, upon what should we rely? Mahādeva said, "If the King wishes to settle this dispute, he should rely on the 'majority decision' (*yadbhūyasikīya*) by casting black and white voting sticks (*śalākā*).
Since the followers of the heterodox faction are numerous, they will side with the Great Heavenly King. Thus, having relied on the majority, the matter was concluded and they returned to the palace.
At that time, the dispute at Kukkutārāma had still not subsided. Then, the various noble ones (*ārya*), perceiving the discord among the assembly, abandoned Kukkutārāma.
When the ministers heard that Udena intended to go elsewhere, they quickly informed the king.

Upon hearing this, the king became enraged at them and ordered that they be led to the banks of the Ganges and placed in a broken boat to drown in midstream. He wished to test whether these men were sages or ordinary people.

As they were about to sink, each of them manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and departed through the air like a flight of geese; however, those who had not yet attained such powers remained behind.
They were also received and transformed into various forms; having completely abandoned the Kukkuṭārāma, they all flew toward the northwest to Kaśmīra.
When the King of Kaśmīra saw this, he repented his faults and built more than several hundred monasteries there.
He then established names for them based on the forms they had manifested. Later, when Mahādeva went out to travel through the cities and towns, a diviner privately...
I have privately recorded this: this son of the Śākyas will certainly meet his end in seven days from now.

When the disciple heard this, he immediately informed his teacher Mahādeva, who said, "I have known this for a long time. He then dispatched his disciples to announce it everywhere among the officials and commoners:
"Beyond seven days, I shall surely enter *nirvāṇa*. When the kings and others heard this, there was none who did not lament in sorrow. When the full seven days had passed, he [the Buddha] then...
When his life ended, they prepared fragrant firewood together to cremate him; yet by various means, the fire could not burn him.
A diviner said to the crowd, "This lowly man cannot endure such superior offerings; one should sprinkle dog excrement upon him.
When they followed these words, the fire finally ignited and, in an instant, consumed everything until it was reduced to ashes. Then, a violent wind suddenly arose.
It was dispersed without remainder; this is the reason for the discord among the Mahādevas, as explained in detail in the ninety-ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the arising of the dispute in the kingdom of Magadha, it is also called the kingdom of Māgadha. Among the four Vedas, it is said that this [place] is "free from poison" (*nirviṣa*);
the old translation "the place where nectar is placed" is also acceptable from a semantic perspective. This is where the various devas and asuras...
In the distant past, beings were heavily afflicted by the poison of attachment, which caused their lifespans to be short.
Brahmā, mindful of this, used a dragon as a cord and a mountain as a drill to churn the Ocean of Milk. At that time, through the karmic power of sentient beings, the ocean transformed into milk;
nectar was obtained and placed in this land, whereby all poisons and harms were eliminated and long life was attained. For this reason, it is called [Lao].
Establishing the Name:

Gandhāra is a region within Northern India that was the native land of Vasubandhu. When he engaged in a debate on the principles of the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā-śāstra* with his preceptor, the latter spoke of "fire and smoke" (*agni-dhūma*).
The King and the non-Buddhists laughed, saying, "One should have said 'smoke and fire' (*dhūmāgni*), not as you heard it."
Vasubandhu bit his tongue in remorse until the end of his days, yet he further engaged in debate with his elder brother to clear his previous disgrace;
he was truly one who never allowed his principles to be distorted at that time. Kaniṣka means "King of Pure Gold" in this language.
The Venerable Pārśva left the household life at the age of eighty and was ridiculed by the youths for his vow, saying:

"If I do not attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa*, become proficient in the Tripiṭaka, sever the delusions of the three realms, acquire the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and be endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*)—such that my ribs do not touch my mat for three years—then may I fail to attain the fruits of the Path.
He subsequently attained the fruits of the Path, became proficient in the Tripiṭaka, and so forth; at that time, people revered him for his virtue.
He was titled the Venerable Pārśva.
"Nüxīng" (聿興) means to initiate or to narrate.
Regarding the "five dreams," according to the lower fascicle of the *Māyā-sūtra*, on the night of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Māyā obtained five [dreams] while in the heavens.
Regarding the evil dreams: first, he dreamed that Mount Sumeru collapsed and the waters of the four oceans dried up;

second, he dreamed that various rākṣasas, holding sharp swords in their hands, were vying to gouge out the eyes of all sentient beings, at which time a black wind blew the rākṣasas back toward the Snowy Mountains;
third, he dreamed that the gods of the desire and form realms suddenly lost their jeweled crowns and tore off their necklaces. Not...
1. She sat peacefully upon her seat. 2. She dreamed that the King of Cintāmaṇi Jewels was atop a high banner, constantly raining down precious treasures to provide for all beings;

then four poisonous dragons spat fire from their mouths, blowing the high banner down and violently snatching the Cintāmaṇi jewel away with fierce winds, which swept it into a deep abyss. 3. She dreamed that five lions came through the air and bit Māyā.

Milk entered his right side, and his body and mind experienced pain as if pierced by swords and blades; having seen this dream, Āniruddha came and informed him that the Tathāgata was entering *parinirvāṇa*.
Regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*):

first, the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), which examines and determines what is correct and erroneous, and investigates and analyzes what is true and false; second, the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), which thoroughly explores and elucidates the five [aggregates]...

1. The sublime principle of cause and effect; 2. The science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), including incantations for restraining malevolent spirits, medicinal herbs, stones, acupuncture, and moxibustion; 3.

The science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), including technical skills, mechanical devices, the principles of yin and yang, and calendrical calculations; 4. The science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), including the interpretation of glosses, the definition of characters, and the classification of linguistic branches;
[and 5. the inner science]. Fearing that his teacher might harbor resentment or dread, or fearing that other arhats might harbor resentment or dread, the author of the treatise...
Fearing that the Arhat might harbor feelings of resentment or envy, the Master [Sthiramati] also adopts this view.

Regarding the necessity of severing the conditions for the outflows (*āsrava*): the "outflows" here refer precisely to the conditions that moisten rebirth. To emerge from the three realms, one must first sever these conditions of the outflows that moisten rebirth;
the primary cause for severing these outflows is pure wisdom (*viśuddha-prajñā*). The above constitutes the commentary’s established principle regarding the way pure wisdom severs the outflows.
The treatise (*śāstra*) correctly elucidates wisdom (*prajñā*); that which arises below it is the person, Vasubandhu, who composed the treatise. Based on the treatise, pure wisdom is generated.

Some commentators explain that the teaching of the treatise is called the "condition for severing delusions," but this is likely not the correct meaning; the treatise correctly elucidates wisdom, and it is only from that point downward that the composition of the treatise is brought forth.
Please examine this carefully.
The four Āgamas—the Long, the Middle, the Mixed, and the Numerical—this treatise is the key to all these sūtras and śāstras.

Since the Blue Lotus ceased its smile, the Buddha possesses two types of wisdom: first, the Fundamental Wisdom, also called the Wisdom of the Essential Body, Non-conceptual Wisdom, and the Wisdom of Awakening from Sleep;
second, the Subsequently Attained Wisdom, also called the Wisdom that Comprehends the Conventional and Awakens Sentient Beings.

The wisdom-lotus opens to reveal wisdom, just as when a worldly lotus opens to reveal the lotus seed within. This refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) which, upon opening, establishes the manifestation of all phenomena from the Buddha’s own nirvāṇa;
because he no longer further preaches the Dharma, it is called "cessation of the smile. Here, "smile" means "opening.

The people of the Jiang and Chu regions explain that the Buddha’s eyes were like blue lotuses; they claim that whenever the Buddha wished to preach the Dharma, his eyes would first smile. This interpretation is incorrect.

Regarding "the white tuft eclipsing the color": when the Buddha intends to preach the Dharma, he first emits light from his white tuft. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he no longer emits such light; this is what is meant by "eclipsing the color.
Second, the two types of wisdom differ because both are attained through the severance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Because one severs the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that cause rebirth, one realizes true liberation; because one severs the cognitive obstructions that hinder understanding, [one attains omniscience]."
Thus, he attained Great Enlightenment.
Regarding those who rain down discourse on the three kinds of excellence: during the Kalpa of Formation (*vivartakalpa*), there appeared a non-Buddhist teacher in the world.
In Sanskrit he is called *Kapila*, which means "yellowish-red"; because his hair, eyebrows, and facial complexion were all yellowish-red, people of the time called him by that name.
The "Yellow-Red" (Huang-chi-se) Rishi is a corruption of what was anciently called the Kāpiḷa Rishi. Among his later disciples, the foremost of the eighteen schools was named Vārṣagaṇya;
because he was born during the rainy season (*vārṣika*), his followers were called the Rain-Followers (*Vārṣagaṇya*).
In Sanskrit, this is *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*, which is translated as "Number-Treatise" (*Sāṃkhya*); it refers to that which [discerns] by means of wisdom.
Because one repeatedly classifies all phenomena (*dharma*) based on enumeration (*saṃkhyā*), and because this treatise (*śāstra*) can produce such enumeration, it is called Sāṃkhya.

The author of the treatise and those who study it are called Sāṃkhya masters. The composition of the *Pañcaviṃśati-tattva-śāstra* (Treatise on the Twenty-five Principles) is also called the *Saptati-kārikā* (Seventy Verses);

this is precisely the Sāṃkhya system. This treatise contains twenty-five principles (*tattva*). The first is the Self (*ātman*), which has consciousness (*cetanā*) as its essence; it desires to experience external objects.
When the object-field [is perceived], the three *guṇas* undergo transformation. Regarding the two aspects of *prakṛti*:

the ancient masters called it "the hidden nature" (*míngxìng*) when it has not yet produced the great elements (*mahat*), etc., and they named it "supreme nature" (*shèngxìng*) once it has produced the great elements, etc., because it is a collection of superior differences.

Thus, the specific names for *prakṛti* are the three *guṇas*. In Sanskrit, they are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. *Sattva* means "sentient being" (*yǒngqíng*) as well as "courageous and vigorous. Here, we take the sense of "courageous and vigorous."
Next is *rajas*, which here is translated as "subtle" (*wei*) or "dust" (*chenpen*); it takes the sense of dust. Then there is *tamas*, which is translated as "darkness-dullness" (*an dun*);

its essential nature is dull darkness, and its formal name is "valiant-dust. Regarding the term "darkness," the three qualities (*guṇas*) are, according to ancient names, "staining, coarse, and black," while in modern names they are "yellow-red and black.

The old names for them are "joy, sorrow, and indifference" (*sukha, duḥkha, upekṣā*), and they are also called "greed, hatred, and delusion" (*lobha, dveṣa, moha*). The old translations were "pleasure, pain, and equanimity."
Because these three *guṇas* are the cause of birth and death, the *puruṣa* (the self) by its very nature contemplates the objects of liberation;

thus, the *guṇas* transform the self into an object, binding it so that it cannot attain liberation. Later, through the cultivation of the path born of weariness with those objects, the self ceases to contemplate objects;
its own nature remains unchanging, and being freed from the bondage of objects, it immediately attains liberation. The non-Buddhists first contemplate eighty thousand *kalpas*.

I do not know whether that which is called *māyā* (the primal nature) is like my ministers and assistants, or if it constitutes the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) that follow me. Third, from *prakṛti* (self-nature) arises the Great One (*mahat*);
because the external objects of thought arise from the three qualities (*guṇa*), the essence is "Great. Fourth, from the Great One arises intellect (*buddhi*);
because within eighty thousand kalpas there is that which is perceived and known, whereas before those eighty thousand kalpas there was no perception, it is termed *māyā*. Fifth, from...
The five *tanmātras* (subtle elements) arise from the Intellect (*buddhi*): namely, color-form, sound, odor, taste, and touch. These are the primary causes (*bhūta-kāraṇa*).
From these five *tanmātras*, the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) arise; these are the derived phenomena (*vikāra*). From the five gross elements, eleven faculties (*indriya*) arise:

the seven [sensory] faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, the organ of excretion, and the organ of procreation—and the four [active] faculties—the hands, feet, the organ of speech, and the mind (*manas*), which is the faculty of internal reflection. These constitute the twenty-three principles (*tattva*).
All these are transformations of impermanent form (*rūpa*). The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are capable of creating turn back into the color red and can form the eye;

the eye can see forms and sounds. The element capable of creating space (*ākāśa*) possesses sound; from sound, the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is formed, and the faculty of hearing can hear sounds.

Fragrance (*gandha*) can create earth (*pṛthivī*); because earth abounds in fragrance, earth forms the nose (*ghrāṇa*), and the nose can perceive fragrance. Taste (*rasa*) creates water (*ap*); water abounds in taste.
Water can form the tongue; the tongue can taste flavors. Touch can produce wind, because there is much touch [in] wind. Wind can form the body; the body can perceive touch.
The five sense objects together give rise to the five great elements. The five great elements together form the five organs of action.
As for the organs of action, they are the tongue that cuts meat, the hands, the feet, the large path, the small path, and the organ of mental equanimity. If I were to experience them...
Regarding external objects: they proceed from the former to the latter. If the self does not experience them, they revert back from the latter into the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

This is analyzed through four propositions: 1. That which has the power to transform: namely, the Primordial Essence (*pradhāna*). 2. That which is transformed by another: namely, the eleven faculties. 3.

That which both has the power to transform and is transformed by another: namely, the intellect (*buddhi*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*). 4. That which cannot transform: [the self].
He did not follow the teachings of others; rather, he held that the self (*ātman*) was the creator.

Fearing that his body would perish upon death and that his knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) would not be transmitted, he questioned Maheśvara regarding the method for attaining eternal life. At present, on this continent, beneath Mount Vindhya, he eats the *śeṣamūla* fruit;
when unripe it is green, and when ripe it is reddish-white. When first eaten, it is sour and bitter, but once consumed, [it provides immortality].
If one obtains water, it is sweet; if one eats this fruit, the mind attains long-term stability. [However,] his mind was not yet resolved, so he went again to inquire further.
[Vasubandhu] then caused a great stone to be manifested, square and round in size like a single bed. He told the gatekeeper:
"If anyone asks you about the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) and you cannot answer, write down their question upon this stone. Later, Vasubandhu’s younger brother, Āryadeva, arrived.
The Bodhisattva Dignāga then asked: "Regarding your assertion that the self (*ātman*) is the agent, is it the experiencer?

He replied: "It is the experiencer. He asked again: "Is it permanent (*nitya*) or impermanent (*anitya*)? [Dignāga] wished to say "permanent," but [the opponent] did not answer. [Dignāga] said: "If it accepts objects, then if you say it is impermanent, the meaning of 'self' is not established.
[The opponent] replied: "It is permanent, because of inference (*anumāna*). [Dignāga] refuted this, saying: "Your thesis that the self exists is a subject (*dharmin*) which must be impermanent."

The formal argument (prayoga) states: "Because it perceives external objects"—this is the reason (*hetu*). The corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) states: "Just as in the *Vedanā-skandha-sūtra*, after several days [of practice], one does not obtain stones;
instead, sweat flows, sounds are made, and with thunderous roars, [the body] naturally breaks apart. Thus, the treatise says: "Dignāga first established the three members [of the syllogism]:
'Milk-stones resounded on the mountain.'"
Regarding the teaching of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*): at the end of a kalpa of formation, there appeared a non-Buddhist teacher named Vaiśeṣika (formerly called Shushi Shi;
here translated as "Excellence in Discourse"). He composed the *Ṣaṭpadārtha-śāstra*.

Because it is superior among all treatises—either because its principles surpass those of the Sāṃkhya school or because the person who composed the treatise on the six categories was preeminent—it is called the Vaiśeṣika. It is also called *Uttara*... [text fragment].

*Luojia* (路迦) is translated here as "owl" (*xiuliu*); the older transcription *youlujia* is an error. It refers to a creature with a hideous form that terrifies pregnant women, causing them to miscarry;
for this reason, it hides during the day and emerges at night. When people set out food at night, it immediately hides;
when no one provides offerings, it seeks out rice from the husks ground in mortars or winnowed in threshing floors to eat. For this reason, it is also called *jianna*.
I here refer to the *Śāli-stamba-sūtra* (The Rice-Stalk Sūtra); the old translation as *Khaṇḍa-ta* is an error. He composed the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma-śāstra*.
"Dhara" in Sanskrit is translated here as "Lord" (*pati*), and "Tattva" as "True Principle" (*satya-artha*), which refers to the meaning of reality. It takes nine categories as its substance:
earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, self (*ātman*), and mind (*manas*). These are eternal. When the world forms, they aggregate; when it disintegrates, they scatter.
The atom (*paramāṇu*) is indestructible and serves as the substratum (*āśraya*)—the Sanskrit term *guṇa* being translated here as "substratum" or "basis"—for twenty-four phenomena.
This refers to the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*), which has these twenty-four phenomena as its essence. The verse states: Color, taste, odor, and tangibility;
number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, volition, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, motion, merit, and demerit.

And "performing an action" (*karma*) corresponds to the preceding nine categories of phenomena as explained in the *Ṣaṭpadārtha-śāstra*. Here, *karma* is translated as "action" (*zuo*) or "deed" (*di*).
Its meaning is the category of activity; its essence consists of the five factors: taking up, setting aside, contracting, extending, and moving.

Apart from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karma*), there are five distinct factors that cause substance and quality to perform actions. Third, *sāmānya* (Sanskrit) is translated as "universal characteristic" (*zongxiang*).

The *Satya* (Truth) is the "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) category; the ten-fold discourse on it is named after this treatise. The "General Category" (*sāmānya-pada-artha*) is identical to the aforementioned [categories of] substance, quality, and action, which cannot exist of themselves.
It exists because there is a separate "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), which is the fifth *viśeṣa-satya*—here translated as the "Distinct Characteristic Truth" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-satya*).

This is the "Identity-and-Difference Category" (*tad-atad-pada*). The seventy-fold discourse on it is named the "Universal Differentiation Category" (*sarva-vibhāga-pada*), which is distinct from substance and quality.
Apart from karma, there exists a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Just as humans are the same [in their humanity], there is a distinct principle of similarity that causes them to be the same;

and just as humans differ from animals, there is a distinct principle of difference that causes them to be different. In reality, among the three categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), each possesses both general and particular similarities and differences.

Sixth is *samavāya-tattva*, here translated as the "truth of non-obstruction" (*anāvaraṇa-tattva*); it is a category of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that enables substances and the other categories to... [not to be separated].
This treatise is established through their separation, just as the union of father and mother can produce a child, or the union of earth and water can produce all things.
To compose this *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma-śāstra* (Treatise in Six Sections), it was essential to have a single person transmit and receive it who must possess seven virtues:

first, being born in a central land; second, belonging to a noble lineage; third, possessing the causes for tranquility; fourth, having perfect physical marks; fifth, being intelligent, eloquent, and quick-witted; sixth, [possessing] a virtuous nature...

Having practiced gentleness and perfected the seven qualities of great compassion, during the period of decline at the end of the kalpa, there was in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra a brāhmaṇa named Maṇava (translated as "Youth").
This Maṇava had a son named Pañcaśikha (translated as "Five-Crested"), who had five points on his head;
his hair formed five curls. Although he possessed the seven virtues, his faculties were somewhat slow to ripen because of their depth.
His wife was difficult to convert. Later, while they were playing and competing for flowers, she became weary of him.
He then thought to himself, "Where is that seer from days past? The seer, possessing supernatural powers, arrived at that very moment.
He was welcomed to their residence, where he expounded the Six-Line Treatise (*Ṣaḍpādābhidharma*). Among the eighteen schools of the later age, he was the foremost, known as Vatsīputra.

Regarding this, it is said that Huiyue composed the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ten Categories), which divides the categories of "sameness" and "difference" into two, and further adds three categories:
"possibility," "impossibility," and "both.

As for the phrase "because of studying the path of treatises," one interpretation states that "treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to verbal discourse, while "path" (*mārga*) refers to the principles explained by the Tripiṭaka.

Regarding the compound "the path of discourse" (*vāda-mārga*), it is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound consisting of two parts: first, "path" (*mārga*) in the sense of a track or way, which carries the meaning of a basis;

second, "discourse" (*vāda*), which refers to the place traversed by the wisdom of the practitioner. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound, wherein "discourse" itself is the "path."
"Mooring" (*po*) refers to the appearance of being tossed about by flowing water; it signifies that within the True Dharma (*saddharma*), false dharmas (*mithyādharma*) arise.
Regarding "powerful outflow" (*balānuvṛtti*): "power" (*bala*) means that which cannot be bent or subdued; the sūtra-teachings produced thereby are likewise unbendable.

"Outflow" (*anu-vṛtti*) refers to a category or kind, meaning "to flow forth," or alternatively, "equal" (*sama*) carries the sense of "drawing forth. This is consistent with the previous sūtra passage concerning the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
Regarding the production of specific and general characteristics: form and sound are specific characteristics, while impermanence and so forth are general characteristics.

"One who has eyes" refers to a person possessing wisdom; when such a person analyzes various phenomena through this treatise, it is like a person with sight obtaining a lamp in a dark room and thereby seeing all manner of forms.
That which is without self-image consists of the Three Dharma Seals. When the teachings of the Tripiṭaka are conjoined with these three seals, they constitute the True Dharma: 1.

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*) refers to the conditioned, such as the Five Aggregates; this is like the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, which mentions the first [seal] to include the latter two. 2. "Nirvāṇa is quiescent" (*nirvāṇaṃ śāntam*) refers to the unconditioned;

this is like the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (or *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*), which mentions the last [seal] to include the first three. 3. "All dharmas are without self" (*sarvadharmanairātmyam*)... [is]... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on the Three Dharma Seals, drawing parallels between the Tripiṭaka teachings and specific treatises.)
The general classification into conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is the broadest category mentioned here, as it encompasses the other two divisions.

Regarding the division of the scriptural traces into eighteen schools: immediately after the seven days [of schism], there were already the names of two schools due to the maintenance of the teachings by five individuals;
beyond one hundred years, following the four prior schisms of the Great Assembly, there occurred the subsequent seven schisms.
The former nine and the latter eleven [schisms] arose from five points of contention among the Mahādevas, resulting in the division into two schools:
first, the Mahāsāṃghika, who were the many disciples—both ordinary and noble, learners and non-learners—assembled for the council outside the stone chamber;

second, the Sthavira, who were the thousand non-learners assembled for the council inside the stone chamber. This occurred within the second century, following the first century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Within the various schools, due to many disagreements arising among the noble ones, the śrāvakas, and ordinary people, they were initially divided into nine schools. First, because of differences in their established tenets, three schools branched out:
1. The Ekavyāvahārika (One-Description School): Because all mundane and supramundane phenomena lack substantial reality and exist only as provisional designations, they are called the Ekavyāvahārika.
They are named after their specific tenet. In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* and by Paramārtha, they are called the "Adherents of One" (*Ekavādin*).
The two schools of the Language Section (Vākyakāra) are the Lokottaravāda and the Lokavāda.

[They hold that] mundane phenomena arise from afflictions and inversions, and thus lack substantial reality and exist only nominally; supramundane phenomena do not arise from inversions, and thus are substantially real.
The school known as Mañjuśrī-nāma-praśaṃsaka is called the Satyārthika-Lokottaravāda; this is a corruption of the Sanskrit term. These are the two schools.
They derive their name from their founder, known as the Kukkutika school. In ancient times, there was a rishi who begot a son by a hen; this was a lineage of rishis among the Brahmins.
According to the *Tattvārtha* (True Meaning), they are called the Pāṣaṇḍaka-vāsin (Dwellers on the Ash Mountain) school. Neither the original phonetics nor the meaning support such a claim;

they merely propagate the Abhidharma while not propagating the Sūtras and Vinaya, because these [latter] are considered the expedient teachings of the Buddhas. Thus, they deviate from the fundamental [teachings].

Because their tenets were distinct, they resided separately. Furthermore, from the Mahāsāṃghika school emerged one named the Bahuśrutīya (The Many-Heard). They were so named because they were extensively learned and possessed vast knowledge;
the name was established based on their virtue. During the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a rishi in the Snowy Mountains who wore garments of tree bark and entered the Mahāsāṃghika order.
He saw only that which propagated shallow meanings, so he further recited other doctrines—both those that were profound and those that were not—which surpassed his original [school].

The three divisions that share the same *sabhāgatā* are the Mahāsāṃghika, the Sthavira, and the Sarvāstivāda. Furthermore, from the Mahāsāṃghika there emerges another school called the Prajñaptivāda (the School of Designation);

they maintain that both mundane and supramundane phenomena possess a subtle designation (*prajñapti*), which is established as the name for "True Reality" (*tattva*). [Note: This name does not appear in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*.

When two hundred years had passed since the four major schools were established, a certain master emerged named Mahādeva, who resided on Mount Caitya; this mountain was richly endowed with many [relics/stupas].
Regarding the prohibition of the five points of Mahādeva, there was debate over what was permissible and what was not, leading to the division into two schools:
those residing in the western mountains were called the *Aparaśaila* (Western Mountain) school, and those residing in the northern mountains were called the *Uttaraśaila* (Northern Mountain) school;

later, this [latter] was named the *Caitika* (or *Caityaśaila*) school. Within two hundred years of the Sthavira school, they remained in harmonious unity as a single flavor, primarily propagating the Sūtras.

The Abhidharma treatises were considered the primary [teaching] and the Sūtras and Vinaya the secondary; this was the case until the beginning of the third century, when Kātyāyanīputra left the household life and propagated the Abhidharma-piṭaka as the primary teaching, while the Sūtras and Vinaya became secondary. Having thus deviated from the original intent, the school split into two:

the first was named the Sarvāstivāda (All-Exists School), also known as the Hetuvāda (Exposition of Causes), because they maintained that all established phenomena possess causes and conditions; the second was named the Himavat (Snowy Mountains), which remained the original [lineage].

Most of those who held the views of the Sthaviras and were proponents of the theory of learning migrated to the region known as the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), where they came to be called the Sarvāstivādins.

From this group, one school emerged named the Vātsīputrīyas. In ancient times, there was a rishi who became infatuated with a heifer and fathered a son; from that time on, the lineage of that rishi was all called "Vatsiputras.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that during the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Vatsiputra who converted to Buddhism and left the world.

The school originated from the back gate, and its followers were unceasing; eventually, they divided into branches that became renowned from afar as the Three Calf Schools (*Trivatsa*). From these four divisions emerged one Dharma:
the Superior School (*Uttarīya*), so named because its members possessed the Dharma that stands above all others. Second was the Noble Lineage School (*Bhadrayānīya*);
"Noble" (*bhadra*) refers to the masters of the school, while "Lineage" (*yāni*) is a term for descendants—meaning they are the descendants of those noble Arhats. Third... [text fragment ends].

The Saṃmitīya school (Saṃmitīya-nikāya) is so named because it "destroys wrong certainty" (*saṃmita*); that which is measured by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is free from error is called "right" (*sam*), meaning that its certainty is without error, hence the name Saṃmitīya.

Regarding the four sub-sects: the Kāśyapīyas, the Avantakas, the Vātsīputrīyas, and the Dharmottarīyas. As for the Mahīśāsakas, they are so called because their leader resided in a mountainous region with dense forests;

these four schools originally recited the *Śāriputrābhidharma* together, but as the wording and meaning became somewhat diminished, they later each composed their own treatises and extracted from the sūtras.
Because their interpretations were mutually contradictory, they eventually formed four schools. Furthermore, there was a school that emerged called the Mahīśāsaka;
a king who had renounced the world to propagate the Buddha-dharma converted his own native land, and for this reason it was named the Mañjuśrī School, also known as the Bhūmi School.
From the Mahīśāsaka school, one further school emerged called the Dharmaguptaka, also known as the Dharmaguhya; "Gupta" (密) carries the meaning of a secret treasury.

1. They likewise possess five [categories]: the Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and Mantras; because they contain all things like a treasury, they are called the Dharmaguptaka (Dharma-treasury).
2. Furthermore, at the end of the third century, a school emerged known as the Kāśyapīya.

In ancient times there was a rishi whose body was golden in color and who could drink the light of the sun and moon; the founder of this school was his descendant. 3. At the beginning of the fourth century, there was...
One school emerged that was named the Sautrāntika (Sūtra-measure), so called because it takes the sūtras as its authority;
these twenty schools each held different tenets, as described in the *Śāstra on the Wheel of Tenets* (*Zhenglun shu*).
The commentary states: "The establishment of eighteen schools is based on the final enumeration; when the two original schools are included, they total twenty."
Regarding the designations "mother" and "daughter," the woman herself is one; it is through different perspectives that she receives the two names of mother and daughter.
The dharma-substance is one, yet through different perspectives at earlier and later times, the teaching of the three periods of time is established.

Dharmatrāta’s view is like that of the non-Buddhists who claim that by abandoning the nature of darkness (*tamas*), one attains the great substance of light (*sattva*); thus, the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) undergo transformation and are impermanent.
Regarding the statement that "all three time periods possess the characteristics of the three time periods": within the phenomena of a single time period, there are already all three time periods.
Take the past, for example: it is called "past" because it possesses the characteristic of the past.

Yet, since it does not exist apart from the characteristics of the present and the future, is it therefore the past, or is it the present and the future? If the past contains phenomena, they ought to be named as present or future. Why is this so?

Because they do not depart from the characteristics of the present and the future, they are illustrated by the analogy of their conjunction; the two periods of time, the present and the future, are refuted in the same manner. [Objection:

Within a single dharma of one period, there would be the fault that the three periods of time exist. Since the past and future extend over many moments, the meaning of the three periods of time is established;
however, the present is but a single moment—how can it possess the three periods? [Response: Although the present is a single moment, because it is viewed in relation to what precedes...

The latter is not the same as the former; the three mindfulnesses (*smṛti*) in the sūtra are all subsumed under the present. To refute this, one might say that the present should likewise possess the three time periods (*adhvan*).

As for "sūtra" (*sūtra*), it has the meaning of threading together and upholding; the Sūtra Piṭaka (*sūtrapiṭaka*) explains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it elucidates the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) according to their respective contexts.

Those sections that correspond to the *śāstra* (commentaries) are subsumed under the Tripiṭaka; those sections consisting of questions and answers belong to the other two Piṭakas. This treatise (*śāstra*) is subsumed under the Piṭaka of Treatises (*śāstrapiṭaka*).
Since this treatise explains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is nevertheless included within those two Piṭakas—the Sūtra and Vinaya Piṭakas.

Question: Since the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) have already been clarified, why is this work alone called a "treatise" (*śāstra*)? Answer: For one reason, it correctly explicates wisdom (*prajñā*); for another, it clarifies wisdom extensively while [the others] clarify it only slightly.
The title is derived from the *Treatise on Many Subjects*.
Those with countenances of doubt and guests waiting for a resolution were all great virtuous men of former times.
He who obtained white jade from the green mountains was Bian He of Lantian; because he possessed virtuous character from his youth, he served under the state of Jing.
Shan obtained a jade disc of one chi and three cun and presented it three times to the state of Chu—first to King Zhao, then to King Jing, and finally to King Ping;
on the third presentation, he offered it. The Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty obtained this treatise to serve as a model for his predecessors.
Regarding "obtaining the dark pearl at the Red Water," the *Zhuangzi*, in the "Heaven and Earth" chapter, states:
"The August Emperor traveled north of the Red Water, ascended the Kunlun heights, looked southward, and upon his return, he lost his dark pearl. (The commentary notes: Red is the color of the South;
the mind is the treasury of the South. The nature of water is to flow, yet its position lies in the North—how much more so for a deluded mind that pursues external objects!

The "dark realm" (jing-an) refers to the region of Northern Water (Bei-fang yan chi-shui), which is the North; Mount Kunlun is the body, and "mysterious" (xuan) signifies the cause that is profound and far-reaching.
The "pearl" (zhu) is a precious treasure. Now, desiring to transform the derivative back to the fundamental and analyze the true to seek the Way, one looks southward toward the place of return.
The South is the place where truth is sought and the direction for attaining the Way. One must employ wisdom to seek it.

Yet it could not be found (meaning it cannot be sought after; one must sever all deliberation to obtain it). Even if Li Lou were sent to seek it, he would not find it (for it is not a color that can be grasped through visual clarity).
Even if Qi Kou were sent to seek it, he would not find it (Qi Kou refers to eloquence; it cannot be sought through verbal discrimination).

Then, when Xiang Wang was sent, Wangxiang obtained it (Xiang Wang is one without a mind; it is obtained through non-mindfulness). The Emperor said, "How extraordinary! Only Xiang Wang was able to [attain it]."

If one attains the "mysterious pearl" (xuánzhū), how much more so can the virtuous predecessors of this land resolve doubts regarding the Tripiṭaka, like the Elephant-Nettled One (xiàngwǎng) obtaining the pearl?

To briefly explain the title of the work: first, there is a general explanation of the three characters *Abhidharmakośa*; second, beginning with "untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-prajñā*), there is a detailed explanation.

The detailed explanation of the three characters is divided into four parts: 1. Regarding "untainted wisdom" (*anāsravaprajñā*) and below, this is the detailed explanation of the character *pratī* (correspondence).

2. Regarding "dharmas are of two kinds" and below, this is the detailed explanation of the character *dharma*. 3. Regarding "that which is called 'abhidharma'" and below, this is the general explanation of both characters *abhidharma*.

4. Regarding "the treasury has two meanings" and below, this explains the three characters *abhidharmapiṭaka*. Question: Within the Four Noble Truths, there is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). What is this cessation?
The Truths themselves are Nirvana. When untainted wisdom contemplates the Four Truths, it is already directed toward Nirvana;

why, then, must one speak of being "directed toward" it as something distinct from the contemplation itself? The answer is that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) realized by the three fruits and four candidates for the fruits is termed "cessation through discernment" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and "unconditioned disjunction" (asaṃskṛta-visaṃyoga), but it cannot be called "Nirvana" because the afflictions have not yet been exhausted.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized by one who has attained the fourth fruit may also be termed the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and *nirvāṇa*.

From the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up until the ninth moment of the vajra-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), although those in the three fruits and four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) contemplate the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), they are termed "contemplating in opposition" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) because their minds do not yet incline toward it. At the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), however, [this changes] all at once.
The arising of eighty-nine faculties capable of attaining the eighty-nine grades of unconditioned phenomena is termed "nirvana with remainder" and "nirvana without remainder.

That is to say, from the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) onwards, when one gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), looking toward the realization of nirvana with remainder, it is "confronting" (*pratimukha*);

looking toward the realization of nirvana without remainder, it is "directed toward" (*abhimukha*). Thus, [the former] is directed toward the state with remainder, while [the latter] is directed toward the state without remainder.
Although they differ, they share the same essence in being the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); yet, because they are realized and manifested at different times, they receive two distinct names.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states that the "repository" (*kośa*) refers either to the basis (*āśraya*), just as a "sword repository" (*asi-kośa*) is so called; these two phrases explain the name "repository" as the basis.

Alternatively, it clarifies that the second [work] cites the meaning of that [first work], stating that this treatise was composed based upon it; thus, it explains the relationship between the root treatise and this commentary (*mūla-śāstra* and *vṛtti*).

Regarding the reason for being the basis: by means of the *Abhidharmakośa*, this treatise is explained as a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive compound) based on its taking the name of the entire root text, the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and the four truths and nirvāṇa expounded in that root text are called "Abhidharma" (the higher dharma), and this treatise takes that as its basis.

Furthermore, the root text is also called the "Treasury of Abhidharma" (*Abhidharma-piṭaka*), meaning it is a treasury; since this treatise contains that root-text Abhidharma, it is [also] called the Treasury.

Regarding the meaning of "Treasury" (*piṭaka*), it takes its name entirely from that of the root treatise. Master Guāng’s *Elephant-Sword* commentary explains that "Treasury" refers to the correspondence between the Dharma and its realization;
thus, the name of this present treatise, *Abhidharmakośa*, adopts the single character "Treasury" (*piṭaka*) from the root treatise, *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, to form a *tappurisa* (possessive) compound.
Furthermore, the first and second phrases of the *Nyāyānusāra* are interpreted as *tappurisa* compounds.

This is not so; rather, the explanation of the meaning of the *Śāstrasaṃgraha* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) constitutes the first two lines of the *Nyāyānusāra*, while the subsequent lines provide the definition of "possessing" (*sattva*), which corresponds to the fifth and sixth lines [of the *Kośa*].
Furthermore, the section refuting the meanings of "lineage" (*gotra*) as "element" (*dhātu*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*) constitutes the formal inquiry:
why does the Master not employ the twenty-two categories to differentiate the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the five aggregates (*skandha*)?

In the "Chapter on Aggregates," there is merely a classification of the eighteen *dhātus* under the name "Chapter on Elements. To answer this: first, regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), both their names and their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are narrow;

for the names "five aggregates" do not encompass the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and thus both their names and natures are narrow. Although the twelve bases (*āyatana*) do encompass the unconditioned, their names alone are narrow.
Since both aspects are broad in the case of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), they are analyzed by means of twenty-two categories.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) correspond to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*); reflect deeply on how the five aggregates and twelve bases also comprise twenty-two categories.
It is easy to understand that the first eight chapters clarify phenomena (*dharma*), while the chapter "Refuting the Self" (*Pudgala-pratiṣedha*) clarifies the principle of selflessness (*anātman*).

This proceeds from the shallow to the profound; alternatively, it may be because phenomena are explained first and the principle later, hence the "Refuting the Self" chapter is explained last. Or, it may be that the first eight chapters clarify [the nature of] the self.
In the *Siddhānta*, the subsequent "Refutation of the Self" (*Ātma-parīkṣā*) clarifies that the external world precedes the internal;

the "Elements" (*Dhātu*) and "Faculties" (*Indriya*) chapters clarify generally that there is no mutual obstruction between the particular and the universal, while the final six chapters clarify individually that there is no mutual obstruction between the universal and the particular.

The "Elements" chapter clarifies that the essence is not obstructed by its function, and the "Faculties" chapter clarifies that the function is not obstructed by its essence. The first three chapters clarify individually that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is not obstructed by the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

The final three chapters clarify the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) without obstructing the existence of the outflowing (*sāsrava*). The "Chapter on the World" (*Loka-varga*) clarifies the fruit without obstructing the existence of causes and conditions;

the "Chapter on Karma" (*Karma-varga*) clarifies the cause without obstructing the existence of fruits and conditions; and the "Chapter on Latent Tendencies" (*Anuśaya-varga*) clarifies the condition without obstructing the existence of fruits and causes.

The final three chapters should be understood according to this principle. Now, this outline of the text is based on the primary subject matter, categorized according to the [classification of] realms (*dhātu*).
Although this section has utility, it is an incidental clarification based on two grounds. While the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Treatise on Categories) is small in scope, its utility is clear;

therefore, we do not categorize it as having utility merely because of its minor scope or incidental nature. Question: In the separate explanation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) results, there are both sentient beings and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*).
Why, in the separate explanation of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), is there no mention of an uncontaminated world? Answer: Because the Noble Ones (*ārya*) first [attain] separately...
The "Vessel" does not depart from abiding within the triple world. Based on this, Master An Faxi previously divided the text into three parts:

the Introductory Section (Nidāna), which explains the reasons for the arising of the teaching; the Main Body (Śarīra), which clarifies the benefits of untainted wisdom; and the Final Dissemination (Pariṇāmanā), which exhorts the upholding of the tradition in future generations.
In the West, Bandhuprabha, in his *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, likewise divided it into three parts, though the names differ slightly in meaning.

Thus, there are three parts: first, the section on the causes and conditions for the origin of the teaching; second, the section on what is taught by the two types of noble scripture; and third, the section on practicing according to the teaching. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* contains the "Chapter on Refuting the Self" at its conclusion, which clearly belongs to the *pariṇāmana-parivarta* (section on the dedication of merit).

The first thirteen characters indicate the person who has accomplished the virtues; the subsequent thirteen characters clarify the three virtues accomplished by that person. Here, the person is presented first, followed by the virtues, signifying that virtue exists only after there is a person.

Within the latter thirteen characters, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is presented first and the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) afterwards, because the virtue of wisdom is unique and not shared with the virtue of abandonment.
Because these are shared, it first clarifies the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*)—whether as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Since the conditioned merit of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) exists first and the unconditioned follows later, it first clarifies the merit of wisdom and subsequently the merit of cessation. Furthermore, wisdom is the cause and cessation is the fruit;

only when the former two exist can the third, the merit of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), exist. Regarding the initial word "all" (*sarva*), there are three ancient interpretations: the first says "all" [refers to...].
Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas of the three periods," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the term "all" (*sarva*) refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

It further explains that this is intended to manifest that his own teacher’s essence is supremely exalted, transcending all other noble assemblies; the intent of the *Nyāyānusāra* is identical to this.

Furthermore, when Vasubandhu composed his treatise, wishing to transmit the holy teachings, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One. Second, regarding the word "all," it includes the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say of themselves, "Our teacher also possesses the three virtues; why does Vasubandhu not pay homage to him?

Regarding the Master of Treatises' marking of the letter *pra* (*praṇamya*) as possessing the three virtues, he pays homage in three ways: first, it accords with his mother; second, the son of the Master composed the treatise and inscribed the letter *pra* at its head;
third, his intention was that for sentient beings of shallow faculties, the Buddha would provisionally manifest in that form to lead them into the correct path.
The Dharma also possesses these three qualities. To refute the latter two explanations, it is said that the Buddha has three bodies;

yet, while the latter two interpretations claim these are merely the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), they argue that by taking refuge in the *nirmāṇakāya* alone, one sufficiently encompasses the true Buddha. Why, then, would this lead the Master [Vasubandhu] to take refuge in external non-Buddhists and all sentient beings?
Therefore, we know that the latter two [interpretations] are incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "the two types of ignorance are both able to obscure the true meaning," etc.: these two ignorances are both able to obstruct the true meaning and to obstruct the true insight within the internal mind.
Question: Since all [objects] of every kind are the objects of apprehension (*ālambana*) for these two ignorances, which of these objects of apprehension is broader and which is narrower?
Answer: "All" refers to those not included within the five categories (*pañcavarga*), namely space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The ignorance that is not subsumed under the Four Noble Truths and is defiled does not take space (*ākāśa*) or analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object.

Since all types of non-defiled ignorance can act as obstacles to [the knowledge of] all phenomena (*sarvadharmas*), one knows that "all darknesses" (*sarvamoha*) is narrow while "all types" (*sarvākāra*) is broad.
Now, these two types of ignorance are explained here with respect to their objects of delusion because their characteristics are obscure and difficult to discern.

Therefore, regarding what has been misunderstood, let us examine the question: Why are space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) not included within the five categories? The answer is:

Suffering (*duḥkha*), Origination (*samudaya*), the Path (*mārga*)—which is the contaminated path—and Cessation (*nirodha*) as that which is realized through cultivation, are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Space and non-analytical cessation are not the cessation that is realized;

thus, they are not included in [the category of] Cessation. Furthermore, they are not included in the other three Truths. As for those who hold that [non-analytical cessation] has inferior wisdom as its essence, the ancients cite the *Vibhāṣā*...
The eleven masters all refute this, asserting that it is not the correct principle. Now, citing the twenty-eighth point of the *Nyāyabindu*, it says:

"Regarding flavors and so forth, when one does not diligently seek [to understand] them, there arises an inferior wisdom (*hīna-prajñā*) along with phenomena of a different character (*vilakṣaṇa-dharma*).

Furthermore, due to this inferior wisdom, one again fails to seek [understanding], and together with these phenomena of a different character, they act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) to produce subsequent moments that are even more inferior and lack diligent seeking."

When wisdom is understood in this way, the successive connection of cause and effect from beginningless time has become established as a nature through habituation; this is termed "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).
Subsequently, at the stage where afflictions are exhausted, because one no longer diligently seeks wisdom, one is unable to discern [the true nature] regarding the flavors and so forth;
this is termed "ignorance. Second, it refers to the non-defiled minds of sentient beings while they are in a state of possessing afflictions, and...
The continuum, having been perfumed by the intermingling of various afflictions (*kleśa*),

gives rise to non-defiled minds and their attendants that possess the capacity to produce afflictions and manifest characteristics resembling them; because they arise in succession through the power of repeated practice,
even a body and mind free from faults are still said to "possess habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), whereby one remains unable to fully comprehend [the true nature of] flavors and so forth.
At the time of the Vajra Path, if one is a Buddha, [the seeds] are completely severed; if one is of the Two Vehicles, they are partially severed.

Between these two explanations, the former takes the distinct characteristic of not diligently seeking wisdom as the cause that induces [the result], while the latter takes the intermittent arising of prior and subsequent afflictions within an undefiled mind to perfume [it].
This commentary also calls this "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*); it is precisely the second explanation that is correct.

The author of the *Lǐchāo* (Lǐchāozhǔ) explained the preceding passage by stating that "continuity" (*xiāngxù*) refers to the body, encompassing both the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the mental continuum.

Now, our Master explains that "continuity" refers specifically to the succession of neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). As for those categorized as wholesome or neutral, because the power of neutral minds and mental factors is weak, they are permeated by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the claim that they may also be associated with the wholesome—as in the case of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—this was the position held by the ancients.
When an *aśaikṣa* wholesome mind manifests, there are no indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds or mental factors; there are only wholesome minds and mental factors.

Since these cannot discern objects such as flavor or potency, it is known that wholesome minds are likewise non-defiled and free from ignorance. Regarding the acquisition of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the formless realm possesses only the maturation-indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*);
[this] is acquired only simultaneously. In the desire and form realms, there are the remaining three types [of indeterminate]; it is not stated that they are common to all three [realms].
Because it is attained [in the formless realm], the "bases" (*āyatana*) are cited by way of the formless; thus, the Jewel is described as being of the Aśaikṣa (Non-learner).

If a mind that resembles a tainted wholesome mind does not cognize objects such as "tasting" (*āsvādana*), this proves that non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) extends to both the wholesome and the untainted Aśaikṣa states.

Furthermore, when an untainted meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is present, one likewise does not cognize objects such as "tasting," and thus non-defiled ignorance also extends to the untainted. Moreover, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, regarding extreme fragrance and stench...

Since entities do not ultimately perfume one another, how could that which is non-cognizant (*avijñapti*) not be untainted? Furthermore, when one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) gives rise to a wholesome mind, it is not called "Buddha" because he does not cognize its taste and so forth.
This is because one beyond training has not yet abandoned his physical basis (*āśraya*), whereas a Buddha has already abandoned his physical basis.
Moreover, a Buddha does not arise as one beyond training; rather, he arises [as such]. Therefore, when he gives rise to a wholesome mind, he does not cognize its taste and so forth.
The object itself is not called the Buddha. Regarding the question of what is subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, five of the indeterminate types are included. Why? Because their intrinsic nature is dull and obtuse.
As for the deportment (*airyāpathika*), it is like Mahākāśyapa, who in five hundred past lives had been a dancer; upon seeing the Buddha Piṅgala, he suddenly began to dance while playing the lute.
Regarding those such as the artisan Piṅgala, who called upon the river goddess as "servant-girl" and commanded her to "cut off the water quickly so that I may cross the river";

and regarding those with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as Maudgalyāyana manifesting his power to take lotus roots, or Piṇḍola taking a bowl—all such instances cited previously are the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the five types of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states. Regarding the phrase "extremely distant and obscure," etc., the "etc. includes [other similar cases].
Regarding the remaining nine objects, the *Nyāyānusāra-kārikā* states: "Taste, potency, ripening, quality, time, place, number, measure, and similarity. The commentary explains:
