This is because the four characteristics acquired upon sound are produced by the power of the mind. Consequently, they are able to follow the sound in conforming to the three natures. Thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, it is established that the four characteristics acquired upon sound are able to follow the sound in conforming to the three natures. There is no fault whatsoever. This concludes the section on the characteristics acquired upon sound. Next is the section on the characteristics acquired upon dharmas. The four great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as name (*nāman*) and so forth, lack power in relation to sound; they are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and are not spoken of as having the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) in accordance with sound.

The four great elements possess power in relation to sound because they are simultaneous causes; thus, they can directly depend on the fundamental dharma (*mūla-dharma*) to arise. Furthermore, they possess power in relation to the fundamental dharma and are spoken of as having the three natures in accordance with sound.

Regarding odor (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*), since the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) lacks the nature of "provisional nutriment" (*paribhoga-āhāra*), there is no provisional nutriment of odor or taste therein. Therefore, they are absent.

Question: Since tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) is also of the nature of a "nutriment" (*āhāra*), the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) should lack tangibility. Answer: There is tangibility in the Form Realm, but it is not of the nature of a nutriment.

It consists of the primary tangibles (*bhūta-spraṣṭavya*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), such as clothing. Since odors and tastes have no function apart from being nutriments, they do not exist in the Form Realm. Question:
If odors and tastes have no distinct function apart from food, then for those in the Form Realm, the nose and tongue would have no objects to apprehend; thus, these two [faculties] should not exist.

Question: If the essential substance (*mūla-dravya*) of the faculties serves to adorn the body, and there are two faculties [in the male and female], why is it sufficient for them to have merely the supporting bases (*āśraya*) for the faculties?

What necessity is there for the essential substance of the faculties themselves? Answer: In the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), there is no essential substance of the male or female faculties, nor are there even the supporting bases for those faculties;

yet, the essential substance of the faculties must exist for the body to possess the supporting bases for the faculties. Question: Since the male and female faculties in the Form Realm serve no purpose, they are absent from the body. Is this not so?
Regarding the separate bases of the nose and tongue, what prevents them from having the function of adorning the body even when separated from the physical form?

Furthermore, in the case of those destined to die within the womb, the six sense faculties serve no purpose; why then must they arise? The answer is that while the various faculties within the womb have their causes, they lack utility.

This is the same for the visual faculty of females, males, and those in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), as well as for odors and tastes. Thus, the two faculties of nose and tongue have their causes but lack utility.
There is nothing here that does not accord with reason: because craving for the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) acts as the cause for the production of superior karma;

because by attaining the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one craves the internal body; and because the male and female faculties depend upon sexual desire, which does not exist in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and thus those two faculties are absent there.

Those factors within the dharma-realm that are subsumed under the Truth of the Path consist of the ten great ground dharmas, the ten great wholesome dharmas, the four mental applications (vitarka and vicāra), the four characteristics, acquisition, non-informative matter, and the untainted; all other factors are tainted.

Regarding the statement that "the five consciousnesses possess only vitarka and vicāra," the *Śāstra* (commentary) explains this using two reasons to establish that the five consciousnesses are indeed associated with vitarka and vicāra.

The *Nyāyānusāra* refutes these two reasons as follows: 1. It is directly perceived that the subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within the internal sphere of the desire realm is constantly associated with vitarka and vicāra;

this refutes the first reason (the aspect of association). 2. In the two higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and above, the mental consciousness operating in the external sphere would necessarily possess vitarka and vicāra; this refutes the second reason (the aspect of the external sphere).

[This refers to] the "transforming cause" (*pariṇāma-hetu*). His own commentary explains: "Because the five consciousnesses share the same basis (*āśraya*) as vitarka and vicāra—namely, the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna—and because they are always associated [with them], the statement [regarding the mental consciousness] follows the pattern of vitarka and vicāra. Anahbuddhi offers this defense:

"Although the internal mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the Desire Realm lacks the external mode of operation, it possesses coarse aspects of activity and therefore has both vitarka and vicāra; whereas the mental consciousness from the Second Dhyāna upward, although..."
Because they turn toward external objects and lack coarse mental aspects, the five consciousnesses are devoid of vitarka and vicāra. Master Bao explains these two reasons in this treatise as follows:

he uses "coarse mental aspects" to explain that the five consciousnesses possess only vitarka and vicāra, and uses "turning toward external objects" to explain that while the mental aspects of the five consciousnesses are coarse, those of the sixth consciousness are not, because it functions by turning toward internal objects as well.

"From this point on, the three realms all pertain to the three grades" explains that the latter three realms traverse the various stages and pertain to the three grades, thereby interpreting the verse regarding how the latter three realms pertain to the three grades.

"From 'subsumed within the dharma-realm' and 'non-associated dharmas' onwards" specifically clarifies that within the dharma-realm, with the exception of vitarka and vicāra, the remainder are... [not associated].
The corresponding unconditioned non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and other dharmas do not pertain to all three categories. Regarding sustained thought (*vicāra*),
which was previously explained as being included within the dharma-element among the sixty-three factors, it has not yet been clarified whether this sustained thought—
being excluded from the first three categories— is subsumed under which category.

In a single moment of mind and mental factors, there are no two [factors] such as sensation (*vedanā*) that arise simultaneously; likewise, vitarka and vicāra do not arise at the same time with two distinct entities.
Therefore, it is said that there is no second vitarka, etc. The *Nyāyabindu* (or *Siddhānta*) refutes this, asking:
"Even if there were a second, how could they be associated (*samprayukta*)? He himself explains: "That is to say, a self-entity does not associate with itself."

For this reason, it is said that the preceding meaning is reiterated below to clarify that, within the subsequent three realms, when discussed according to their specific dharmas, four categories are established each in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna.

The aspect of seeking and investigating is called "discriminating wisdom" (*vikalpa-prajñā*); furthermore, mindfulness (*smṛti*) receives the name "discrimination" because it possesses the functions of discernment and retention.
As for their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): vitarka and vicāra are essentially the capacity for seeking; that which is able to seek is precisely conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Question:

Since *saṃjñā* (perception) can grasp images, *vedanā* (feeling) can experience, and *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction) can maintain [its object], why are they not considered conceptualization? Answer: Conceptualization is defined as that which excludes what is evil and accepts what is wholesome.

*Vedanā* and *saṃjñā* cannot exclude evil or accept the wholesome; furthermore, *adhimokṣa*, being in a state of non-decision, is unable to provide a definitive seal of maintenance. Therefore, they are not conceptualization.

Therefore, it is not called "discrimination. Question: Since wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) arise with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), how can they not be considered discrimination? Answer:
Because the five consciousnesses are subtle and weak, although wisdom and mindfulness exist simultaneously with them, they are not termed the two types of discrimination. Question:

If that which is appropriated by mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as their support is called "appropriated" (*sopādāna*), then in the two states of non-consciousness (*acittaka*), the five sense organs and the four objects would be non-appropriated, as there is no mind present.

How can that which is appropriated by mind be called "appropriated" (*upātta*)? Furthermore, since the six present consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not arise; thus, it does not appropriate the five sense organs as its basis.

How then can it be said that the mind and mental factors are called "appropriated" because they appropriate [the organs] as their basis? Answer: First, because the five sense organs and the four objects are not mutually... [text fragment ends].

It is distinct from those two; it belongs to the category of appropriated [dharmas]; thirdly, because the substance of the faculties and the life-faculty are always present when consciousness arises, they can serve as its support—meaning that consciousness does not arise of itself in the absence of these other conditions.

That which causes each [part] to arise in its own continuum is precisely "arising"; that the axe and so forth divide [the body] into two segments, each of which undergoes the transition of its own four characteristics, is called "arising in its own continuum.
Question: The five sense-faculties are invisible and resistant matter (*rūpa*); because they are designated as "pure" (*viśuddha*), they cannot be cut.
Furthermore, if the limbs were separated from the body, there would be no faculties, and thus they are not subject to being cut, just like the body-parts of those in hell.

If each of the thousands of segments possesses the faculty of touch (*kāyendriya*), it would follow that they must experience suffering, as they would otherwise be indistinguishable from insentient matter (*asattva*).
If they possess the faculty of touch, their substance would necessarily be subject to being cut. [This is] due to the power of karma; they differ from humans in this regard.

Furthermore, in the hells, the faculty of touch must certainly exist, because—as will be explained in the subsequent text—the three factors of lifespan (*āyuḥ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) mutually support one another, and thus the faculty of touch must necessarily be present. This is because of the [necessity of] material food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Furthermore, because all beings in the hells experience suffering, they must possess a physical body. If those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) in hell lacked the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it would be impossible for them to have a physical form or skeletal structure.
Since they do possess the life-faculty which sustains the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), they necessarily exist as embodied beings.

Moreover, the lifespan in hell is fixed and cannot be terminated by killing—just as among the ten paths of action, the five such as killing, stealing, and so forth, do not apply to hell-beings. Although their bodies...
Between the two separated parts, there must necessarily be a connection via the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), just as there are fibers connecting the middle of a severed lotus stalk.
If both segments were to move independently, like two sections of a snake, it would be because they are sustained by the power of wind (*vāyu*).
Should these two segments each come to life on its own, other sentient beings would then rely upon them to take birth.
Vipāka (maturation) encompasses both cause and effect; here, we take the effect and not the cause.
Puṣṭi (nourishment) encompasses both the nourisher and the nourished; here, we take the nourished and not the nourisher. Niṣyanda (outflow) also has two types:
first, that which is subsumed under vipāka and puṣṭi, which we do not take; second, that which is neither vipāka nor puṣṭi, such as the airyāpathika (postures), which we do take.

There are two kinds of "real entities" (*vastu*): first, those that possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which are called real; these are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and are not grasped [as such]. Second, those that are not subject to transformation by the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which are called real;

these are grasped. Furthermore, there are two kinds of moments (*kṣaṇa*): first, moments of arising and ceasing, which are not grasped; second, those that do not arise from a cause of the same class (*sabhāgahetu*). The former is the first [kind].
This refers to appropriation at the very moment [of rebirth].

Now, wherever there is a place of birth through maturation (vipāka), there must necessarily be nourishment (aupacayika); however, wherever there is nourishment, it is not necessarily the case that maturation is present—for instance, the divine eye of Aniruddha and others did not exist previously.
The cause is either wholesome or unwholesome, while the fruit is neutral; since the nature of the cause differs from that of the fruit, they are designated by different names.

Because it can bring [the fruit] to maturity, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). When referring to the cause, it is termed "maturational cause" (*vipāka-hetu*); when referring to the fruit, it is explained accordingly as "maturational fruit" (*vipāka-phala*). Thus, the single character "arising" (*jāti*) definitely belongs to the fruit.
The second explanation concerns the difference in the functional power (*śakti*) between the two stages of "taking the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*) and "giving the fruit" (*phaladāna*).

It states that the power at the time the karma is first created is different from the power at the time it is about to yield its fruit; thus, they are distinct in name. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* offers another explanation:
the fruit arises only after a long period has passed since the cessation of the cause that brings it to fruition, being separated from that cause.

Regarding those that can nourish and are common to all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*): among the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*), the first two are neutral by nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*); the third and fourth pertain to all three natures.

When the treatises state that "those which can nourish are common to the three natures," this is said in reference to the four conditions collectively. Because they are nourished by causes and attain growth, they are called "nourishing" (*aupacayika*).
This "nourishing" is established based on the "ripening" (*vipāka*). External non-sentient things lack ripening and likewise lack the nourishing. The mind [is not so].
Although mental factors (*caitta*) possess maturation (*vipāka*), they lack physical form and substance; because they do not cause growth or increase, they lack nourishment (*aupacayika*).
Nevertheless, from a specific perspective, they do indeed provide benefit.

Regarding sound, there is no maturation-born [sound]; if there were, then "sound" as the subject (*dharmin*) would have to be without maturation, which contradicts the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated as follows: first, because...
Because it functions according to one's will, it is illustrated by the analogy of the Noble Path; because it is intermittent, it is illustrated by the analogy of a flash of lightning.
If [the voice] were not a maturation (*vipāka*), how would one reconcile this with the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*), which states:

"By practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and abstaining from harsh speech, one attains the mark of a Great Being: the Brahma-like voice"? The treatise explains this through two meanings, the first of which is as follows:

Furthermore, the first transmission consists of the performance of karma; the second transmission consists of the acquisition of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) as maturation (*vipāka*) resulting from that karma;
the third transmission consists of the production of sound through the mutual impact of those maturation-born great elements.

Since sound does not arise directly from karma but is mediated by the maturation-born great elements, the treatise states that it is "not of maturation. Second, it is said to belong to the fifth transmission.
After the maturation primary elements (*vipāka-mahābhūta*), the nurtured primary elements (*aupacayika-mahābhūta*) arise as the third transmission;
after these nurtured primary elements, the outflowing primary elements (*naiṣyandika-mahābhūta*) arise as the fourth transmission, and only then does sound arise as the fifth transmission.

Because it is separated by these three intermediate transmissions and does not arise directly from karma, it is not a maturation result (*vipāka*). Within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this excludes the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

The ten great wholesome courses of action, the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas), the acquisition (prāpti), the path (mārga), and the non-informative (avijñapti) are all non-momentary; the rest are momentary.

Regarding the designation "mind" (*manas*) in relation to what follows: this refers generally to the present mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). Because it is difficult [to distinguish otherwise], that which serves as the support for the subsequent moment of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is designated as "mind."

Regarding the statement that "the name 'consciousness' (vijñāna) is designated in anticipation": this means that consciousness is named in anticipation of its arising based on past mental factors (manas). Question:

Regarding dharmas in the future, do they abide in a sequential order or do they abide without a sequential order? If they abide in a sequential order, then future dharmas would abide according to that sequence, and thus there would be homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) in the future.
If they abide in a sequential order like the nine grades (navavidha) of dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti), [then such causes exist].

If it is argued that the lowest-of-the-low grade of concentration arises first, and then—due to the sudden absence of conditions—the middle-of-the-middle grade does not arise, and thus the first [moment] takes the lowest-of-the-low as its cause, how can one say that it does not arise from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)? The answer is:

in the future, there is no sequential abiding; now, at the very first moment of arising, if the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) has not yet occurred, no untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma has previously entered the present.
Question: It is said that worldly [dharmas] are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), yet they are called "ultimate" because they do not arise from a homogeneous cause.
Since the sharp path of the future exists alongside the dull path of the future, once the sharp path has arisen, the dull path will certainly not arise.

To which of the five categories does this future dull path belong? Answer: It is included in the category of outflow (*niṣyanda*). These five categories encompass all phenomena (*dharma*). Question: As stated above...

When the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) of the present moment is of an inferior grade, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering of an inferior grade in the future will certainly not arise.
How, then, can it be said that there is no "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)? It is because two conditions establish a "moment": first, it must not be produced as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*);
second, it must be present activity. Since these two conditions are lacking in the case of the future patience regarding the dharma of suffering of an inferior grade, it is not a "moment."
Regarding "now attaining accomplishment": the characteristic of arising is called "attainment," while that which exists in the present is called "accomplishment.

As for the phrase "attaining the superior dharma," "attainment" refers to the category of the act of acquiring, whereas "taking up the substance of the dharma" refers to the actual entity. Here, the two time periods of the present and the future are combined and presented together as "now attaining accomplishment."

Regarding the statement that "these twelve bases (dhātus) are internal because they are the supports for the mind's apprehension": Question: The past mental faculty (*manas*) is called "internal" because it serves as the support for the present six consciousnesses.

However, the present six consciousnesses have no [past] mind as their support; therefore, they should not be classified as "internal. Answer: The essence of the mental faculty is not separate from the essence of the six consciousnesses.

Therefore, the six consciousnesses are also termed "internal. If this were not the case, there would be no eighteen elements (*dhātus*) in the present. Question: Regarding the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the mental factors (*caitta*).

Question: Since mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously with the mind and are included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are called "external," and since these mental factors serve as the support for the mind-king (*cittarāja*), while the mind-king serves as the support for the mental factors, the mind-king should also be called "external.
Answer: The mind-king universally serves as the support for all three natures (*tridhātu*); because its nature is always fixed, it is called "internal.

Mental factors, however, do not have a fixed nature in their relationship to the mind-king; if they are wholesome (*kuśala*), [they may serve as the support for an unwholesome mind-king]. Therefore, they are not designated as "internal."
The mental factors (*caitta*) associated with unwholesome or neutral minds cannot serve as the support (*āśraya*) [for these universal factors], because the supports of mental factors are not fixed.

They are called "external" because the ten great ground factors (*mahābhūmika*), while being fixed as the support for the mind-king (*cittarāja*), differ in nature from the forty-six mental factors—namely, the thirty-six indeterminate ones—which disrupt the uniformity of their class; thus, they are also termed "external."

Regarding the discussion on the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) being "fixed" (*niyata*): the five consciousnesses take the five objects as their respective conditions without confusion; thus, the five consciousnesses are called "fixed.
However, the five objects themselves cannot be called "fixed," because they serve as the objective conditions for both the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Since the five consciousnesses only take their own specific objects, they are termed "fixed"; here, the five objects are designated as "fixed" in reference to the fixed nature of the five consciousnesses that apprehend them at the time of their perception.
This is called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā). Question: The five objects are also apprehended by the mental consciousness; in relation to the mind, why are the five objects not called "homogeneous"?

Answer: Although they are apprehended by the mental consciousness, the reason the five objects are not called "homogeneous"—despite being apprehended by the mind-faculty and the mental consciousness—is that they are not apprehended by their own respective faculties and consciousnesses.
Therefore, when the mind-faculty and the mental consciousness apprehend the five objects, all six faculties are [involved].
At the time when the five consciousnesses and so forth arise, the mental faculty (*manas*) and the consciousness are designated as "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) because they share a single function;
thus, they are called homogeneous. Although the six faculties are conditioned by the mental faculty and the consciousness, they are not designated as homogeneous;
this is because the six faculties and the consciousness are termed "homogeneous" only in relation to their capacity to grasp objects (*ālambana*), and not in relation to being objects themselves.

Even though the five sense organs (*indriya*) are capable of apprehending objects, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) used here refers to the supporting consciousness while simultaneously including the supported organ.
The phrase "even though" (*tsui*) below explains the preceding text regarding the relationship with the apprehending consciousness. Question:

When the mental organ (*manas*) and consciousness do not take the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*) as their object, are the mental organ and consciousness then termed "homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*), and is the dharma-sphere not [considered] the object of the mental organ?

Furthermore, regarding the statement that consciousness takes the dharma-dhātu as its object, it should be understood as including both the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous) aspects. To answer this: there is not a single dharma-dhātu that is not included. In response to the lower [objection], it is said that the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) takes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as its essence.

At the same time, when the mental king (*citta-rāja*) is accompanied by the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), and the applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), these four characteristics arise simultaneously.

These function as the simultaneous cognitive objects (*ālambaka*). Just as the five sensory consciousnesses take the five sense-objects as their objects, when they are present and attached, they take those five objects as their cognitive domain. Thus, one enters [into the realization].

The past is ultimately not an object of [the five] consciousnesses; although the mental consciousness takes dharmas as its object, when the five consciousnesses arise, the mental consciousness does not take dharmas as its object.

Once dharmas have passed into the past, the subsequent moment of the contemplation of non-self arises, capable of taking all dharmas of the three times as its objects, because even past dharmas are taken as objects by the contemplation of non-self.
Therefore, the dharma-realm is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) if it can be taken as an object by the moments of mental consciousness.
One should reflect so that when the five consciousnesses arise, the mental consciousness does not arise; thus, the mental consciousness is brought to an end.

It is established that the mental consciousness possesses both the state of being "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the nature of the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*). The first moment of thought acts as the objective condition (*ālambana*) but does not act as the subjective condition (*ālambaka*).

The second moment of thought, however, is able to take the preceding first moment’s contemplation of non-self as its object; thus, the second moment’s contemplation of non-self takes the first moment’s contemplation of non-self as its object.

Regarding the conditions and the object of cognition, based on the manifestation of the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*), it is established that the scattered mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of cognizing the three periods of time by itself.
This means that when auditory consciousness arises for one who does not see form, visual consciousness does not take form as its object; this is what is meant by "not seeing form.

Other objects, such as sound and so forth, are to be understood accordingly. Alternatively, it may be that the twenty types of form and the twenty types of cognizing consciousness are fixed in their mutual correspondence.
From the consciousness of visible form (*rūpa-vijñāna*) onward, the remaining nineteen [consciousnesses] are all termed "not seeing" visible forms, sounds, and so forth; this is explained by analogy.
For example, the visible forms below the great ocean and the visible forms at the center of Mount Sumeru are never seen by any eye and are always termed its *sabhāga* (homogeneous).

Question: Is it not the case that these are the objects of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*)? Answer: First, they are not seen because there is no benefit [in seeing them]; second, they are not seen because [the divine eye] does not perceive them at all times.
The divine eye arises, yet because it does not see when no Buddha is present, it is termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Herein, regarding the sense-faculty of the eye, the six faculties—both those that see visible forms and those that do not—are explained as being either homogeneous or non-homogeneous.

Regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it has already been explained that the eye sees [objects] of its own level and lower levels; here, the six objects (*ṣadviṣaya*)—both homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*)—are clarified.

Regarding the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness, their homogeneity (*sabhāgatva*) is threefold; here, the homogeneity and partial homogeneity of the six consciousnesses are clarified.

Regarding "further mutual interaction": the faculties (*indriya*) serve as the support (*āśraya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which depends upon them (*āśrita*), and form (*rūpa*) serves as the object (*viṣaya*). The conjunction of these three factors is termed "interaction.

Regarding "having already performed their functions," each performs its own specific function; this differs from the first [category] mentioned previously, for the former was defined in terms of the characteristics of the three factors.
To perceive forms in accordance with [the object] is itself the functioning [of the sense organ].
As for the mutual induction of characteristics: the similar (sabhāga) induces its own similar, and the similar induces the similar.

Furthermore, regarding mutual connection: it is difficult for that which is of the same class (*sabhāga*) to see visible forms; rather, it is the sense organ, the object, and consciousness that are mutually connected.

Fifteenth, regarding those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): the five faculties, the five objects, and the wholesome or neutral mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) serve as the objects of focus for cultivation.
Alternatively, that which acts as the perceiving subject is bound by the object; the five consciousnesses associated with greed and other afflictions are bound by association;

and that which takes defilement as its object is bound by the object. These delusions that act as the perceiving subjects are abandoned through the path of cultivation, and are thus called "abandoned by cultivation."

Regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as being common to the three types of abandonment: within the dharma-realm, there are the indeterminate [afflictions]—greed, hatred, doubt, pride, the great affliction of ignorance, and the defiled wisdom of the universal ground (mahābhūmika)—which constitute the five views (*dṛṣṭi*). These ten are the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*).

The remaining nine universal afflictions, the five [mental factors of] investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*), torpor (*middha*), the two [factors] of the great unwholesome ground, and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of acquisition (*prāpti*)—these are associated with the aforementioned delusions of view.

These are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). Those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) include: the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), vitarka, vicāra, middha, kaukṛtya, the ten afflictions of the great ground (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the five great afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*), and the two minor afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*)—these ten being bound by association with greed and so forth; the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*);
vitarka, vicāra, middha, kaukṛtya, and the ten wholesome and neutral factors of the great ground; and fourteen factors belonging to the limit of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) state.

The associated non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the non-informative matter of the Prātimokṣa, the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the innate (*sahaja*) non-informative matter, and the non-informative matter of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)—these various dharmas take greed and so forth as their objects;
this is called the "bond of the object" (*ālambana-bandhana*), which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). That which is not abandoned includes:

the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), vitarka and vicāra, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the informative matter associated with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-vijñapti*), the limit of the untainted (*anāsrava-anta*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These are not abandoned.

Furthermore, the Sautrāntika school maintains that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), bodily and vocal karma, and the fruits of the miserable realms (*apāya*)—which are incompatible with the initial patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)—are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).

Question: If it is held that what is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*), that which is not produced by the six [consciousnesses], and matter (*rūpa*) are certainly not abandoned through seeing, then defiled states (*kliṣṭa*) should [likewise] not be abandoned through seeing.

Furthermore, regarding the sixth birth, non-material dharmas should be understood as being abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). The answer states that they are not "defiled" (*sāsrava*) and thus are not abandoned through seeing;

it does not say that all defiled things are abandoned through seeing. As for the three types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, they simply do not arise due to the absence of the supporting body and conditions;
they are not directly abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

First, regarding Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), it is said to pervade the three stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth; this reveals that there are distinctions among the three stages of ordinary learners (*pṛthagjana-śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), and that these are categorized into three types because they arise through gradual cultivation.
Question: What is the difference in the objects (*ālambana*) perceived by the eight views? Answer:

The five defiled views (*kliṣṭadṛṣṭi*) are like traveling on a path at night when there are clouds. Right View is like traveling at night when there are no clouds. The view of one in training (*śaikṣadṛṣṭi*) is like traveling during the day when there are clouds. The view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadṛṣṭi*) is like traveling during the day when there are no clouds.
Just as there is a distinction between superior and inferior before and after a cloudless day, so too there is a difference in the objects perceived by the wisdom and vision that arise.

Regarding the correct doctrine of the *Vibhāṣā*: Vasumitra holds that it is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) that sees; Dharmatrāta holds that it is the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that sees; Ghoṣaka holds that it is the wisdom associated with eye-consciousness that sees;

the Sautrāntika school holds that it is the simultaneous conjunction of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-saṃnipāta*) that sees; and the Vātsīputrīya school holds that it is the mind and mental factors simultaneously [that see].
I have refuted this view of "seeing"; other [objections] should be refuted accordingly. Question: If that is so, then that which performs the determination [of an object] is called "seeing.
Since the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) does not perform such determination when seeing form, it should not be called "seeing. The Sautrāntika objects:

If you say that the faculty is material (*rūpa*) and does not see what is obstructed—just as glass, crystal, mica, and the like, which are material, do not obstruct the eye-faculty—then [the objection remains].
Regarding how the sense-faculties can see objects even when separated by mica and the like, he answers himself:
because the light [passing through] mica and such is unobstructed, visual consciousness is able to see walls and other objects; however, where light is obstructed, visual consciousness cannot see.
According to the Vātsīputrīya school, the two eyes do not see simultaneously due to the distance between them, but rather because of the rapidity of the two eyes.

The term "simultaneous" (*yugapat*) refers to occurring at the same time. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* refutes this by asking: "If a servant is struck with a staff, how can both feet experience pain simultaneously when their locations are separated?
Furthermore, since the two eyes are distant from one another, why should it not be possible for them to see simultaneously?

This treatise states that vision is clear when using both eyes, whereas it is not clear when using only one; therefore, we know that both eyes see together. If it were not so, [vision would not be clear].
How can there be a distinction between clarity and dimness when both eyes see at the same time?
Furthermore, in the following section, the Master himself explains: "Once both eyes are opened, when one eye is touched, one sees two moons;
when not touching the eye, one sees the original moon; and when touching the eye, one sees the new moon. If it were granted that both eyes see simultaneously, then [the distinction would be lost].
When one touches with one [eye] and sees two moons, that calf’s rescue is likewise due to both eyes; it is not the case that they see them simultaneously.
The counter-argument states: "Since they are not seen simultaneously when one is closed, then even when touching with one [eye], one should see two moons.

Because one does not see two moons when one [eye] is closed while touching, it follows that it is precisely by means of both eyes seeing simultaneously. Master Guṅgāraprabha (Guang Fashi) explains that the eye being touched [is the one affected].
The movement and shifting of the sense organs induce the mental consciousness to see two moons.
The Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists claim that all six sense organs apprehend objects that have reached them; that is, distant forms and sounds must enter the eyes and ears before one can see or hear them.

This is refuted as follows: if all six sense organs apprehended only objects that have reached them, then one should be able to see the medicinal ointment within one's own eye; yet, since one does not [see it], [the claim is false].
Because one perceives medicine and other such objects from a distance, it is known that the eye, ear, and mind apprehend objects without reaching them.

Regarding the three faculties that apprehend objects by reaching them, according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, they also apprehend objects without reaching them; for the translucent purity (*rūpaprasāda*) of these three faculties is not something that can be touched.
This is because, in the Sarvāstivāda school, atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not touch one another; if the faculty and the object were to reach each other, it would imply that atoms touch one another.

Suppose a single atom is divided into four parts: the nose can apprehend fragrance by traversing three parts; the tongue apprehends flavor by traversing two parts; and the body apprehends touch by traversing one part. These are explained as "apprehending objects through contact" based on their relative proximity. As for the eyes and the body, they cognize objects through non-contact (*aprāptaviṣaya*); thus, there is no sequence of before and after. Regarding the other three [senses], they cognize through contact. This being the case, let us set aside the nose for a moment; as for the two faculties of the tongue and the body: [The tongue] apprehends flavor by traversing two parts; [the body] apprehends touch by traversing one part. Regarding which arises first based on the original intention to grasp either of these two objects: whichever is stronger between the cold and the hot will first give rise to body-consciousness.
If the two objects are equal in strength, tongue-consciousness arises first. Furthermore, if it is a new object, one obtains the taste first;
if it is an old object, one obtains the touch first.

Regarding "equal magnitude" (*samapramāṇa*): for instance, when the sense organs such as the nose consist of one hundred atoms (*paramāṇu*), they can grasp an olfactory object consisting of one hundred atoms.
If the olfactory object is large, the preceding moment of consciousness first grasps half of it, and the succeeding moment grasps the other half;

because the sense organ rapidly produces consciousness, it is said that they occur simultaneously. If the object is small, the organ produces consciousness from its own half [of the object] to grasp it; this is called "equal magnitude."

However, among the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), it is accepted that the first four both produce consciousness in their entirety and produce it partially; yet it is not accepted that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) produces consciousness in its entirety.

This is because, for example, if the body of a hell-being were to produce consciousness in its entirety, it would immediately disintegrate. Thus, we know that regarding humans, the body-faculty does not produce consciousness [in its entirety].
Even if the first four faculties have the body-faculty as their support (*āśraya*), even if they were to produce [consciousness] in its entirety...

The arising consciousness does not disperse from the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), as there is no other material faculty (*rūpendriya*) to serve as its support. Question: Regarding the arrangement and dimensions of the five faculties, what are they?
Answer: First, concerning the four [sensory] particles that support the faculties: the eye is like a thin peach pit; the ear is like a rolled birch bark;

the nose is like a pair of fingernails; and the tongue is like a curved blade. As for the body-faculty, it does not reside in a single location such as the feet, but dwells throughout the entire body, just like the body itself.

Regarding the measurement of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is explained in terms of its substance and its physical basis (*āśraya*). One theory states that the substance of the eye-faculty resides in a layered accumulation upon the *tāla* fruit and other supports.

Another view holds that it is distributed laterally upon the "root-support" (*upastambha*), like the filaments on a fragrant flower. Because it is covered by a transparent, clear film, it does not scatter;

for since the substance of the faculty is pure and subtle, being covered by this pure and transparent film, it is able to see forms. The other four faculties should be explained according to this same principle.

Regarding the statement that both rely on two conditions, Vasumitra says: "The faculty sees, not consciousness. Consciousness arises from six conditions: the faculty, the object, space, light, attention (*manasikāra*), and the immediately preceding mind (*samanantara-manas*).
If it is the ear-faculty, there are five conditions for hearing sound; among the six, light is excluded. For the nose, tongue, and body faculties, [the same applies].
The mental consciousness has four conditions; it can smell odors and taste flavors. Among the six [conditions], space and light are excluded.
Here, only the sense faculties and their objects are mentioned, while others are not, because factors such as space and light are not fixed;

they are not mentioned, for example, like those who travel at night who do not require light, or seeing objects in water, or seeing objects through mica or lapis lazuli where space is not required. Attention (*manasikāra*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are also not mentioned.
The six consciousnesses are said to have universal objects of perception, yet this is not explicitly stated here.

Since it is asked whether consciousness follows the sense organ—just as the mental consciousness relies on the mind-organ (*manas*) and varies in clarity according to the mind-organ—is it not the case that when the body is damaged, the visual consciousness sees [this] and the mental consciousness immediately becomes unclear? This would mean the mental consciousness changes in accordance with the body-organ (*kāyendriya*).

How can it be said that the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) is "reversed" according to the will? It is because when the body-faculty is impaired by diseases such as wind-disorders (*vāta*), the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) simultaneously experiences a painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*).

Upon entering the past [moment], this is called the "reversal of the faculty of mind. Subsequently, the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) arises in the following moment based upon this reversed faculty of mind;

this is precisely what is meant by the reversal of the faculty of mind according to the will. Question: If the preceding moment of the faculty of mind is tainted (*sāsrava*), how does the second moment of painful sensation [arise]?

When the dharma-knowledge-acceptance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is untainted (*anāsrava*). How then can the tainted mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) serve as the support (*āśraya*) for the untainted mental consciousness?
The answer is: it is merely explained that the dullness of the [mental] faculty conforms to its support; this is not based on all cases.

Just as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) five faculties serve as the supports for the five consciousnesses of the three natures (*tridhātu*), so too does the tainted mental faculty serve as the support for the untainted mental consciousness.
[This is] the basis.

According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, when a hand and a drum each produce their own sound through the mutual conjunction of their respective four great elements (*mahābhūta*), because the sound of the drum is great while that of the hand is small, one hears only the sound of the drum and not the sound of the hand.
Question: Can the eye-faculty of a higher realm see that which belongs to a lower realm?
Question: Since the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of a higher realm is subtle, it should be able to perceive the coarse tactile objects (*spraṣṭavya*) of a lower realm. Answer:

The eye is a cognition that perceives objects at a distance (*viprakṛṣṭajñāna*), and thus it can see the coarse forms of a lower realm; however, because the body-faculty is a cognition that requires contact (*saṃyuktajñāna*), it does not perceive the coarse tactile objects of a lower realm.

Regarding those who are "equal" in their engagement with meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), they may be identical in four respects: first, the body; second, the arising [in that state]; third, the entry into the first dhyāna; and fourth, the observation of the objects of the first dhyāna.
Because these four are all the same, it is called "equality of ground" (*bhūmi-samatā*).

Alternatively, they may differ: for example, when one's body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and one enters the first dhyāna to observe phenomena of the desire realm, at the very first moment, the body remains as it was.
Regarding the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) belongs to the first dhyāna from the second moment onward;
as for the body and mental objects, these two belong to the desire realm, while the mind-faculty (*manas*) and the mental consciousness are said to belong to the first dhyāna.

If one contemplates the phenomena of the first dhyāna, then at the very first moment, the mental consciousness and its mental objects belong to the first dhyāna, whereas the body and mind-faculty belong to the desire realm. From the second moment onward, [the subsequent moments] likewise arise.

When the mind is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the body belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the mental faculty (*manas*), mental objects (*dharma*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) belong to the first dhyāna.

If, from the second moment onward, one arises in the second dhyāna or higher, the body still belongs to the desire realm, the mental faculty belongs to the first dhyāna, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) belongs to the second dhyāna;
as for mental objects, they may pertain to all three stages. The rest should be understood accordingly. The same principle applies when entering a lower stage from a higher stage.
Regarding the time of rebirth: if the [mental] states are identical, there is no principle for death to occur when a mind belonging to a different level arises;

this is because one who dies while in the desire realm and is subsequently reborn in the desire realm has all four [bases—body, sense-faculty, consciousness, and object] belonging to the same level. Alternatively, if they are different:

if one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the first dhyāna, then the mental faculty (*manas*) belongs to the desire realm, while the body, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the mental objects (*dharma*) belong to the first dhyāna. This constitutes "descending from a higher level to a lower one."
This is according to this explanation.

● Regarding the first chapter, "The Chapter on the Faculties" (*Indriya-varga*), the commentary is divided into three parts: (1) explaining the title, (2) the purpose of its inclusion, and (3) the detailed analysis of the text. Its essence pervades the three periods of time, and its function is broad.
Only the present [faculty] is narrow; the subsequent explanation clarifies the nature of the faculty (*indriya*).
Because its essence and function are both preeminent, it is "illuminating" (*prakāśana*); this illumination is precisely what constitutes "predominance" (*ādhipatya*).

Thus, the name "faculty" is here explained by means of the sense of predominance. Question: Does feeling (*vedanā*) consist of experiencing? Does perception (*saṃjñā*) consist of grasping images? Can false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) sever the roots of goodness?
Question: Since *nirvāṇa* is the most supreme among all phenomena, it should be established as a faculty (*indriya*). Answer:
Among all phenomena, these twenty-two faculties are the most predominant; they are like a lion among lions, being the most excellent.

At the beginning of the kalpa, all human bodies were alike in that they possessed both sexual organs; it was only later that distinctions arose, such as those termed "brave" or "timid. This is what is meant by the "difference of sentient beings.
The "difference of discernment" refers to [distinctions] based on the eyes and other faculties.

Regarding that which sustains the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*): for example, when one gives rise to an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*) or a wholesome or defiled mind of its own level within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there is no distinct ripening-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) mind.
If the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) did not exist, what dharma would one designate as "birth in the formless realm"?
It is precisely by means of this life-faculty that the various faculties are designated, and thus one speaks of "receiving birth in the formless realm."

One who can read the past *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) is able to read it in anticipation of what preceded; one who can maintain it relies on the present substance, which is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
As for the reader of the continuity, just as the life-faculty arises at the second moment following the first moment of death, one who approaches [a new birth] has the life-faculty arise.
Because the present five aggregates are maintained by the present life-faculty, they are able to continue and obtain the past five aggregates.
It is the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
As for the path (*mārga*), it leads [beings] forward; it is able to universally take all objects as its domain, and thus is called "universal grasping" (*parigraha*).

Its activity possesses power and efficacy, and is therefore termed "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*). It functions in accordance with its respective objects, and is thus called "concomitant functioning" (*anuvartana*).

Regarding the phrase "it is traditionally said" (*kila*) placed at the beginning of the verse: the intention of the Master [Vasubandhu] is to adopt the meaning of the latter section concerning the "seeing by consciousness.

Among the four meanings, the unique function of sustaining the body is the consciousness that depends [upon the sense organ], not the sense organ which is the support. The Master refutes these two positions;

thus, he states at the head of the verse "it is traditionally said," as the *Nyāyānusāra* explains: "The initial statement 'it is traditionally said' indicates that it is the latter teaching regarding the seeing by consciousness."

Master Paramārtha says that this master was a Sautrāntika. The term "attainment" (*prāpti*) has four meanings, such as adorning the body; if any one of these is present, it suffices for the definition.
Because the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is associated with the nine faculties in the ninth path of liberation, it is called the faculty of one who has already known.
It is able to give rise to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the eighty-nine categories of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which is termed "attaining nirvāṇa."

Regarding "abandonment and establishment": "abandonment" refers to abandoning ignorance (*avidyā*) and the vocal apparatus; "establishment" refers to establishing the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

Alternatively, when analyzed according to the seventy-five dharmas, one may also abandon the remaining sixty-two non-faculty dharmas because they do not serve as the support for the mind, and instead establish thirteen dharmas as the twenty-two faculties.

Regarding the refutation of the five faculties of action: the vocal organ is like the eye; it does not require training to be able to see forms, whereas speech requires training before it is accomplished.
Furthermore, since vitarka and vicāra can produce speech, these should be established as faculties.
The bird that holds objects with its beak does not require hands; the snake that moves by gliding on its belly does not require feet.
Furthermore, since the hands and feet are themselves the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), their various extensions and contractions are subsumed within the body-faculty.

If excrement were like an object falling through space, one would have to establish a "space-faculty" (*ākāśendriya*); furthermore, according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, if there were wind that was discarded [as waste], one would have to establish a "wind-faculty" (*vāyvindriya*).

As for the female and male faculties, they are simply the substance of the visible and resistant form-faculties (*rūpendriya*); the experience of pleasure does not arise from the four objects (*viṣaya*), but rather from form itself.

Furthermore, because ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links] lack mental stability, they are like formations (*saṃskāra*), which arise from ignorance but cannot themselves serve as the roots for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth;
since their basis is unstable, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as the fundamental basis of sentient beings: although the external six objects are insentient and thus more limited, the four sensory objects are subsumed within the internal body because they depend upon the six faculties for their establishment;
therefore, the six faculties are the fundamental basis.

Regarding this purity (*śuddhi*), there are two types: first, that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called pure, referring specifically to the mental faculty (*manas*); second, that which is free from the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*) is called pure, referring to all six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
The contaminated provisions (*saṃkleśa-saṃbhāra*) should be explained accordingly. Alternatively, some interpret these three as being exclusively the mental faculty. Question:

If feeling (*vedanā*) is established as a faculty because it serves as the cause for the five dull proclivities (*paryavasthāna*), why is perception (*saṃjñā*) established as a faculty because it serves as the cause for the five views (*dṛṣṭi*)?

Regarding the reason why "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is not established as a root: the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that among the afflictions, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is predominant because the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the primary cause for the arising of rebirth;

therefore, craving is established as their root. When it comes to the arising of afflictions, ignorance (*avidyā*) is predominant, whereas when it comes to the arising of rebirth, craving is predominant.
Craving is predominant for two reasons: first, it can produce the six sense bases; second, it can maintain the six sense bases. Perception is not so established.

Furthermore, because wholesome perception (*saṃjñā*) and right wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*) are capable of eclipsing defiled perception and eclipsing perversions (*viparyāsa*), they are not established as faculties (*indriya*);
this is because they do not possess predominance (*ādhipatya*). Other dharmas should be explained accordingly based on this principle.

That which takes consciousness as its essence refers to the sixth consciousness, by which one flows through the five destinies, abandoning a previous destiny and taking up a subsequent one in an uninterrupted stream; this is due to consciousness.
"Flowing into birth" refers specifically to birth from a womb or from an egg, excluding moisture-born and transformation-born beings, because they do not receive a womb.
Regarding the cessation of birth: "cessation" refers to *nirvāṇa*. Because one does not give rise to further birth, one attains the "attainment of non-arising.

Through the five factors beginning with faith during the stage of application (*prayoga*), which possess utility, they serve as the basis for the unconditioned attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*); only then can birth be brought to an end.

The three paths are all termed the "group of those fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*). Under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), [the acquisition] first arises through the faculty of "knowing what is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvya-jñendriya*);
it is only upon this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [attainment] that [the acquisition] subsequently arises.

By means of the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātāvīndriya), one causes the abandonment of the afflictions to be severed through cultivation, so that the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) arise and abide in succession.

Because of the possession of the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñendriya*), one again attains the acquisitions of the unconditioned; only then can one give rise to the manifestation of the dharmas of the four dhyānas and experience them in the present body, which is called "experiencing happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

It is precisely for this reason that the sequence is established in the Sūtra: because all six faculties equally serve as the basis for the substance of saṃsāra, the Sūtra teaches the mental faculty (*manas*) as the sixth, following the bodily faculty (*kāyendriya*).
"Body" (kāya) refers to the basis; that is, the five consciousnesses serve as the basis for sensation.

Within the first five consciousnesses, there may be one instance of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and within the sixth consciousness, there may also be one instance of equanimity. Since both are alike in being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), they are established together as a single faculty of equanimity.
Agitation and surging are termed "joy" (*prīti*) because they arise from conceptualization; tranquility is termed "bliss" (*sukha*) because it arises following a superior object.
In the third dhyāna, mental satisfaction is combined with this tranquility and termed "joy," while the tranquility itself—being non-conceptual like the five sensory consciousnesses—is termed "bliss."

The eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are called "knowing" because they possess decisive determination regarding the objects of the four truths. The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are not "knowing" because they have not yet achieved decisive determination.
When that practitioner correctly gives rise to patience, they form the cognitive engagement (*ākāra*) of "the truth of suffering is not yet known," which is termed "not-yet-known.

Subsequently, at the stage of knowledge (*jñāna*), they will certainly know the truth of suffering; this is termed "to-be-known. Taken together, these are called the seven knowledges of "not-yet-known and to-be-known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*).

It is not appropriate to call the correct knowledge of the principle of the Four Truths "unknown" (ājñā-ājñeya); because it arises during the interval between the eight patiences (kṣānti), it shares the name "unknown" with those eight patiences.

Since the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) has already known the Four Truths through realization, the present path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) again gives rise to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) that knows the objects of the Four Truths. This is what is meant by "knowing."

Because he has already known the objects of cognition, he is called "one who has already known. Question: Regarding the contemplation of the truths during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are three aspects:

first, the abandonment of afflictions; second, dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); and third, the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*). Why does this text mention only the abandonment of afflictions and not the other two?

Answer: Regarding the refinement of the faculties, one fears the regression of afflictions. As for dwelling in happiness in the present life, this is also included within the meaning of abandoning afflictions, as it constitutes a superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
The Path-encompassing [knowledge] refers only to the abandonment of afflictions, which already includes the other two.
Alternatively, one who has practiced this knowledge until it becomes their nature is said to possess the perfected mastery-nature by constantly practicing the two knowledges.

Or, to re-explain the previous point: "knowing what was already known" is precisely the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), or by practicing this knowledge of exhaustion, one becomes of sharp faculties and attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
It is the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Regarding the "roots of the person within the three paths" (the path of those who have not yet known what is to be known, those who already know it, and those who possess complete knowledge),
this refers to the nine faculties associated with the three paths that are capable of severing the afflictions.

The nine faculties beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*) and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) constitute the essence [of these states]. Those that arise during the four stages of preparatory practice (*prayoga-avasthā*) are tainted (*sāsrava*).

As stated in the treatise: "The fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) and the mundane [attainments] involve objects; by observing the exhaustion of one's own life-span, one performs the rite for prolonging life."
One must possess six conditions: first, excellence of person, meaning an Arhat (excluding those in the three lower fruits);

second, excellence of liberation, meaning one who has attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) (revealing the "liberated-in-both-ways" [ubhayatobhāga-vimukta] and excluding the "liberated-by-wisdom" [prajñā-vimukta]); third, excellence of cultivation, meaning mastery over the mind (excluding the "occasionally liberated" [sāmayikī-vimukti] and taking the "unshakable" [akopya-dharman] nature);
fourth, excellence of the field of merit, meaning giving gifts such as robes and alms bowls to the Saṃgha or to an individual (excluding other objects). [The remaining four...]

1. Superiority of the person (*pudgala-viśeṣa*): [The donor] becomes a monk, whereas others are merely in states such as the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). 2. Superiority of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*): Having given the gift, he makes a vow and enters the "limit" concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*)—this distinguishes it from other bases that are not superior.

3. Superiority of the transformation of karma (*karma-pariṇāmana-viśeṣa*): Having arisen from that concentration, he thinks in his mind and speaks with his voice, "May all my karmas capable of producing the maturation of wealth be transformed so as to produce the fruit of the maturation of longevity. At that time, those karmas of wealth are all transformed to produce longevity.

Regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), through the power of meditative concentration and aspiration, one may transform karma for wealth so as to obtain the fruit of a five- or ten-year lifespan.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: through the power of concentration and aspiration, one induces the arising of a life-span from past non-life-deadening karma.
This, however, differs from the original vow; the vow stated that one would transform karma for wealth into the ripening fruit of a lifespan. Others say that it is by... [text ends]
Question: Now, since giving brings about the attainment of life, and one also gives for the purpose of relinquishing the end of life so as not to shorten it, we know this is incorrect.

Question: Is this prolongation of life an *vipāka* (maturation) result? Answer: It is merely through the power of meditative concentration, giving, and so forth, that wealth-producing karma is transformed to produce the fruit of longevity;
thus, it is also a *vipāka*. Furthermore, the fruit of wealth is also produced by the fulfillment of past karma.

Nor is it the case that multiple karmas project a single birth, as in the case of matter (*rūpa*), which is obstructive by its nature; through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is rendered non-obstructive.

One cannot say that matter is non-obstructive [by nature], yet this is likewise so: through the power of the gift of concentration, wealth is transformed into longevity. One cannot say that this is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
If the life-force of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has not yet expired, and they have no connection with the world, the method of application follows the six conditions mentioned above.

That is to say, he transforms the fruit of longevity into the fruit of wealth. As for his retaining or relinquishing his life-span, only those among humans in the three continents who have attained *asamayavimukti* (liberation not dependent on time) and have achieved the *prāntakoṭika-samādhi* (the meditative concentration of the ultimate limit) possess mastery over meditative absorption; therefore, the World-Honored One retained [his life] for three months. This indicates that he has attained mastery over death.
If he were to reduce it by less than three months, his benefit to sentient beings would not be complete. As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120: [text omitted].

One tradition states that the World-Honored One’s lifespan was one hundred and twenty years; because the time spent practicing the causes [of Buddhahood] was extensive and his physical stature was unequal to that of ordinary humans, it differs from the lifespan of humans by a third. Another tradition states it was one hundred years;

although the time spent practicing the causes was extensive, as it was equal to that of humans, he relinquished a fifth part of his lifespan. Question: What is the distinction between the formations of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and the formations of lifespan (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*)?
Answer: According to the following text, since the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is itself longevity (*āyus*), we know that longevity is identical to life.

One explanation states that past karma produces longevity, while present conditions extend life. As for the statement "retaining many formations of longevity," this is because a single moment of life cannot be retained, as its nature is impermanent.
Question: Both life and the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) are both projecting fruits (*ākṣepaka-phala*); why is this so?
Therefore, it is said that one merely prolongs life (*āyus*) and not the life-constituent (*nikāya-sabhāga*). To answer this:

the cause for the mutual similarity of desire is called the "life-constituent" (*sabhāga*), while the cause that sustains warmth and consciousness is called "life" (*āyus*). The preceding text explained that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) causes the life-constituents to endure; it did not say that it prolongs the life-constituents.
The Sarvāstivāda school explains that *daurmanasya* (mental grief) is not a *vipāka* (maturation) because it is abandoned through the renunciation of desire; thus, it cannot be a maturation.

Regarding the various factors such as the material faculties and the mind-faculty (*manas*), each may be of two types: the seven material faculties—eye and so forth—and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are *kuśala-vipāka* (maturations of the wholesome) if one is in the human or celestial realms, but *akuśala-vipāka* (maturations of the unwholesome) if one is in the woeful states (*durgati*). As for the mind-faculty (*manas*), it is of both types of maturation in both the wholesome and unwholesome states.

The five destinies (*gati*) are all the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome states when associated with joy, pleasure, or equanimity; the five destinies are all the maturation of unwholesome states when associated with suffering.
Within the happy destinies, those who possess both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) are produced solely by unwholesome karma as the basis for the fruits of female and male. Question:

Since mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration are all universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) and thus pertain to all three moral natures, why does the treatise state that they are "only wholesome"? Answer: This refers to their limited [application].
The faculties are established by taking the side of the wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*), because they do not include the defiled or the neutral; thus, they are said to be of "wholesome nature.

Regarding the fact that grief (*daurmanasya*) is not neutral, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 144) states: "Furthermore, it is not the case that [grief] is obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).

The two views of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm are of an obscured-neutral nature, and they function as modes of elation (*prīti-gati*), whereas grief functions as a mode of dejection (*daurmanasya-gati*)."
Because their characteristics are dissimilar and they do not correspond, [the mind] is not "obscured" (*nivṛta*).

It is not the case that the mental states of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) involve the turning of afflicted discrimination (*vikalpa*), for deportment and the like turn spontaneously (*anābhoga*).

This is as when one thinks, "I am not equal to the Buddha or the bhikṣu Aśvajit," while in a state of correct deportment; at that time, it is not [afflicted] deportment. When deportment and the like actually arise, discrimination has already ceased.

The breaths (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) are not "resultant-of-communication" (*vyākṛta-phala*), because they arise from a concentration that is "resultant-of-communication," and because they are associated with the equanimity (*upekṣā*) of one who is free from desire and sorrow;

thus, they are not neutral (*avyākṛta*) as a maturation (*vipāka*). They lack female and male [faculties] because they are free from sexual desire. As for the absence of the odors and tastes in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there would be no nose or tongue faculties [there].

To explain again: furthermore, because the bodies of women and men are ugly, [it is argued that these faculties must be absent]. But how could the Buddha, who possesses the mark of the elephant king’s concealed organ (*kośopagata-vasti-guhya*), be considered ugly?

The *Nyāyānusāra* itself explains that the previous statement is correct: while those born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) possess the two faculties of nose and tongue and thus receive the physical substance of these two faculties, they lack the substance of the two sexual faculties because they are devoid of the female and male faculties. Question:

Since the two sexual faculties are absent, how can the Sūtra state that "it is impossible and there is no occasion for a female body to become a Brahmā, but it is possible and there is occasion for a male body to become a Brahmā"?

Question: How can there be the designation "male" in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) if it lacks the sexual organs? Answer: Because the characteristic of maleness exists, it is designated as "male"; this does not mean that the sexual organs themselves exist. Furthermore, regarding the absence of suffering:
because the five consciousnesses do not exist in the form realm, they lack a basis for suffering; therefore, the suffering that depends upon them [the consciousnesses] is also absent. If that is so—
The first dhyāna has three types of consciousness; therefore, the first dhyāna should have suffering. To explain this again: suffering arises from objects that are disagreeable.
Since there are no unwholesome things to serve as disagreeable objects, although there are three types of consciousness, there is no suffering.
The mind-faculty (*manas*) and the three feelings (*vedanā*), when they are with-outflow (*sāsrava*), are subject to abandonment through both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

These four faculties, when with-outflow, pertain to all three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*): as wholesome (*kuśala*), indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and associated with afflictions (*kleśa*). When they serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*) for afflictions, they are termed "bondage by way of the object" (*ālambana-bandhana*).

If they are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), they are bound by association (*saṃprayoga*) with the afflictions abandoned through cultivation; this is termed "abandonment through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). If they arise in association with the afflictions abandoned through seeing, they are termed [abandonment through seeing].
The associated fetters (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*) are abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

As for sorrow (*daurmanasya*), it is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and pervades both the wholesome and unwholesome natures; when wholesome, it serves as the object of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and when unwholesome, it arises through association.
The seven types of material faculties (rūpīndriya) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) serve as objects of perception for the afflictions of the bhāvanā-heya class.

The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), which pertains to all three moral natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—serves as an object of bondage for the afflictions of the bhāvanā-heya class; that is to say, when it is defiled in nature, it constitutes both an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and an associated bondage (saṃprayoga-bandhana) for those afflictions.

The five faculties beginning with faith serve exclusively as the objects of the afflictions abandoned through cultivation; these afflictions that take them as objects are called "abandoned by the path of cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya).

Regarding the statement that at birth one does not obtain mental equanimity: this is because [at that stage] it is defiled; here, however, it clarifies the acquisition of the maturation (vipāka) [of equanimity]. At birth, there is nothing else.
Regarding the four feelings: because birth-and-death consists only of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), one cannot obtain faith and the other [faculties];

furthermore, because the mind at the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi-citta*) is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), the linking mind is a contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and lacks the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). As for the remaining material faculties, they are acquired only at the very end of the fifth stage.
Regarding the fact that those born by transformation do not attain equanimity at will, the explanation is the same as before.

As for the mind at the moment of death, it pertains to all three natures; this first clarifies that death occurs with a defiled or neutral mind, and it is taught that the five faculties such as faith are absent.
The explanation for the two lower realms should be understood accordingly.
Regarding those who pass away in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is not said that they die with joy or pleasure; their death and rebirth occur only through the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, in the form realm, there are no female or male faculties, and one dies with a defiled or neutral mind, lacking the five [faculties] such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth.

Regarding the four ways of gradual death: those who die from the upper part [of the body] lack the four faculties beginning with the eye; those who die from the lower part lack the two faculties of female and male.

As for the attainment of the fruits, one does not take the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) into account. The eighty-nine categories of unconditioned states (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are divided into the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

The eighty-nine categories of uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) and paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) constitute the realizing wisdom (pramāṇa-jñāna); these are the eighty-nine paths of liberation.
