When one realizes these eighty-nine categories of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) through the substance of conditioned fruits,

how many of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are associated with these eighty-nine realizing wisdoms as they collectively realize these eighty-nine categories of unconditioned phenomena to constitute the four fruits of śrāmaṇya?
For example, the first fruit has eight categories of unconditioned phenomena as its substance, and this occurs at the sixteenth moment of mind.
Regarding the eight types of unconditioned [attainments] (*asaṃskṛta*) above, there are eight instances of "attaining for the first time" (*prāpti*) that arise simultaneously and belong to the body.

When one attains those eight types of unconditioned states, it is said that this person has attained the first fruit (*phala*). As for the fifteenth and sixteenth moments of mind, with how many faculties (*indriya*) are they associated in common realization of these eight types of unconditioned states as the first fruit? The latter three fruits should be explained according to this principle.

Because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises based on the stage of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*), it is associated with the mental state of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*); thus, the mind and its mental factors, such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, are simultaneous.

Regarding the attainment (*prāpti*) of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is identical to the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) in that it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*); the uninterrupted path induces that attainment.
Birth serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for that [subsequent state].

These two support one another: the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) eliminates afflictions like driving out thieves, while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes cessation like closing the door; this mutual efficacy is termed "mutual support."
Regarding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*): it is that which possesses the power to act as a cause; its non-obstruction of arising constitutes the efficient cause.
Its ability to sustain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitutes its power.

As for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) severing afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not differentiate between the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*); rather, they consolidate them into nine grades. Having severed three grades, they enter the path of seeing.

One who is called "partially free from desire" (*ūrdhvabhāgavītarāga*) has severed six grades [of afflictions] and subsequently enters the path of seeing; one who is called "doubly free from desire" (*dvibhāgavītarāga*) has severed nine grades;

and one who is called "completely free from desire" (*sakalavītarāga*) has severed all. In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 148, the ninth question asks: "Of those entering the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), who enters the fundamental [dhyāna] and who does not?

The answer is: "Those with much joy (*abhirati*) generally enter, while those with much aversion (*vidveṣa*) generally do not. Some say that those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) enter, whereas those with dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) do not.
The three explanations provided [by previous commentators] do not enter into the core meaning; they are all general and lack critical evaluation.
This treatise, based on the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), explains that there are three instances of falling back and three instances of realization, each using a single faculty.
When these three instances are combined, it is said that eleven faculties are involved.

This passage explains that there is the possibility of falling away from the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) when it is realized by means of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), whereas if it is realized by means of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), there is no such falling away.

If one realizes [the fruit] by means of the faculty of pleasure, this refers to the case where an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has already exhausted the afflictions of the two lower dhyānas and below;

subsequently, relying on the third dhyāna, they enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and directly realize the third fruit [of non-returner] through "leaping" (*vyutkrāntaka*). This occurs because they did not previously attain the first two fruits, but instead proceeded directly to the third.
One who attains the first fruit is certain not to fall back; if one were to fall back, what fruit would they fall back to?

Since they have not yet attained the first or second fruits, this text provisionally cites the case of those who transcend by means of the faculties (*indriya-samāpatti*) as proof that those who realize through joy or equanimity are likewise certainly not subject to falling back.
By analogy with this, those who transcend to the second fruit are also certainly not subject to falling back, because it is their first attainment.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, there is no falling back" clarifies the sequential attainment of the third fruit. It allows for the possibility of falling back;

having fallen back and attained the two preceding fruits, one attains the third fruit again by means of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) belonging to the *anāgamya* stage. There is no case of attaining it again by means of the faculties of joy (*prītīndriya*) or pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
The first fruit is attained solely through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) based on the *anāgamya* concentration. The second fruit is based on the *anāgamya*.

Regarding the third superknowledge (*abhijñā*), which realizes both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths, it pertains to six stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the fourth fruit, which realizes both contaminated and uncontaminated paths, it pertains to nine stages and consists exclusively of the uncontaminated path.
As for the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi-vibhāga*): The first case concerns a path that is mixed with respect to the stages but unmixed [in its nature].
The second case concerns a path that is mixed with respect to the stages but unmixed [in its nature], which refers to the fourth fruit. The third case... [text fragment] ...the fourth fruit.
When the stages (*bhūmi*) and paths (*mārga*) are both mixed, this refers to the third fruit; when the stages and paths are both unmixed, this refers to the first fruit.

This is not the case for those who have previously abandoned desire. Below, there is a further explanation regarding those who leap over (*vyutkrāntaka*) the second and third fruits; the first three [stages] apply to all locations.

The phrase "those who possess [them] and so forth" refers to those who definitely achieve [the faculties]. This clarifies that while the achievement of the faculties is certain, all others are exclusively non-retrogressive.

Alternatively, regarding the meaning of the "gate of the fixed quantity of the faculties": among the twenty-two faculties, when one achieves the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), how many faculties are simultaneously achieved at that time?

The rest should be explained accordingly. For instance, when achieving the five [faculties] such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, this is based on the case of a person who has severed the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

Those who do not possess the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Those who do not possess the first four faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are those who have passed away from the higher realms.

Those who do not possess the male or female faculties are those who have passed away from the lower realms; furthermore, this refers to those born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), who do not possess the female or male faculties, and those born in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), who likewise do not possess the first seven material faculties. Furthermore, those who have become detached from desire (*vītarāga*) do not possess the faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) or suffering (*duḥkha*).

When joy (*prīti*) is abandoned, the third dhyāna is established; when pleasure (*sukha*) is not yet established, the fourth dhyāna is established. For the remainder of the text below, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) should be understood according to this principle.

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is established in seven [realms]. Regarding the four faculties such as the eye, they are excluded based on the perspective of passing away from the higher realms. The female and male faculties (*strī- and puruṣendriya*) are excluded based on the perspective of [passing away from] those [lower realms].
This concludes the explanation regarding death at the lower levels.
Regarding the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), they do not include the four faculties such as the eye, nor the female or male faculties.

This is because, for those who die at a higher level and enter the state of a noble one (ārya) with a mind superior in its aversion to birth and death, there are no longer the four faculties such as the eye; whereas for those who die at a lower level and enter the state of a noble one, there are no longer the female or male faculties. *Bā* [end of section].

The *Śāstra* (Treatise) states: "It is traditionally taught that those with a deep-seated mind weary of birth and death are superior to those who attain the state of an Arya at the end of life, because for the latter, rebirth after death is uncertain.
Therefore, there are no [new acquisitions of] the four faculties such as the eye, nor the two faculties of female and male.

As for the principle that one who lacks form cannot attain the dharmas of an Arya, this refers to those who are congenitally impotent or whose organs have been damaged. This refers to those who are "formless" (*anākṛti*) among the two types of eunuchs.
The statement that "two are untainted (anāsrava) and eleven are non-corporeal suffering" refers to those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as a result of the third or fourth fruit.

Regarding persons who have severed their roots of goodness (samucchinnakuśalamūla), this is to be understood according to the following text; based on the three continents, both men and women [are included], and since they lack roots of goodness, they constitute eight [categories] without male or female [gender].
Regarding the "equal faculties" (samarūpa): by analogy with the attainment of the noble state, one who dies from a higher realm lacks the four faculties such as the eye;
one who dies from a lower realm lacks the male or female faculty. Commentary, Volume Four (Root Section, Part Two).
*Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*: Question: For what reason is this treatise on co-arising factors (*sahabhū-dharma*) and subordinate causes (*hetu-pratyaya*) composed?

Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting heterodox tenets and manifesting correct principles (*nyāya*). That is to say, there are those who maintain that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise spontaneously or from a single cause;

this treatise is composed to demonstrate that these conditioned phenomena arise from various causes and conditions, such as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), and so forth. Therefore, this treatise on co-arising factors and causes was written.
This is a discussion based on conditions (*pratyaya*).

For instance, just as characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ, so too do their arisings (*utpāda*) vary; that is, while the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*) differ in their characteristics, there is likewise a distinction in the manner of their arising.

According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, this verse explains that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are no sound-aggregates; "desire" refers to the desire realm, "subtle" (*aṇu*) refers to the atom (*paramāṇu*), and "aggregate" (*saṃghāta*) refers to an aggregate formed by seven atoms.
This treatise states that these seven atoms of form exist simultaneously, and are also accompanied by smell, taste, and touch—each also being seven—thus totaling twenty-eight atoms (4 × 7).
These are comprised within the derived matter (*bhautika*), and each individual atom [possesses all four types of derived matter].

Each [element] has its own primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that act as its creators; thus, there are many atoms (*paramāṇu*). Now, when it is said that there are "eight things," this is stated according to their common categories;
in reality, there are many dharmas. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 90) asks: "What is the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*)?

If the four primary elements that create the body-sense organ (*kāyendriya*) were to create the sound, there would be the fault that the cause is few while the result is many. If, on the other hand, separate primary elements arise..."
When these great derived elements strike one another, they produce sound;
when this sound is again struck by further great derived elements, it produces yet more sound, which would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. The critique states: One should explain it thus:

within the bodies born in the desire and form realms, there are many instances where the four great elements strike one another and produce sound, and others where they do not. According to this text, such is the case.

These sounds produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are merely manifest sounds; wherever there is sound, there are necessarily eight entities (*aṣṭadravyaka*), whereas the distribution of these eight entities is not fixed.
This treatise’s discussion of the eight entities is based on the *Vibhāṣā*’s explanation that when the four great elements do not strike one another, they do not produce sound.
If it is said that there is sound, this refers to the manifestation of sound. The *Vibhāṣā* states that sound is always accomplished (*nitya-siddha*).
This refers to the general discourse on these eight matters for all people; "the absence of sound" refers specifically to the non-emission of the four great elements from a single body.

Regarding the statement in the verse that it concerns the subtle [matter] of the desire realm and not the form realm, this is because fragrance and taste do not exist in the form realm, whereas they are prevalent in the desire realm.
The explanation for the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) follows that of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding the eight substances, these are explained in terms of external insentient matter;
regarding the nine substances, these are explained in terms of the internal sentient material body.

Regarding the four faculties being distinct: the locations of the four faculties upon the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are each separate; one cannot add the ear-faculty and so forth to the eye-faculty to constitute eleven.
Because the meaning of "sound" is latent within the faculties, external non-sentient things produce manifest sounds that can be known, whereas the seven internal material [faculties] are not so.
To resolve this difficulty regarding how the sense bases (indriya) can possess sound, it is said that sound is produced by the great elements (mahābhūta) that are appropriated (upātta).
Alternatively, this passage cites the presence of sound within the internal body to show that for external non-sentient matter, the principle may be inferred from the internal case.

That the mind-king and its mental factors arise together is stated here in terms of their general characteristics; however, if they are explained according to their specific categories within the three natures, it is as analyzed in the text concerning the "wholesome mind arising with twenty-two [factors]" and so forth in the section on the co-arising of meditative concentrations.

Regarding "sentient beings are not [identical to] the state of being sentient": the discussion of sentient beings having acquisitions (*prāpti*) holds that within the category of sentient beings, there are simultaneous acquisitions of both the dharma and the acquisition itself; however, when acquisitions arise before or after [the dharma], they are not simultaneous.

As for the statement "mental factors (*caitta*) are, for now, five," the word "for now" (*tāvat*) indicates that the list is not exhaustive; this treatise clarifies that beyond these five stages, there are further...
There are eight indeterminate stages (*aniyata-bhūmi*) because they exist outside of the five [defiled] stages; thus it says "for the time being" (*tāvat*).

Alternatively, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the latter part of this treatise, there are further stages of longing (*abhinandana*) and aversion (*vidveṣa*) that exist outside of the five matters; the verse says "for the time being.

Or, as the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (132) states, there are further stages of concealment (*mrakṣa*) and non-concealment (*amrakṣa*) that exist outside of the five stages; the verse says "for the time being. This treatise refers to...

Among the forty-six mental factors (*caitta*) of the second dhyāna, there is not a single factor that is exclusively of the nature of being obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);

these two natures are not mentioned for this stage. Question: Sensation (*vedanā*) and the others pertain to all three moral natures; thus, sensation and the others are called "great factors" (*mahābhūmika*).

The mind-king (*cittarāja*) also pertains to all three moral natures; why is the mind-king alone called a "great factor"? Answer: Because two mind-kings do not arise simultaneously, they depend upon one another as support and supported.
The mind-king (*cittarāja*) is not defiled by itself; it is in dependence upon the mind-king that mental factors (*caitta*) obtain the designation "great dharmas" (*mahābhūmika*).
The mind-king does not depend upon the mental factors, nor do the mental factors obtain the designation "ground" (*bhūmi*) [independently].

According to this treatise, only the mind-king is called a "ground. However, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 16), both the mind-king and the mental factors are designated as "grounds," because...

Because these two factors depend upon one another, and because this same principle applies to the "simultaneously existing cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*) discussed later in this treatise, all subsequent stages should be explained according to this interpretation.
Question: When there is doubt regarding existence or non-existence and it has not yet been resolved, there is no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*);
therefore, resolute conviction should not be a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*). Answer: There is a seal of existence; furthermore, there is a second [point].
Regarding the doubt that there are no mental seals (*mudrā*) and that two successive moments of thought are not identical, one can indeed attain resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

As for the fundamental school’s position, they do not establish mental factors (*caitta*) at all; rather, they maintain that what are called "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth are merely specific differentiations of the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

This is refuted by the later school, which argues that if this were so, the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations would not exist within the five aggregates. Consequently, the later school establishes feeling, perception, and formations as three distinct aggregates among the five.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Some maintain that there are no mental factors (*caitta*) distinct from the mind (*citta*). [However,] these are definitely capable of causing the mind and its mental factors not to be distracted within a single moment of thought;

they do not cause them not to be distracted across successive moments of thought. Question: Regarding the two lower meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), it is said that there are the two mental factors of joy (*prīti*) and aversion (*daurmanasya*).
Within these forty-six [mental factors], to which category do they belong? Answer: The *Nyāyabindu* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*, here referred to as *Zhènglǐlùn*) states: "Joy..."
That is to say, when taking virtuous qualities as an object, one develops revulsion [toward saṃsāra], which causes the mind to take the faults and disadvantages of the afflictions as its object;

these two cannot arise simultaneously. This is an incorrect statement in the treatise, for it speaks of "both" (*ca*) and uses that term to indicate by implication that longing and revulsion do not coexist, because their natures are mutually contradictory and because they are both wholesome in nature.
Thus, the author of the treatise includes them within the category of the "great wholesome ground" (*mahā-bhūmika-kuśala*) by means of the word "and" (*ca*). *Pā* (the commentary).

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (143) and the *Nyāyānusāra* also state this. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* (35) states that the mental factor of fear (*bhaya*) is of either defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature.
This treatise [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] mentions it briefly and does not discuss it as being included within the indeterminate stages (*aniyata-bhūmi*).

Question: Since the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) is itself cultivation (*bhāvanā*), why do you say that one should cultivate all wholesome factors while remaining detached from cultivation?

Question: Is there a distinct substantial entity of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) apart from these? Answer: This heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the nature of focused attention upon the collection of wholesome phenomena that constitute its causes.
As for mental pliancy (*citta-karmaṇyatā*), it is the cause of physical and mental well-being; "physical" refers to the lightness associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.

"Peace (*praśrabdhi*) is not the physical body, as in the case of 'bodily sensation' among the five types of sensation (*vedanā*). The Sautrāntikas maintain that what is called 'peace' is simply the light and agile touch of the wind-element upon the body when one is in a state of peace.
Question: "If it is associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), how can it be established as the factor of enlightenment of peace (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: "Peace associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not even considered a factor of enlightenment, let alone that which is associated with the five sensory consciousnesses."

Regarding the question of how these two—equanimity of application (*upekṣā-prayoga*) which lacks the nature of alertness (*apratibodha-svabhāva*), and mental attention (*manasikāra*) which possesses the nature of alertness (*pratibodha-svabhāva*)—can arise together within a single moment of mindfulness (*smṛti*):
The answer is as follows: One has the quality of being startled-awakened (*saṃvejana*), while the other lacks the quality of being startled-awakened.

Since their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct, what contradiction is there in their arising simultaneously? Mental attention is functional (*savyāpāra*), whereas equanimity of application is non-functional (*nirvyāpāra*). When mental attention is active, it performs its function.
If two entities that lack functional utility exist simultaneously, why would this not accord with existence? Regarding the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*):

there are those that are exclusively wholesome but not universally wholesome, namely the two types of existence consisting of longing and aversion; those that are universally wholesome but not exclusively wholesome, namely the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) which pertain to both;

those that are neither exclusively wholesome nor universally wholesome, namely the ten great wholesome factors (*mahākuśala-bhūmika*) and [the factors] other than the wholesome; and those that are neither [exclusively wholesome nor universally wholesome], namely vitarka, vicāra, sleep, and the unwholesome.
It functions across all three natures and is not exclusively wholesome; it does not pervade all stages and is not universally wholesome. Regarding the "great afflictions," there are six;

the "unwholesome" consists of two; the "minor afflictions" consist of ten; and the remaining four are indeterminate. The statement "wholesome" already excludes those that do not enter these four categories.

"Physical unserviceability" refers to the five consciousnesses and is termed "body" (*kāya*) because it is not the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*), just as with "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*). This refers to the term "defiled."

Regarding the fourfold classification of those factors that are both obscured and unwholesome: The first category consists of those that are pervasive defilements but not exclusively defiled; these are the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

The second category consists of those that are exclusively defiled but not pervasive defilements; these are the ten minor afflictions (*upakleśa*), the two indeterminate factors—greed (*lobha*) and anger (*pratigha*)—and the [remaining] three among the indeterminate factors:
pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and [the other two]. The third category consists of the six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). The fourth category is as follows: [none].

The factors of concentration (*samādhi*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), torpor (*middha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), the ten great wholesome factors, and joy (*prīti*) and aversion (*daurmanasya*) do not enter these four categories;

this has already been excluded by the term "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*). Regarding the four categories of the great unwholesome ground (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*): the first category follows the same principle, yet its unwholesome nature is not universal (*avyāpaka*).

The first phrase consists of the seven [mental factors] beginning with anger (*krodha*) and the second phrase of hatred (*dveṣa*); these are pervasive unwholesome factors that are not exclusively unwholesome.
The third phrase consists of the six factors beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) and delusion (*moha*), which give rise to both vitarka and vicāra; these belong to the two types of unwholesome stages.

The fourth phrase refers to the remaining three secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the indeterminate factors, and the other seven [factors]; these are the ten great wholesome ground factors, as previously distinguished.

Furthermore, the arousal of the mind toward the prosperity of others is called *krodha* (anger); the concealment of one's own committed transgressions is called *mrakṣa* (concealment); the attachment to wealth and dharma is called *mātsarya* (avarice);

the resentment toward the excellence of others is called *īrṣyā* (envy); the stubborn persistence in not relinquishing [one's views] is called *pradāśa* (malice); and causing harm to others is called *vihiṃsā* (cruelty). These are the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

"Enmity" (*upanāha*) does not include the first [meaning] and the third meaning; "resentment" (*pradāśa*) does not include the second and third meanings; "deceit" (*māyā*) falsely manifests intimacy while harboring hatred; "guile" (*śāṭhya*) is the discrepancy between mind and speech; and "conceit" (*mada*) is the attachment to one's own qualities.
Pride (*māna*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) lack the first and the third meanings, respectively; regret (*kaukṛtya*) lacks the second and third meanings. This...

Regarding the statement that *middha* (sleep) lacks three characteristics: according to the following passage, the pride (*māna*) and *middha* to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), as well as the autonomous secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), all arise solely in the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*). Based on this text, *middha* arises solely in the mental faculty;

however, although it occurs only in the mental faculty, there are instances where it does not coexist with ignorance (*avidyā*), such as wholesome sleep; thus, it lacks the second characteristic. That it arises in the mental faculty is established by this text.
The foregoing clarifies the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*): the "universal" factors pervade all minds; the "great wholesome" factors pervade all wholesome minds;
the "great afflictive" factors pervade all defiled minds; and the "great unwholesome" factors pervade all unwholesome minds.

These ten lack the four aforementioned characteristics [of being universal across all stages], and are thus termed "minor afflictive ground" (*parīttakleśabhūmi*) and "indeterminate ground" (*aniyatabhūmi*), as they do not enter into these five grounds.
Terms such as these are called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).
Regarding the phrase "those of this class": this treatise determines that these minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise individually and are not identical; they constitute a specific category.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 11, states: "In addition to these ten, there are further mental states such as intolerance (*akṣānti*), lack of joy (*arati*), and outburst of anger (*krodha*)."

Those which belong to the category of the minor ground of afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*)—namely, intolerance (*amarṣa*) and lack of joy (*arati*)—are included within this [category of] envy (*īrṣyā*); and outburst (*pragādha*) and anger (*krodha*) are subsumed under resentment (*āghāta*).
These arise in association with the mind-king (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*), and do not arise through their own independent power. There are twenty-nine such factors:

ten from the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*), ten from the great wholesome ground (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), six from the great afflictive ground (*kleśamahābhūmika*) excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), two from the great unwholesome ground (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), and the two of discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*).

In the second phrase regarding sleep (*middha*), there are fifteen [factors] that arise through their own power and are not associated: the ten minor afflictions (*upakleśa*), the ten indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), and the remaining five.
Among these, the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) within the two types of wisdom (*prajñā*) arise through their own power; the others arise through association.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) arises both through association when it is common (*sādhāraṇa*) and through its own power when it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). The fourth phrase refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) itself.
At times, *kaukṛtya* (remorse) increases. *Kaukṛtya* is the state of regretting or not regretting having performed an evil deed;

it is said to occur "at times" because such a mind does not exist during a wholesome state. An "evil deed" (*kaukṛtya*) refers, for example, to an evil act committed yesterday. Both the "evil" (*ku*) and the "deed" (*kṛtya*) pertain to the object of yesterday;
they are called "evil" in the sense that, when viewed from the perspective of today, they are not in accordance with one's wishes. Today’s [wholesome] mind does not regard them as such.
The mind arises with regard to the object of regret (*kaukṛtya*) as its condition; taking the name of the object in its entirety is the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.

The second explanation is that *kaukṛtya* is the basis and regret is the dependent; now, calling "regret" by the name "bad action" (*kaukṛtya*) is like mentioning the village—the basis—upon which a person depends, and thereby referring to the person who has come in. This is an instance of mentioning the basis to indicate the dependent.
The third explanation by Venerable Muniśrī concerns the result of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) taking the cause of regret (*vippaṭisāra*) as its name.
That is to say, regarding both non-performance and performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, "wholesome" and "unwholesome" refer to a single performed action.
"One who does not act" refers to one who does not perform good deeds but instead performs evil deeds; the subsequent mental regret for this is called "good or evil *kaukṛtya*" (remorse).
The phrase "at a previous time" and below explains the three preceding lines. [Question: Regarding the mind toward the two matters already performed, good and evil...

Regarding the statement that "remorse can be named as the two types of *kaukṛtya* (evil-doing), both good and evil": how can remorse for not having performed good or evil deeds be called the two types of *kaukṛtya*, good and evil?
The answer is: regarding a deed not yet performed, if the mind feels remorse, regretting not having done what was good is called "good *kaukṛtya*";
regretting not having committed what was evil is "unwholesome *kaukṛtya*. As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 37) states: "There are four [types of *kaukṛtya*]..."
There are four distinctions regarding remorse (*kaukṛtya*): 1. There is wholesome remorse arising with respect to wholesome objects, such as regretting not having performed much wholesome action;
2. There is wholesome remorse arising with respect to unwholesome objects, such as regretting having previously committed evil; 3.

There is unwholesome remorse arising with respect to unwholesome objects, such as regretting not having committed more evil; 4. There is unwholesome remorse arising with respect to wholesome objects, such as [regretting]...
It refers to the performance of wholesome deeds and so forth.

Regarding "unshared" (*āveṇika*), the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 48) provides two interpretations: first, it states that unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) is abandoned solely through the path of vision (*darśana-heya*) and does not associate with the ten fundamental afflictions;
thus, it is called "unshared. If, however, it associates with the seven self-power afflictions such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth...
Because it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) by way of association (*samprayoga*), it is not "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).

Second, some say that unshared ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) is that which is abandoned through both seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation, and which does not associate with the ten root afflictions;

it is called "unshared" because it associates with anger (*krodha*) and so forth, as these are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). In this treatise, we follow the latter explanation and accept unshared ignorance.

This is because clarity (*pramāda*) arises in association with the secondary afflictions of torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*). Question: At what stage does non-associated ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) arise? Answer:
It refers to when, while giving rise to right view or wrong view and so forth, the mind becomes weary while contemplating the principles of the Four Noble Truths;

at that time, the inability to endure [the truth] and the lack of understanding constitute non-associated ignorance. According to the Sautrāntikas, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Both *daurmanasya* (dejection) and *kaukṛtya* (remorse) are common to both the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the other natures;

however, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that *kaukṛtya* is associated only with *daurmanasya* and never with the indeterminate, as explained previously in the section on the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). Regarding sleep (*middha*), if it is without dreaming, it is invariably of an indeterminate nature;
if there is dreaming, its threefold moral nature is determined according to the specific object dreamed of. [Question: How does *kaukṛtya* relate to the faculties?

Among the ten fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), the remorse (*kaukṛtya*) associated with ignorance (*avidyā*)—but not associated with the other nine afflictions—is said to arise simultaneously with twenty-one mental factors (*caitasika*).
If this were so, then the aforementioned "unshared" (*āveṇika*) ignorance should likewise be accompanied by twenty-one factors, including remorse.

Why, then, does the treatise state that there are twenty? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains the verse as follows: "In the case of unwholesome [ignorance] that is unshared and associated with views..."

Regarding the "only twenty": when it is associated with unwholesome views, there are twenty mental factors arising together; when it is non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*), there are twenty-one mental factors arising together.

Since it is already accepted that ignorance can be associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), and remorse consists of twenty-one [factors], what prevents remorse from being associated with ignorance, such that ignorance would then consist of twenty-one? This was the second of the two positions in the earlier *Vibhāṣā*.

The uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) is included among those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because it is admitted to be associated with twenty-one mental factors, including the six such as delusion (*moha*).
Therefore, according to this treatise, wherever there is remorse (*kaukṛtya*), there is necessarily ignorance; however, where there is ignorance, it does not necessarily entail remorse.
Among the forty-six mental factors (*caitta*) of the first dhyāna, thirty-four are present; in the intermediate dhyāna, there are thirty-three;

from the second dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are thirty mental factors. Within the five categories of mind in the desire realm, the unwholesome category of mind does not exist in the higher realms;
the remaining four categories of mind arise together with their associated mental factors.
This is explained approximately according to the system of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It is traditionally said that the Bhikṣu Aśvajit entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the Jeta Grove and contemplated how to inform the devas and others that the Buddha was superior among humans;
he questioned the Four Heavenly Kings and even Brahmā, but Brahmā sent him back to question the Buddha himself.

Furthermore, although the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute form (*rūpa*), they are extinguished only at the stage of the fourth dhyāna. When the defilements of the fourth dhyāna are completely severed, one is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
this is precisely the place where the four great elements are extinguished.

The commentary states that regarding merit (*guṇa*), the four [factors] beginning with "lack of respect" (*agaurava*) are used collectively for explanation; likewise, regarding a person of virtue, these same four are applied collectively.
To lack respect for virtues or for those who possess them; to have no veneration for virtues or for those who possess them;

to feel no sense of dread or difficulty regarding virtues or those who possess them; or to be without dependence upon virtues or those who possess them—whether it be a lack of respect or veneration for virtues, or a lack of dread, difficulty, or dependence regarding those who possess them—to have such an attitude toward both virtues and those who possess them is what is meant by a lack of shame (*ahrīkya*).
This is the object (*viṣaya*).

The evil fruits of the present and future two lifetimes are the "object of fear" (*bhayasthāna*), because they can give rise to the mental factor of fear. Therefore, the name of the offense is now called the "cause of fear," while the experience of the fruit of that offense is called "fear.
Question: If one perceives cause and effect and yet does not feel fear, is this not a form of unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*)? Wisdom exists... [text fragment ends]
If one sees [the fault] yet does not fear the cause and effect, this is ignorance (*avidyā*). How is this related to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*)? [The answer is:

Shamelessness has a distinct mode of activity (*ākāra*) and a separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it acts as a cause for the production of both unwholesome discernment (*daurprajñā*) and ignorance.
Because unwholesome discernment attributes the merit [of the action] to its source, it is said that shamelessness does not fear cause and effect. Question: Does this refer to self-observation?

Regarding how shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) arise simultaneously: the answer is that this is stated in terms of their predominance. When one observes others, it is not that one does not observe oneself;
and when one observes oneself, it is not that one does not observe others. Therefore, they can arise together.

Regarding the distinction between *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought): since their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are explained as being identical to those of *vibhakti* (discrimination) and *mada* (intoxication)—namely, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and elevation (*unnati*)—their essential natures (*svabhāva*) should not be different.
Question: Since the characteristics of *vitarka* and *vicāra* are mutually contradictory in being coarse and subtle respectively, how can they arise together in a single moment of mind?
Answer: It is like butter on water; due to the sun shining upon it from above while water rises from below, there appear two colors—one congealed and one liquefied. These two colors [coexist].
If two colors that are mutually contradictory can arise simultaneously, what prevents vitarka and vicāra—which are mutually contradictory as coarse and subtle—from arising at the same time?

If that were so, then the substance of ghee would not have states of solidification and liquefaction, for since water and sunlight also possess solidification and liquefaction, it would follow that the essence of vitarka and vicāra is neither coarse nor subtle.
Regarding this, the *Nyāyānusāra* explains: "It is like water and vinegar being in equal proportions."

When they are mixed together, one perceives only the sour taste and does not perceive the taste of water; yet it is not that the substance of the water is absent, for the function of the vinegar increases [the perception of sourness], while the functions of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) diminish [the perception of water].
When vitarka increases, the function of vicāra diminishes, and when vicāra increases, the function of vitarka diminishes. That which increases among the two is analogous to the vinegar.

Furthermore, just as greed and delusion may simultaneously possess their own substances and are admitted to arise at the same time, yet one can say of a state that "it possesses greed" without calling it "possessing delusion."

Regarding the statement that vitarka (applied thought) is coarse while vicāra (sustained thought) is subtle: this means that in their causal operation, vitarka has a strong function of seeking, whereas vicāra has a strong function of examining;
both entities exist simultaneously.
Pride (*māna*) consists solely in looking down upon others, while self-satisfaction (*mada*) consists solely in one's own haughty exaltation.
In Sanskrit, *citta* means "mind" (*xin*); it signifies that which accumulates and gives rise to the three types of karma along with the mental factors (*caitta*).

In Sanskrit, *manas* means "intellect" (*yi*); it signifies the function of deliberation. This differs from the aforementioned "mind," which refers to the sense of volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*).
In Sanskrit, *vijñāna* means "consciousness" (*shi*).

Regarding those that possess a basis (*āśraya*), the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) alike have the six sense-faculties as their bases. When various treatises speak of them having a "single common basis," the ancients said:
"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies upon the mental faculty (*manas*), while the five sensory consciousnesses rely upon the five physical faculties and the mind.

Thus, the five sensory consciousnesses actually have two bases; how then can one say they have a single common basis? In truth, there are two, and this is stated here specifically with respect to the six consciousnesses.
Each [school] asserts "the same basis" (*ekāśraya*) according to its own root-texts. Baoyun says: "Not so.
'The same' means that the two dharmas—the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the mental factors (*caitta*)—share the eye-faculty as their basis at one and the same moment;

this is called 'the same. It is based on the fact that the mind-king and mental factors exist at the same moment and are inseparable that they are called 'the same,' not by taking them to have a single shared locus of support."

Regarding "having the same object" (*ekālambana*): although it is accepted that minds and mental factors arise by taking multiple objects, they are called "having the same object" based on their taking a single form-object.
The *Ratnākara* states that this is because the mind-king and its mental factors are inseparable within a single moment;

thus, even if they take multiple objects, they are still called "having the same object" because they are inseparable, rather than being called "having the same object" based solely on a single form-object.

Regarding those that share the same aspect (*ākāra*): although mind and mental factors arise by taking many objects and manifesting many aspects, this is explained based on the case of taking a single form (*rūpa*) and a single aspect.
Thus, it is said: "Even if the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) were to produce ten kinds of aspects, the mental factors would do likewise."

Now, based on the fact that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are inseparable in terms of their support (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), and mode of activity (*ākāra*), they are said to be "identical";
it does not mean they are identical in the sense of relying on the same faculty, taking the same object, or arising with the same mode of activity.
Regarding "factors dissociated from mind" (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*): the term "dissociated from mind" excludes factors associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta-dharma*);

"formations" (*saṃskāra*) exclude matter (*rūpa*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as these are not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). This commentary explains: "That which does not correspond with the mind is called 'dissociated from mind';
this refers to the objection that [if it were merely dissociated], it would include both material phenomena and unconditioned phenomena."

Regarding the phrase "the categories such as the [three] marks and the group of names": this treatise explains that all fourteen non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) belong to the same category.
Furthermore, within the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, there is also the factor of "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*), which exists outside the fourteen; this is also a member of the same category as these fourteen.

The commentary on the *Śāstra* is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the verses; second, the citation of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The commentary states: "Regarding this, when the acquired phenomena reach the present world, they are termed 'accomplishment' (*samanvāgama*).

This ancient master’s explanation takes the essence of the acquired phenomena as they enter the present and names this "accomplishment. Furthermore, he explains that there are three types of future acquisition and two types of non-acquisition.
Regarding the attainment of distinct abodes (*prāpti*), it is said that those attained in the future arise as one; however, the arising [of attainments] in the three time periods is not fixed.
This is because the preceding [attainments] are determined by the following treatise: attainments arise in the three time periods and are not fixed;

they are not co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the primary dharma, but are termed "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "possession" (*samanvāgama*) based on their capacity to acquire the primary dharma. As for the ancients, they took the acquired dharma itself to be what is named "attainment."
That which is attained is precisely what should be acquired; it must be a dharma such as form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), and it should not be a non-associated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, since non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) are dharmas that do not arise and do not enter into the present, how can one establish them as "non-acquisition" or "non-possession"?
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains: "There are dharmas that have never been acquired since beginningless time; now, for the first time..."
To "attain" means to acquire for the first time what was never previously attained and had been abandoned; it is called "attainment" because it is accomplished, not because it was already possessed.
It is not "non-attainment"; by this principle, one should understand that non-attainment is the opposite of attainment.
Question: Why is it not called "attainment" (*siddhi*) at the moment of acquisition? Answer: What is the harm in calling it "attainment" at that very moment?

If one were so, there would be the fault that a single body would simultaneously be both ordinary (*pṛthagjana*) and noble (*ārya*). For example, in the case of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), the present body has already attained the state of an ordinary person;

yet, because the future *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* and the subsequent dharmas have been acquired within the body, it would also have to be considered as having attained the noble dharmas. If [the noble state] were [already] attained at the time [of the mundane dharma], then...

If this "attainment" were to mean that one simultaneously achieves the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and achieves untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), then there would be no distinction between the ordinary and the noble.
If it meant achieving the phenomena of another's body, there would be the fault of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) becoming confused.

If it meant achieving what is not a phenomenon, there would be the fault of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) being confused, as it would be subsumed under both sentient and non-sentient things. Question: If a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) achieves the seven treasures, is this not [the same]?

Question: Does this mean that he achieves mastery over the bodies of others and insentient things? Answer: Regarding the Universal Monarch (cakravartin), it is through the connection with past karma that produced his marks that he causes the seven treasures to appear;
these seven treasures are "achieved" as a conventional designation, but it is not that he achieves mastery over them.

Excluding those noble ones who, while still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) from their previous stage as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and have not yet attained analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) up until the moment of the dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*); these are excluded and not included.

However, for those who previously abandoned the afflictions through the six types of practice and enter the path of seeing, analytical cessation is attained at the very first moment of the dharma-patience regarding suffering.
Regarding other sentient beings: first, those noble ones (ārya) from the stage of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) onwards;

second, those who were previously in the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), severed their afflictions, and entered the state of a noble one at the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti); and third, ordinary beings who sever their afflictions through the six modes of practice—all of these achieve cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Space is not the same as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), nor is it the same as cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Their realization differs;

while the latter is attained by the absence of conditions, non-possession (*aprāpti*) is entirely absent in both cases. This is because there is possession (*prāpti*) regarding untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*);

thus, when a noble one (*ārya*) gives rise to a conventional mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*), they are not called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because the prior and subsequent possessions of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*) reside within their continuum. Question: Since space has no possession, should "non-possession" not be established for it?
The answer is that because "attainment" (*prāpti*) does not exist, "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) likewise does not exist.
The thesis clarifies that attainment and non-attainment are established as mutual opposites; this explains that where there is no attainment, there is also no non-attainment.

Since you establish "great non-attainment" by opposing it to "great attainment," why do you not establish "small non-attainment" by opposing it to "small attainment"? Answer: If one proceeds from the perspective of the particular...

By reversing the meaning of the characteristics, one obtains "small non-possession" (*aprāpti*); if it is "great non-possession," one does not obtain [the former]. If there is small non-possession, the fault is as described below.
The second section, citing the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, is divided into two parts: first, citing the *Vibhāṣā* to explain "possession" (*prāpti*);
second, citing the *Vibhāṣā* to explain "non-possession" (*aprāpti*). The preceding text is divided into two parts: first, explaining that which can possess.

Regarding the acquisition of the two types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) among the dharmas obtained, this section is divided into two parts: first, citing the text; second, the commentary and explanation. In explaining the non-acquisition, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited;
the following classification is based upon that.

The phrase "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) and so forth includes those born of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those born of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), those not resulting from repeated practice (*a-bhyāsa-janita*), and those that are neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).

There are obscured and unobscured-neutral forms. Regarding "obscured form," this refers to when the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna gives rise to afflictions such as greed, which induce the two types of karma—of body and speech.
From the Second Dhyāna upward, there is no mind that initiates karma, because [the afflictions there] are not of a nature to do so.
Furthermore, the views of self-identity and extremes (*satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the Desire Realm are of an obscured nature and cannot initiate karma, as will be explained below.
"Because the superior conditions are lacking" means that while conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has, since beginningless time, performed the six modes of practice to abandon the afflictions,

causing the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) to also abandon the afflictions in the future— such that there would be one category of conventional knowledge and its five aggregates as the basis existing simultaneously with the five aggregates that are the basis for the three types of subsequent knowledge—
and thus entering the present life through the power of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
The homogeneous immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) draws forth the basis for the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), which first enters the present;

however, the basis for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) cannot arise [simultaneously]. Since that basis is lacking, the conventional knowledge does not arise because it lacks a present substantial entity;

furthermore, since it lacks a basis, it does not arise either. Another interpretation holds that future conventional knowledge arises in the same moment as the three types of subsequent knowledge, depending on the present.

In the five-aggregate body, when the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) first arise, they take the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of the present body as their support; thus, the present body itself is absent as a support, which is called the "deficiency of the superior condition" (*viśiṣṭa-pratyaya-vaikalya*).

Regarding the phrase "because there is an actualization of the object" (*vastu-abhisamaya*): although conventional knowledge differs from the three types of subsequent knowledge in being either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it functions in the same way [in its realization].
Because it involves the task of abandoning afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, "the tasks regarding the truths are complete" means that the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) have completed their tasks regarding the three truths.
"Because there is no further realization of objects" refers to the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the second point, "because of the realization that there is no universal application": the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) realizes that the path is not universal because there are many spiritual lineages (*gotra*).
This explains why the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is not universal: first, because the lineages of the three vehicles are distinct and do not cultivate one another;
second, because within the śrāvaka lineage itself, there are six types of lineages which likewise do not cultivate one another; and third, regarding these six types...
Within the *parihāṇadharman* lineage, there are nine types of lineages; because they do not cultivate [the antidotes] simultaneously, it is called "multiplicity of lineages. Question:

Since conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) does not arise, how can it coexist with the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)? Answer: It is like the case where ten thousand soldiers together capture a commandery and its districts;
even if half the men have already died, a decree is issued to grant all of them official rank. Although ten thousand soldiers may die, the title is bestowed upon them all.

Regarding the distinct categories of birth, they are equivalent to worldly knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) and the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). As for whether they are produced or not produced, that which has the capacity to acquire them—that is, their acquisition—is what constitutes their equivalence.

This includes the prātimokṣa vows and so forth, namely the unmanifest forms (*avijñapti*) of the eight assemblies, as well as the unmanifest forms of evil and those belonging to the intermediate category.
Furthermore, regarding wholesome and unwholesome manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), it corresponds to the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

It includes the Path of Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Dharma (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth; the second fruit (*phala*) at the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*); the third fruit at the ninth uninterrupted path;

and the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*). Simultaneously with these, one attains the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the morality associated with the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*), and the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) of the Great Ground.
The wholesome [states] consist of ten types of vitarka and vicāra, as well as the mind-kings (citta-rāja).

Fifth, all meditative absorptions (samādhi), excluding one moment of the path-of-classification patience (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti) and the second fruit; sixth, all uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) except for the third and fourth fruits;

ninth, all other scattered wholesome states, all defiled dharmas, and the entirety of the neutral states of deportment (airyāpathika), craftsmanship (śailpasthānika), and supernormal fruition (nirmāṇa-phala). Small [wholesome states].

Regarding the question of how there can be "prior acquisition" (*pūrvaprāpti*) for present patience (*kṣānti*): in response to the question of how there can be both prior and simultaneous acquisition (*sahaprāpti*) for a single moment of present *dharmajñānānvayakṣānti*,
the answer is that it is established based on the two periods [past and future] for the first [patience], while for the present, it is established based on the present itself.

Regarding the statement: "The dharma-body obtained in the future is the same as that obtained prior to the subsequent dharma of the future *dharmajñānakṣānti* (patience regarding the knowledge of dharmas), and it is obtained simultaneously with the present *dharmajñānakṣānti*;
thus, like the present, it is called 'present patience' (*pratyutpanna-kṣānti*), and there are two types of acquisition. Refutation:

How could there be a question concerning the acquisition of the present patience answered by the acquisition of the future patience? Refutation of the second interpretation: How could there be an entry [into the path]...?
Now, it is already established that there is an acquisition (*prāpti*) co-arising with the dharma; however, why does this not occur prior to the present dharma?

Regarding the third interpretation, which holds that the acquisition of the numerous future dharmas that have not yet arisen occurs prior [to those dharmas], the *Prakaraṇapāda* refutes this, stating:
"Even if the acquisitions of the three categories of future dharmas were to arise prior to those dharmas, as long as they are not yet fully exhausted, one cannot [take them as] such."
It is acquired prior to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) preceding the present momentary Patience regarding the Path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*). Master Bao explains:

"Before the present Patience has arisen, there is 'acquisition prior to the dharma' (*dharmapūrvaprāpti*); when this Patience manifests, there is 'simultaneous acquisition with the dharma' (*dharmasahaprāpti*).

Regarding the many future Patiences regarding the Path that are about to arise, it is also possible for them to have two types of acquisition. Here, we are considering how a single moment of Patience in the present life can induce two [types of acquisition].
The statement that "attainment" (*prāpti*) is called "present patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to two distinct attainments; they do not arise as a single attainment within the same moment of thought.
There is absolutely no "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) that can coexist with a dharma—this is a general refutation of the ancient treatises.

Regarding the principle established below, that "the dharma is present before one," that which is "not attained" refers to external insentient matter, the bodies of others, space, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), for which both attainment and non-attainment are absent.

"No. It is not that from the beginningless past... [This is] Master Bao’s refutation of the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty. He argues that future conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) should arise simultaneously with the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*);
however, because it lacks the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*), it does not arise. At all times, there is always the "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) of dharmas that have not yet been attained.
Regarding the phrase "because there is no basis," one enters *nirvāṇa* because there is no basis for a body; therefore, there is no non-possession (*aprāpti*).

For the first five [paths], because they lack discernment (*avikalpa*) and have not yet attained the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), there is always non-possession. After refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), once the knowledge of non-arising is attained, there is possession that replaces the non-possession.

Master Bao says: "Initially, the past afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) were difficult for the Tripiṭaka-master to resolve; he cited this previously."
Regarding the three propositions found in the *Vibhāṣā* concerning dharmas that are not currently acquired (*aprāpta*), there is further a fourth proposition:

"only those dharmas whose subsequent non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) consists of view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) that have already entered the past. This was established by the Tripitaka Master of Tang as a response to an objection.
Subsequently, when the second round of objections was raised regarding future view-delusions that have not yet arisen, the aforementioned fourth proposition was removed.
Furthermore, sixteen characters [are added] to simultaneously refute the difficulty regarding the afflictions of the view-delusions of the two time periods.

Just as with the view-delusions of the Non-Perception Realm (*asaṃjñisattva*), which have been accomplished since beginningless time and are not yet abandoned because they have not been severed by the Path of Seeing—being designated as "not yet abandoned"—they necessarily arise, and it is impossible for them to arise [again].

As for the acquisition (*prāpti*) of future view-delusions entering the past and being exhausted, the reason for the refutation is that [the author] does not intend to say there is no such principle; rather, if their arising-acquisition were to enter the past...
When [the non-acquisition] has been exhausted, one may say "only dharmas. Since this principle does not exist, it is the manifestation of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The abandonment of the afflictions of the two periods—past and future—is, in relation to the past, a non-acquisition subsequent to the dharma;
in relation to the future, it is a non-acquisition prior to the dharma. This is subsumed under the second of the three phrases from the *Vibhāṣā*. Question: Regarding the fundamental dharma...

How are the "minor acquisition" (*anuprāpti*) and "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) established? Answer: Just as the "great acquisition" (*mahāprāpti*) acquires the primary dharma, the "minor acquisition" acquires that great acquisition.
When the primary dharma is lost, there is non-acquisition; when the primary dharma is not acquired, there is great acquisition.
There is minor acquisition that acquires the great acquisition, which belongs to the person. If there is a great non-acquisition, there is minor non-acquisition.

Regarding the fourfold analysis—namely, that when one loses the "great non-acquisition" (*mahā-aprāpti*) at the time one ought to lose the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*), the non-acquisition does not belong to the person and thus the precept should not be lost—the distinctions are as follows:
1. When there is an acquisition of the higher [realms], there is both a great acquisition and a small acquisition. 2. When there is an acquisition of the higher [realms], there is a non-acquisition;
that is, having abandoned both the great and small acquisitions, a non-acquisition arises. 3. When there is a non-acquisition of the higher [realms], there is... [text truncated]
Regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of such [states] by means of the two types of acquisition—the great and the small—and the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of these four non-attainments (*aprāpti*):

when one abandons a non-acquisition, there arises a non-acquisition [of that non-acquisition]. The acquisitions of the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have as their essence the conditioned, untainted five aggregates (*skandha*) of those in training and those beyond training;
the acquisitions of these acquisitions are likewise. All tainted (*sāsrava*) [dharmas] follow accordingly.
The determination of their nature is established because they are produced by the dharmas that have been attained; thus, the two types of cessation are inherently devoid of function.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has its nature defined in relation to the Path, whereas cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not realized by means of the Path, but rather follows the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and the specific nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding "attainment by way of category," this refers to the fact that in the future life there are three groups of attainments which are not intermingled; thus, there is attainment prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously [with the path].

If one realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) via the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*), such as when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) abandons the lower eight stages through the combined abandonment of both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), then...
There are eighty-one grades of afflictions (eight, nine, and seventy-two), and by abandoning these afflictions, one attains eighty-one grades of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding the attainment of this [cessation], if one takes those who have attained the first or second fruit and, by means of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*), become weary of the lower realm and aspire toward the upper, then according to the same principle for abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are likewise eighty-one grades of unconditioned attainments (*asaṃskṛta-prāpti*) as their superior acquisitions.
Among these two types of attainments, half are subsumed under the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), while the other half are non-existent [in that realm].
It is comprised within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), when it is of a lower grade, it clarifies that the untainted path severs eighty-nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) pertaining to the three realms—both those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
There are eighty-nine grades of unconditioned acquisitions (*asaṃskṛta-prāpti*); these acquisitions are untainted and non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), there are eight and nine [moments] each for the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

The acquisitions that acquire these are likewise untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Within the bodies of those in training (*śaikṣa*) of the three vehicles, the acquisitions that acquire the conditioned, untainted five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves also [of the stage of] training.
As for the acquisitions that acquire the conditioned, untainted five aggregates within the bodies of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) of the three vehicles...
"Attainment" (*prāpti*) is also determined according to what is acquired by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are not the [first] three fruits; they are called "non-learner dharmas" (*na-śaikṣa-dharma*) because they are cultivated by those who are not yet in the four paths of approach (*catur-abhimukha*).

They are called "non-non-learner dharmas" (*na-aśaikṣa-dharma*) because they are not cultivated by those who have attained the fourth fruit. Furthermore, the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and that which is not the noble path (*ārya-mārga*)—if...
Generally, regarding the seventy-two types of unconditioned phenomena realized by the Noble Ones, that which is capable of obtaining them is called "acquisition" (*prāpti*).
Those with outflows (*sāsrava*) are termed "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*) because they serve as objects for the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.

As for the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized by those on the path of training (*śaikṣa*), this refers to the eighty-eight types of unconditioned phenomena realized collectively by the three fruits and four candidates; their respective acquisitions follow the nature of what is being realized.
This is subsumed under the stage of one-in-training (*śaikṣa*).

If it is the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized by the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), then for a person who has attained the fourth fruit, at the moment of the ninth path of liberation, they simultaneously obtain eighty-nine categories of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); there are likewise eighty-nine "attainers" (*prāpti*) that can obtain them, and these too are [of the stage of] no-more-learning.
This refers to the inclusion within the [three] trainings.

The afflictions of the paths of seeing and cultivation are termed "dharmas to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation"; that which can attain these [results] above them follows the two delusions and is thus abandoned by those two.

Regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and the acquisition of the uncontaminated path (*anāsravamārga*) that abandons the afflictions—there are seventy-two categories of such acquisitions on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

These two types of acquisition take the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) as their objects; thus, while they are dharmas obtained through the path of cultivation, they themselves are not [afflictions] to be abandoned.
The analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized by the Noble Path is the state wherein the eighty-nine grades of afflictions have been abandoned by the untainted path;

there are thus eighty-nine grades of unconditioned attainments (*anāsrava-prāpti*) that can obtain this [cessation], as well as the subsequent attainments on the eighty-nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

All these attainments are untainted and are not themselves [afflictions] to be abandoned. Regarding all the dharmas mentioned above, one takes the attainment of their subsequent attainment (*prāpti-prāpti*).
This explains that the three trainings and the three types of abandonment do not take the essential substance (*dharmatā*) as their basis.
Although there may be superior grades [of mind], they are still unable to produce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). This is because the mind of concealment (*nivṛta-citta*) is inferior;
and since bodily and vocal actions arising from a mind of concealment are even more inferior, these bodily and vocal actions cannot produce non-informative matter.

Regarding the statement that "because they do not follow the power of the mind and are weak," it is asked: why are the unmanifest (avijñapti) of both good and evil, as well as the two types of manifest (vijñapti) matter of body and speech, classified as non-following-mind matter (*cittānuparivartin-rūpa*)?

Conversely, why is acquisition (*prāpti*) established as following the acquired (*prāpya-anuvidhāyin*), while non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is not classified according to the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*) of the non-acquired phenomenon (*aprāpya-dharma*)?
Why does the verse state that non-acquisition is exclusively pure-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)? Answer: If...

If the nature [of non-acquisition] were determined solely by the dharma that has not been acquired, then the Path of the Noble Ones (āryamārga) would likewise never manifest in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because the non-acquisition of the Noble Path exists within their continuum;
since this non-acquisition is itself untainted (*anāsrava*), the ordinary being would possess it and thus would have to become a Noble One.
Furthermore, a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) possesses the afflictions of the views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) belonging to the two time periods of the past and the future.

Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the higher [stages] within the body: if one were to judge its nature based on whether it is a non-acquisition that is not a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*), then those who have attained the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) would necessarily possess view-afflictions (*dṛṣṭikleśa*).
Furthermore, such a person would be a worldling (*pṛthagjana*); they would lose their status as a candidate (*pratipannaka*) and thus become a candidate once again;

they would lose their attainment of the fruit and thus become one who has attained the fruit; and they would sever their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Because there are these many faults, the three natures are not determined according to the specific dharmas that have not been acquired.

Question: Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), which category among the two—maturation (*vipāka*) or outflow (*niṣyanda*)—is it included within, as it is determined by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
Answer: It is maturation, though not universal; it is immediately categorized as being of the nature of neutral (*avyākṛta*) by way of outflow.
According to those who view things horizontally across time, the future exists after the past and present;

thus, for a single aggregate of dharmas in the future, there is a non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) prior to it. This prior non-acquisition of that dharma is precisely the category of prior non-acquisition belonging to the family of past dharmas.

Regarding the classification by way of nature, there are two types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*): because the two aggregates of the future and the non-acquisition prior to or posterior to a dharma each arise in different locations, there are thus two kinds of non-acquisition.
Sentient beings of the desire realm who do not possess dharmas of the desire realm are like the six classes of gods of the desire realm who do not possess the prātimokṣa precepts;

their non-possession (aprāpti) follows the matter (rūpa) bound to the desire realm that accompanies the body. Sentient beings of the form and formless realms who do not possess dharmas of the desire realm have a non-possession of the unmanifest (avijñapti) that follows its own respective realm’s bondage.

This is precisely because it is not acquired; this explains why non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) follows the specific realm to which it is bound. The dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consist of the four dhyānas along with their concomitant non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);

the dharmas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consist of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). As for the unbound dharmas (*anivṛta*), this refers to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*);
it means that sentient beings within the three realms have not acquired these three types of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, which constitutes their non-acquisition.
Each is bound according to its own respective realm (*dhātu*).

The Sautrāntikas maintain that this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is a provisional designation based upon the form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as long as one has not yet attained the state of an Ārya; once one attains the state of a non-Ārya, it is abandoned.
