Our Buddha, in order to refute that [view] and to demonstrate that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of consciousness is not self-existent, and to refute the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), stated that consciousness does not abide within.

The World-Honored One did not say this because he taught that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) serves as the support for the continuing consciousness in the present, while the past and future serve as its objects;

and that the three aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, in the present, share the same object as consciousness, while in the past and future, they likewise take the past and future as their objects.
Because they possess the sense of being "companions," the four aggregates are established as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), since consciousness resides within them.
Regarding the seven stations of consciousness, if one includes consciousness itself, it refers to consciousness and the four aggregates abiding happily in realms such as those of the gods;
thus, the four [aggregates] are where consciousness dwells.

Regarding the inclusion of the external vessel-world within the preceding realms, there are four modes of birth (*yoni*) and five destinies (*gati*). These do not exhaustively encompass the three realms and five destinies;
rather, the term "four modes of birth" is mentioned therein as being contained within the three realms and five destinies.
Regarding the "four modes of birth" (*catasro yonayaḥ*): "four" refers to the number of births, meaning the various classes of beings;

these different types of birth do not exceed four categories, or because there are many such classes of beings, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). First, listing those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*): they possess four conditions—first, the egg-shell;

second, the womb; third, moisture; and fourth, the place of defilement. Those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) exclude the first condition; those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*) exclude two conditions.
The first two [types of birth] are *upapāduka* (miraculous birth), while the one [type of birth] has three conditions, excluding the previous three.
Vaiśākha is the name of a lunar month; here it is translated as "Nurturing.
The star Vaiśākha can nurture all things, and because it nurtures wholesome dharmas, the name of the star is adopted. All twelve months of the West take their names from stars.

Those born through these four modes of birth can all enter the state of a noble one (ārya) and attain the status of a Golden Wheel-Turning King; once they have attained the state of a noble one, they no longer undergo birth from eggs or moisture.
*Poshadha*—which here means "Pure Abiding"—is that which nurtures merit.
To the north of Jambudvīpa there is a tree with iron blades. When the Garuḍa wishes to eat a nāga, he first perches upon this tree and plunges himself into the ocean;
fanning the water with his wings, he seizes his prey. Among the Garuḍas born by transformation, those who eat nāgas born from all four modes of birth;
those born from eggs eat nāgas born from three modes of birth; those born from moisture eat nāgas born from two modes of birth; and those born from eggs eat only nāgas born from one mode of birth.

Question: Why can the dragons born from the three [other] modes of birth not eat them? Answer: Because they consider themselves inferior. Question: Since dragons born by transformation (upapāduka) leave no physical remains upon death, how can birds eat them?
Answer: There are two explanations. First, it is said that because [the birds] do not know [the dragon is dead], they eat it; there is no fault in this even if it does not satisfy their hunger.

Second, it is said that they swallow the dragon while it is still alive, and this also removes their hunger. Question: Among the four modes of birth, which mode of birth [is the dragon]? Answer: All four.
At most, the answer is that [the majority] includes those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as well as those from the realms of hell-beings and devas;

these two destinies (*gati*) in their entirety and a portion of the other three destinies all include those born by transformation because they arise from the intermediate state. If the intermediate state is excluded from these four, then among the remaining four, those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*) are the most numerous.

The heterodox treatises contain a prophecy stating that after more than a hundred kalpas, a great illusionist will appear in the world who will take birth from a womb; this is intended to refute such slander.

Regarding those who claim he left behind his physical remains (*śarīra*), the Master refutes them by saying: "The Buddha possesses supreme supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and is able to manifest a separate body-relic (*śarīra*) to leave behind."
Regarding the question of why he must dwell in a womb-born existence, the *Nyāyānusāra* refutes the proponent’s argument by stating:

"A distinct transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not the basis for the perfuming of the qualities such as the ten powers; even if one were to leave behind a separate [body], it would not bring about great benefit."

Because there is an interval between the existence at death (*cyuti-bhava*) and the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*), it is called "intermediate" (*antara*). Since it is subsumed within the three existences (*tri-bhava*), it is called "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*).
Question: Birth (*jāti*) and arising (*utpāda*) differ in name but are identical in essence. Since the intermediate existence has already arisen, why is it not called "birth"?

Answer: Although they are not distinct in essence, they differ according to their stages. "Birth" refers specifically to the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*); therefore, the intermediate existence is termed "arising" and not "birth."

It exists. When one plants a seed and awaits the fruit, is there any interval between them? There must necessarily be a continuous succession of factors such as the sprout and so forth. The concordant example is like that between a seed and its fruit;
the discordant example is like that between a substance and its reflection.

Regarding the presence of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) within the fourteen [reasons], the fourteenth is a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) because it is shared by both those who maintain that there is an interval and those who maintain that there is no interval between successive births. As for the analogy of the original object and its reflection:
from the perspective of the original object relative to the reflection, the successive birth [of the reflection] constitutes an interval.
Regarding the arising of a distinct color: a "distinct color" refers to an image-color that exists apart from its underlying substance. This color is conventional (prajñapti).
If it were not a conventional color, how could another real image-color arise in the same location as the real color of the mirror?

Since the color of the mirror's surface and the image-color each rely upon their own four great elements (mahābhūta), we know that the image-color exists only conventionally. Second, in the case of a single body of water, on both banks...
1. The appearance of color and form within water is called the second [case]. 2. Within a mirror among shadows, light and color arise simultaneously with the shadow;

therefore, the reflected image of light and color is a provisional existence. 3. When the two images of a human face and the moon appear in a mirror, there is both the human face and the surface of the mirror;
that which is near is the image of the face, and that which is far is the image of the moon. This is the first [case].
The location, the mirror, the water, the reflection, the clarity, and their being a single place— these are all one. However,
through the conjunction of these various causes and conditions, by means of the distinctions such as the surface of the mirror, the mirror-light reflecting the person,
and the mirror illuminating the person's own eyes, one consequently sees one's own face.
Now, as for the statement that "this perishes while that arises" in order to explain the principle of continuity:
if it is argued that an image appears only from within the mirror because the substance has already perished, then this constitutes the attainment of continuity.
However, while the substance remains, the image appears only within the mirror; thus, the substance and the image are fundamentally distinct categories.
Therefore, we know that it is not a continuous succession.
Among the five types of *anāgāmin*, it is stated that one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate heaven.

If this were the case, then those who attain parinirvāṇa through birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) and through effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*) would likewise have to attain parinirvāṇa as "born-in-heaven" beings and "effortful" beings; yet such a conclusion is not permitted.
Therefore, it is known that that explanation is incorrect.
"The first noble being is also like this" means that, just as in the case of the first dhyāna, one travels from the desire realm for two million five hundred and sixty thousand *yojanas*—
dividing this distance into three parts— and having traveled eighty thousand *yojanas* into the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one then enters [the first dhyāna].

The time and place of *nirvāṇa* are both near; all virtuous persons should interpret it according to this explanation. Question: When Devadatta entered hell in his physical body (*jāti-kāya*), was there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or not?

Answer: There was an intermediate state. Because of his extremely evil karma, he experienced the fruit of maturation in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) without waiting for the end of his life;
it was not that his physical body entered hell directly. His physical body reached another location, died there, and only then did he undergo the intermediate state.
Regarding those who enter hell to take birth, if one were to enter hell with the very body that was about to be born, then the bodies of the five destinies would become intermingled and confused.

Since it is granted that this [human] body may immediately receive a hell-body due to extreme evil, it should likewise follow that one with extreme goodness could immediately receive birth in a Pure Land with this very body.
Since extreme goodness is not permitted [to result in such confusion], the same applies to the intermediate state of goodness.
He exists. King Yama is also called Yamara, Yamā, or Yamārudra; these are all Sanskrit names that differ in their phonetic weight.
This is translated here as "Twin Kings" (Shuangwang), meaning that the brother and sister together serve as the kings of ghosts. It is also called "Quiet" (Jing).
At every moment, the sinner first receives the womb from his parents; this is called "birth. When one subsequently receives the Dharma, it is called "rebirth.

● In the ninth chapter of the *Treatise*, because the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) share the same projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), their forms are similar. However, because their completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*) differs, that which is consumed [by the former] is [like] flying.
The distinctions lie in the karma, faculties, and so forth.

To raise a hypothetical objection: if the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) were to possess a form identical to that of the previous existence, then suppose a mother dog were to carry five offspring in her womb who all died at once, each falling into a different realm of rebirth;
in each case, an intermediate state would arise for that specific destination. Thus, there would be intermediate states for those destined for hell.
The burning chariots and other such torments should indeed burn the mother’s womb. The first explanation uses a heavy case to illustrate a light one:

if [the intermediate state being] while still residing in its original existence is not burned, how much less would it be burned while residing in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? The second explanation holds that because the karma of the five destinies creates an obstruction, the [karmic fire] does not sprout or burn;

as for the mother’s womb, since it is not said to be obstructed by karma—the intermediate state being being subtle and the mother’s womb being coarse—even if it were not obstructed, it would still not be burned. Therefore, it is not [burned].
This explains that [the statement] regarding karma is a refutation.

For example, if one asks whether it is possible for those who possess a body corresponding to their original form to have their karma for the five destinies fixed, how can one say they are like those with a body corresponding to their original form when the karma for the five destinies is not yet fixed?
The answer is: there is no such thing as karma that is not fixed; even if it were not fixed, one would immediately undergo the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a hungry ghost.
Regarding "illuminating one hundred koṭis": one koṭi is ten billion; one hundred koṭis is one hundred times ten billion, which is the great trichiliocosm.

He illuminates the great trichiliocosm that he transforms. Although these bodhisattvas reside in the desire realm, they are like those in the prime of youth and are not like other people who are five or six years old.
"The great elephant being confined within a room" refers to all sentient beings; "the room" refers to the triple world (*tridhātu*);
"having no door" refers to having no way out; and "a small window" refers to the Buddha-dharma as the means of escape.

Regarding the consecration with ocean water: when a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is about to receive his position, he takes the right horn of a white ox and places within it the seeds of the five grains, filling it to the brim with the waters of the four great oceans.
This symbolizes that the various minor kings of the four continents will ascend the throne for the consecration and receive the royal mandate.

Regarding those who enter the womb as twins: the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) first enters the smaller [womb] and later the larger; upon emerging, it first emerges from the larger and later from the smaller.
Other beings enter through the birth canal and also emerge through the birth canal. The Bodhisattva, however, emerges from the right side and receives the womb-embryo through the right side;

the same applies to Pratyekabuddhas and Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*). According to another explanation in the *Vibhāṣā*, entry into and emergence from the womb are both identical to that of ordinary birth.
The *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* states: "There is no fixed rule regarding entry into the womb, because the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is unimpeded;
nevertheless, it is sustained within the womb by the power of karma.

Regarding those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no intermediate state, because the karma of the formless meditative attainments cannot project an intermediate state, and because the fetters that would cause its arising have already been severed.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "First, it is because the transmigrating consciousness (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*) is obtained at the place of rebirth; second, it is because it manifests the form of the destination.

In the two realms of desire and form, there is [an intermediate state]; however, in the formless realm, one attains birth in a fixed location within the realms of desire and form itself, as there is no coming or going.
Question: When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the realms of desire or form, is there no coming or going?"

Question: Why must there necessarily be an intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? Answer: Because when one dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire or form realms (*kāmadhātu* or *rūpadhātu*), the specific location of rebirth is not fixed.
Furthermore, because one initiates karmic actions, the intermediate state arises. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 68, states:

"If a person dies, even if insects appear on their own face, there is likewise an intermediate state insect; this refers to the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*). As for those going to the three evil destinies, consciousness ceases [at the point of death]."
Since consciousness moves from the feet up to the face, there is coming and going; therefore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists.

That the intermediate state is determinate means that for one who has not yet abandoned the craving of the two lower realms, the arising of existence is determinate. After the intermediate state arises, it shares the same karma as the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) and draws it forth.
Such a being cannot enter the two mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), nor can they realize liberation through both parts (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukti*).

One liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) does not give rise to a mundane mind of a different category; for women and men, there is the definitive meaning that they cannot undergo a change of gender, nor can they abandon the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation.

Those with the divine eye (divya-cakṣus) are able to see the five destinies; those with the eye of the "fundamental existence" (mūla-bhava) of the heavenly realm are able to see the fundamental existence of the five destinies.
Those in the form realm who have received birth in the heavenly intermediate state (antarābhava) possess eyes that can see beings in the five destinies;

yet those with eyes in their original human existence cannot see those in the heavens, nor can those with eyes in the human intermediate state see those in the heavenly intermediate state. This capacity to see the other four [destinies] applies even down to those in hell:

those with eyes in their original hellish existence cannot see the intermediate states of the other four destinies, nor can those with eyes in the intermediate states of the other four destinies see one another.
Upward, even to the World-Honored One (Bhagavān), there is none who can obstruct or suppress it. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 68, asks:

"Between the supernormal power of the realm of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*) and the supernormal power of karma (*karma-vaśitā*) pertaining to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is swifter? It answers: "The supernormal power of the realm of psychic travel is swifter. [The interlocutor asks:

"If that is so, why is it called the 'supernormal power of karma,' and why is it said that upward, even to the World-Honored One, there is none who can obstruct or suppress it? [The answer is: "It is spoken of in terms of the sense of being unobstructed and the force of karma. As for the World-Honored One not obstructing or suppressing it, [this refers to the fact that]..."
"Swiftly" refers to the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).

If it is asked how an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) being can possess the five sense faculties when the previous text stated that they are like their future form, and that there are those who do not possess the five sense faculties in their original form, the answer is:
because the initial karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of the intermediate state is superior and sublime, it possesses the five sense faculties.
Regarding the statement "because one sees there is exiting," this indicates that while there is entry into the red-hot iron [hell], it does not obstruct the process of taking birth;
or, perhaps, because one previously entered the various diamond mountains, they could not block it, for being matured by the coarse and porous [conditions], one is able to exit and enter.
That which is irreversible is so according to the consensus of other schools;

however, regarding that which is reversible—namely, when one perceives an evil sign while not yet having received that [new] body and thus gives rise to slander and the like—it can indeed be reversed. But once the body has been received, it is definitively irreversible.

Regarding those who do not remain for long, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 70, states that after seven days, if the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, one undergoes repeated deaths and births;

however, before long, the conditions for rebirth do converge. Other masters state that one merely dwells temporarily among other beings of the same class, such as a dog dwelling temporarily among wild foxes and the like.
To reverse these two conditions and give rise to a mind of anger simultaneously means:
reversing the previous case where the male feels love for the mother and anger toward the father, and the female feels love for the father and anger toward the mother. Question:

Regarding the later statement that entering the womb is like entering a reed hut and so forth, how does this relate to the earlier statements about conceiving the mother as a wife and so forth, or the later mention of entering a reed hut?
Regarding the statement made in the context of the "entrance into the womb," this refers to the arising of defilement based on the existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

There are two explanations in the treatise: first, that the semen, blood, and so forth constitute the body with its five sense organs through the principle of the destruction of the seed and the arising of the sprout;
second, that the body with its sense organs is formed by distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*), just as there are distinct sentient beings based on the differences in their karma.

The "various sages" are the sages of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); "delighting in tranquility" refers to the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*); and "practicing asceticism" refers to the bodhisattvas.
"Right awareness" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*) means not giving rise to a perverted mind; it is called right awareness because it is not a [merely] wholesome mind.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to affectionate attachment toward their parents, this is a form of rebirth-linking that differs from the perverted attachment of ordinary beings.

Regarding "because of superior merit and wisdom": among the six perfections, the first three are merit and the last one is wisdom; the two in the middle accord with the former and are thus subsumed under merit, while they accord with the latter and are thus included within wisdom.
Regarding "lack of clear comprehension during the three times": if one's merit is thin, in the intermediate state (antarābhava) one perceives oneself amidst great wind, rain, cold, and heat.
Alternatively, if one’s karma leads them to enter through a grass mat or beneath a wall, and they emerge in the same manner;

or if their merit is superior such that the intermediate state being sees itself ascending onto a flower pedestal, entering a hall or palace, and dwelling upon an excellent seat before emerging in the same manner—this is lack of correct awareness (*asaṃprajāna*).
Regarding the statement "because this exists, that exists," some explain it as: because the cause exists, the effect exists; because the cause arises, the effect arises.
Alternatively, it means because the past exists, the present exists; because the present exists, the future exists.
Or, because the past arose, the present arises; because the present [arose], the future arises.
Furthermore, regarding these eight branches as explained in reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 21) states:

"Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases" refers only to the three lifetimes of the desire realm. There are also those who say this sutra applies to all three realms and four modes of birth (*yoni*).

They argue that at the moment of initial conception through miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), although the sense faculties are complete, they are not yet sharp; this is called the initial linking of name-and-form, while consciousness is the first [moment of] rebirth-linking.

The second thought-moment is called *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form). The third thought-moment and those following it, at the stage of intense development, constitute the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 24, it is asked: "How many links of the twelvefold dependent origination are present in each of the three realms?

One explanation states that the desire realm possesses all twelve links; the form realm possesses eleven links, excluding the link of *nāmarūpa*; and the formless realm possesses ten links, excluding both the links of *nāmarūpa* and *ṣaḍāyatana*.

The commentary states: All three realms possess the twelve links. Initially, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), it is consciousness (*vijñāna*). At the stage when [the faculties] have not yet become sharp, it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

At the subsequent stage when the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have become sharp, it is the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no aggregate of form; thus, "name" refers to the four aggregates.

Since there are no five physical sense-faculties, the mental faculty (*manas*) is what is meant by "name"; this is because it takes the mind as its object. The correct principle of this treatise is the same as the previous explanation. Below this:
Regarding the statement that past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the causes and the present five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are the results:

this is explained according to karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*). Furthermore, there are cases where the present five members are not the results of the immediately preceding past ignorance and formations, and the future birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are not the results of the present craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*). This refers to karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman*) as well as indeterminate (*aniyata*) karma.
This is indeed as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: that in one lifetime, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) produce the fruits of the nine stages.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks: "Why is it that the term 'ignorance' (*avidyā*) refers to all afflictions? The answer is: when past afflictions have not yet obtained their fruit, they are clear and sharp;
once they have obtained their fruit, clarity is no longer present and they are impaired. Because of this lack of clarity, they are called "past afflictions."
The general designation for "affliction" (nau) is ignorance (*avidyā*). Even if present ignorance has not yet attained its fruit, its characteristic is still not clear;
if other afflictions were present, they would be clear and sharp.
As for the statement that "it functions simultaneously with ignorance," the *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this, saying: "Afflictions such as greed (*rāga*) follow ignorance..."

It is logically impossible that when ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arise, the formations (*saṃskāra*) would follow the inferior [craving] rather than the superior [ignorance], for ignorance is superior to craving.
If ignorance were to follow craving, then ignorance would necessarily follow craving;
yet if craving and ignorance were to follow one another exclusively, such that they reside solely in ignorance, this is certainly not the case. If [it were so] regarding ignorance...

If craving and so forth are predominant, they should be like a king followed by his ministers; if craving and so forth are superior and ignorance is inferior, then it is like a superior leader followed by inferior attendants.
What is the correct principle for designating the various karmas of past lives as "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*)? The name is established according to its meaning. What is that meaning?

The meaning of "formative activity" (*saṃskāra*) is "to form" or "to construct," in the sense of causing a fruit to arise. Karma from a previous birth that induces results in the present is called "past formative activity";

this refers to karma that has already obtained its fruit, as once the fruit has arisen, it no longer bears the name "formative activity. Present karma whose fruit has not yet matured does not all receive the designation "formative activity" according to its literal meaning;

rather, such karma is designated as "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" or "indeterminate karma. However, when these reach the time of producing their fruit, they all obtain the name "formative activity."

Furthermore, since the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the results of wholesome and unwholesome [karma] are neutral (*avyākṛta*), just like consciousness and the aggregates at the moment of conception (*pratisaṃdhi*), how can these [neutral aggregates] be admitted as the results of wholesome and unwholesome karma?
[The answer is: At the single moment of conception, both the consciousness and the simultaneous [aggregates]...

Since the five aggregates are not the fruit of projecting karma, while the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) are the fruit of projecting karma and are thus maturational (*vipāka*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*), what prevents defiled consciousnesses from being likewise? There is no contradiction.

Regarding "abiding in the faculties of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpendriya*), the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are also included within the stage of name-and-form; thus, it is called "abiding in the faculties of form.
Name-and-form itself begins from the fifth stage; the four stages prior to this are all subsumed under name-and-form.
Within the fifth stage, there are thirty-four days (seven days for each of the first four stages), making thirty-eight days in total across the five stages.

Question: Since the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) within the womb already possesses the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), which gives rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and the sensation of pain or pleasure, how can it be said that the "threefold conjunction" (*trikasamnipāta*) does not yet exist until the stage of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)?
Answer: At the stage of name-and-form, the threefold conjunction is neither constant nor predominant; therefore, the designation "threefold conjunction" is not established.

It is only at the stage of the six sense-bases that this conjunction becomes predominant. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and birth (*jāti*) give rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Only the defiled [states] are [excluded]; in other stages, they may be either wholesome or defiled. Therefore, in the stage of the *vedanā* (feeling) link, the three links of *vedanā*, *upādāna* (clinging), and *bhava* (becoming), as well as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), arise;
these are not subsumed under the *vedanā* link itself. If these three links do not arise, then they are subsumed under the *vedanā* link.

Because the stage of feeling is the longest, the preceding text states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) arise after feeling; this is based on the fact that craving, clinging, and becoming are produced for the sake of a single lifetime. Some say: [this refers to the production of a future life].
If one creates karma over many lifetimes that results in the five destinies, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) arise repeatedly.

While the first moment is called craving, its intensification is called grasping—if this were so, then craving and the consciousness that arises simultaneously would each exist for only a single moment.

The answer is no; since the consciousness of rebirth is necessarily a single moment and there is no second linking of birth, craving and grasping serve as conditions for multiple [subsequent moments].
The objects each last for one *kṣaṇa*, which is equivalent to multiple moments (*nāṇa*).

The manifestation of future birth refers to the fact that when consciousness is strong in the present, it clearly discerns; because the characteristic of birth occurs when consciousness is strong, the manifestation of future birth is shown to exist in the future.

Regarding future old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the four factors from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) up to feeling (*vedanā*) cease first and are then followed by birth; these are designated as the factor of old age and death.

The two factors of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) serve as the cause of birth, while ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) serve as its conditions. If delusion arises, then ignorance is predominant;
if rebirth-linking occurs, then craving is predominant. Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, when any affliction first takes an object, it is termed [ignorance].

The stage when craving increases after its initial arising is called "craving conditioned by grasping" (*upādānapratyayā tṛṣṇā*), because the faults of craving are particularly heavy at that point; thus, among all present afflictions, it is specifically designated by the name "craving.

As for "momentary": in a single moment, a mind of greed performs the bodily and vocal informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) actions, as well as the mental [actions] belonging to the universal mental ground (*mahābhūmika*).

The ten great afflictions (*kleśa*), the six great unwholesome states (*akuśala*), the three types of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) can arise simultaneously;
these numerous factors are assigned to the twelve links [of dependent origination] as explained in the commentary.

Regarding the mention of the four envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth, they are called "concomitant envelopments" because they follow along with [the afflictions]; the other six are "non-concomitant envelopments.

As for their being "all-pervasive throughout the conditioned," this refers to the fact that ignorance and the rest are not said to exist in non-sentient things; regarding their absence within the twelve links [of dependent origination], this refers specifically to birth, aging, and so forth.

The Sautrāntika school refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that the twelve links do not comprise the five aggregates existing simultaneously; they maintain that ignorance (*avidyā*) takes delusion as its object, while formative action (*saṃskāra*) takes volition (*cetanā*) and so forth as its object.

Furthermore, they hold that the fruit of old age and death does not arise from the cultivation of the path, and that birth and death have an end; thus, ignorance has no cause, which is the same as the Mahīśāsaka school.
If one begins with sentient beings and adds the correct principle along with the scriptural authority, there is the fault of deficiency.
By way of the meaning as it is revealed: since feeling gives rise to craving, this reveals that old age and death have ignorance as their cause.

Future old age and death consist of the four factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling; once feeling has arisen in the present, craving is produced. Thus, by means of [the sequence], [the causal relationship is established].

To clarify that ignorance (*avidyā*) arises from birth, old age, and death within the future [existence], one takes the third phrase—“arising from phenomena and from afflictions”—to explain the cause of ignorance;
the remainder is identical to the preceding text and thus follows here. Since the essence of cause and effect is not distinct, how can the two meanings of being both cause and effect be established?
It is like a father who, having been born from another, is called a son when he gives birth to another, and is called a father. This is like the case of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
The arising of consciousness is called the cause; its arising from ignorance is called the fruit. Question: Past and present phenomena have already arisen and may thus be called "dependently arisen.

How can future phenomena, which have not yet arisen, be called "dependently arisen"? Answer: Because they belong to the same category as those past and present phenomena that have already arisen, they are called "dependently arisen."

● In the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) has the nature of delusion and darkness. To say "it does not comprehend" or "it does not know" is to distinguish its essence by way of its function.
It should be understood that among the seventy-five dharmas, only wisdom (*prajñā*) is clarity; the essence of the remaining seventy-four dharmas is [not clarity].
All would not be the clarity of wisdom, but rather all would be ignorance.
If, according to the latter explanation, "clarity" is non-existent, then wherever wisdom is absent, that is ignorance; thus, ignorance would have no essence.
The statement that "everything other than what is separated from light is called ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth" is intended to exclude the two previous interpretations as being incorrect.

Just as when a person has someone as an enemy, that enemy is called a "non-friend," one cannot say that everyone outside of one's own friends—including enemies and all other people—is called a "non-friend. [The same applies here.]
It is not the case that a person cannot be a relative or friend; nor can one who is a relative or friend be called a non-relative or friend.
Since this would be a non-existent thing, how could they be termed an enemy?

It is not permissible for everything outside of truthful speech to be considered untrue; otherwise, the other three types of speech, such as divisive speech and so forth, would not necessarily be unwholesome.
Regarding truthful speech and untruthful speech: furthermore, that which cannot be established as real is called "unreal," which is to say, deceptive speech has no substantial entity.

Moreover, neutral phenomena (avyākṛta-dharma) are not the opposites of wholesome factors and so forth; yet this does not mean they are not matters of dharma-meaning, nor that they are non-dharma-meaning and non-matters.

Regarding the statement that "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise," it means that with ignorance as a condition, volitional formations are produced; with volitional formations as a condition, consciousness is produced, and so forth.

If such unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*) were to be called ignorance, then since wisdom has the function of discernment (*pravicaya*) while unwholesome wisdom lacks this capacity—and thus is no different from a lack of wisdom—it would follow that it is indeed ignorance.
To refute this, [the opponent] says: "It is not unwholesome wisdom, etc. Furthermore, they say: "The characteristics of greed and so forth..."
Since it is both defiled and lacks the nature of a [correct] view, and is not distinct from unwholesome wisdom (*akuśala-prajñā*), it ought to be ignorance (*avidyā*).

As for "relying on the nature of selfhood," this refers to the pride of self (*asmimāna*) among the seven types of pride; because one relies on the self to look down upon others, this "nature of selfhood" is precisely ignorance.
Since ignorance is characterized by a lack of clear understanding, it is similar [to the pride of self]; thus, relying on the self to treat things with contempt is indeed the pride of self.
This is of that same category.
As for the designation "name" (*nāman*), it is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) among the four aggregates;

how can it be called a "name" if the other four aggregates cannot express phenomena? Answer: A name expresses many phenomena, and the four aggregates likewise take many objects according to the six sense faculties.

The upper [realms] are similar to that [the desire realm] in that the term "name" (*nāman*) designates many phenomena; therefore, the four aggregates are collectively termed "name. Question: Among the four aggregates, the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) cannot take objects as their cognitive domain (*ālambana*);

how, then, can they be called "cognizing" (*ālambaka*)? Answer: If "name" exists within the formless realms (*ārūpya*), it is like the case where "form" (*rūpa*) is so named because of its capacity for transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*).

Just as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), past and future atoms, lack transformation and resistance yet are still designated as "form," so too, even though "name" exists in the formless realms, it is nonetheless designated as such.
Among the four aggregates, the four aggregates taken collectively are termed "name" (*nāman*).

Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) possess physical form and substance such that the eye can see them; however, the four [mental] aggregates lack such physical segments, and each must necessarily be made known through names and verbal explanations.
Therefore, the four aggregates are collectively established as "name."

Regarding the "abandonment of the body": the body is the material form-body (*rūpakāya*). When the four aggregates abandon the form-body of the previous destiny and take up the form-body of the subsequent destiny, it is like how a name denotes many phenomena;

thus, the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*). Question: Since the four untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates cannot take up a body in a future destiny, how can the four untainted aggregates be collectively termed "name"? Answer: Because they belong to that same category, even though they do not take up a future destiny.
There is the sense of relinquishing these aggregates.
Regarding "the arising of contact from the conjunction of three": contact arises simultaneously with the conjunction of three, while feeling arises simultaneously with the conjunction of four.

As for the expression "contact conducive to pleasant feeling," it is called "conducive" by virtue of being the cause; it is conducive to pleasant feeling, and thus it is termed "conducive. It is conducive to that which is conducive to pleasant feeling, and thus it is termed "conducive."

This refers to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). Question: If a future dharma gives rise to a present mental consciousness, this would mean the cause exists after the effect, which contradicts the principle of causality.

Answer: There are three kinds of effects: the effect that takes [the cause] (*grāhaka-phala*), the effect that gives [the fruit] (*datta-phala*), and the effect that co-exists with or precedes the cause.

These are the four conditioned effects (*saṃskṛta-phala*). The two [effects] are those realized by means of wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); the third is the effect of conformity (*anuloma-phala*). One must [understand] these accordingly.
This relies on the fact that the fruit [of contact] is realized either simultaneously with its cause or at a subsequent moment.

Regarding the mutual refutations found in the treatises: the two positions of the Sautrāntika school are not established as the fundamental tenet of our own school; rather, we posit that mental factors (*caitta*) do not exist, and that contact (*sparśa*) is a provisional designation for the simultaneous conjunction of the two [organ and object] and consciousness.
Furthermore, the "Later Master" (Vasumitra) posits that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the three [mental factors].
Regarding "contact with resistance" (*sapratigha-sparśa*), the *Nyāya* states: "Alternatively, it is called 'contact with resistance' because it takes resistant objects as its conditions.

As for that which is "superior in speech," this refers to the name (*nāman*) as the expressive agent; since the name is superior to that which is expressed, it is designated as "speech" (*vāk*) by way of its basis (*āśraya*).
For example, in the case of the color blue, there is the expressive name "blue," and the essence [of that name] extends to both visual contact and mental contact.

Regarding the statement that "contact cognizes the designating name which is exclusively mental contact": here, mental contact is designated by the name "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) because it takes this [name] as its object.
Second, because consciousness arises due to speech, consciousness is designated by its cause and called "designation-consciousness.
The contact associated with this consciousness that takes designation as its object is called "designation-contact"; thus, there is also consciousness that is the contact of designation.
The explanation that [feeling] arises conditioned by name and is established as being associated with it is a *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (co-referential) analysis.

Regarding the Sautrāntika position that the preceding moment of contact is the cause and the subsequent moment of feeling is the effect, [the opponent] refutes this, saying: "Suppose two moments take an object as their condition;
the first moment takes a favorable object, while the second moment takes an unfavorable object. Would the feeling of the first moment, which took a favorable object, [then arise from the second?]"

Because the third consciousness arises simultaneously with the second moment of thought as its object, yet possesses a nature that is contradictory to the preceding and succeeding moments—being either contrary or compliant—the mind of the preceding and succeeding moments perceiving their objects is refuted in this same manner.
Thus, the sixth *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) is defined as "perceiving only dharmas" (*dharmālambana*) when it does not involve other objects;

if it includes the objects of the first five [consciousnesses], it is called "perceiving mixed objects" (*miśrālambana*). Regarding the six objects, there are six distinct modes of perceiving each individually. II.
The combination of two conditions constitutes five phrases, up to the combination of six objects which constitutes one phrase.

Regarding the explanation of the term "access" (*upavicāra*): its meaning is that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), together with joy and the other [feelings], relies upon a simultaneous cognition and is called "access" because it discriminates the object;
the second explanation states that joy and the others act as conditions for the mind to range over the object. This is the correct principle, as joy and the others are [themselves] the conditions.
The power [of joy] takes the mind as its condition, causing the mind to range over objects. To refute this argument, it was previously stated:

"If one says that joy and so forth take the mind as their proximate condition when ranging over objects, then mental formations such as perception (saṃjñā) should also receive this name, because they are associated with the mind and proceed by means of the mind."

Although the joy (*prīti*) of the first and second dhyānas lacks the counterpart of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), it is established as "higher" by analogy with the presence of such counterparts in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, the third dhyāna is not established [as having joy] because the desire realm lacks the mental application of pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*). Moreover, while pleasure (*sukha*) is characterized by stagnation, the mental applications (*upavicāra*) are non-stagnant.

Within one's own realm, six types of joy arise upon seeing favorable objects; six types of sorrow arise upon seeing unfavorable objects; and six types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) arise upon seeing neutral objects.

Desire conditioned by the superior births of the Brahma-kings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth gives rise to four types of joy; conditioned by the fruit of non-conception (*asaṃjñiphala*), it gives rise to four types of mental suffering (*daurmanasya*);

conditioned by the five fruits, it gives rise to four types of equanimity (*upekṣā*); conditioned by the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), the absence of location, and so forth, it gives rise to one type of suffering feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*);

conditioned by longevity and other superior births, it gives rise to one type of joy; and conditioned by the absence of volitional activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and so forth, it gives rise to one type of equanimity.

Regarding the twelve [mental applications] that take the desire realm as their object: among the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the first two liberations and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) rely on the first two dhyānas and take the desire realm as their object;

they do not give rise to greed. Six [of these] give rise to joy (*prīti*), while six give rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*). These are the mental applications associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the eight internal [attainments]: the first dhyāna takes the second dhyāna as its superior object and thus gives rise to four types of joy; taking the *nirmāṇa* (emanated forms) as its object results in four types of equanimity.

The case of the form realm taking the formless realm as its object follows the explanation for the desire realm taking the formless realm as its object. Regarding the latter two [dhyānas] taking the desire realm as their object:
there are six, meaning that by taking the emanated phenomena of the desire realm as objects, six types of equanimity arise.
Regarding the four [types of equanimity] that take their own level as an object: they arise from the transformation of the fourth dhyāna and take the four [objects] as their objects.

As for the near-attainment (sāmantaka) of the sphere of infinite space taking form as its object, these four are explained according to the *Vibhāṣā* based on specific objects; if taken collectively, there is only one.

Regarding the formless [realms], because they are distant from the four objects of desire, they do not take the desire realm as their object; the fundamental formless [attainments] and the universal objects do not take the form realm as their object.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that the eighteen modes of mental application (*manopavicāra*) exist as nourishment, and therefore they are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not included herein.
The discordant apprehensions—namely, the tainted wholesome, the defiled, and the indeterminate—are all termed "near-operations" (*upavicāra*).

If one has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, one is said to have not attained the *anāgamya* (preliminary) and other concentrations; this constitutes the non-attainment of a wholesome mind of the form realm.

Within one's own realm, there are both defiled and wholesome-indeterminate [near-operations], whereas in the higher realms, they are exclusively defiled, because such is the nature of those afflictions.
Because they are objects to be experienced [as pleasant], etc., they do not take lower realms as their objects.

Regarding "non-discrimination": discrimination is wisdom (*prajñā*); non-discrimination is delusion (*moha*). Among the gates of the three poisons, these are established as the "near-approaches" (*upavicāra*).
They are called "bases of indulgence" because they serve as the basis for the afflictions of indulgence; thus, the Sautrāntikas maintain that they consist of defiled joy, sorrow, and equanimity.

The near-attainments (*upavicāra*) are that which are to be countered; the grasping of defiled joy, sorrow, and equanimity is called "the counteragent" because it serves as a basis for wholesome dharmas, yet these are not themselves near-attainments.
Other neutral states of joy, sorrow, and equanimity—whether they accord with defiled attachment or are included within the basis of wholesome renunciation—are not near-attainments.
However, the Buddha’s intention was to exclude only those defiled near-attainments; thus, he spoke in this way.

The Master explains that "defiled" and "wholesome" refer to what the Great Master has taught: these thirty-six [factors] exist in each of the three periods of time, thus constituting one hundred and eight feelings (*vedanā*).

As for the arising of phenomena such as afflictions (*kleśa*), it means that from afflictions arise karma, and from karma arise the resultant phenomena such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), just as a sprout arises from a seed.

The fruit arises after the leaf; likewise, because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have suppressed their karma through the afflictions, their karma lacks the suppression of afflictions and thus bears no fruit.
Regarding the "roots of affliction," those afflictions that accord with the stages and the path of seeing are called roots of affliction; the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is able to uproot them.
Just as with various medicinal herbs, for which the ripening of the fruit constitutes their final stage— once the herb has produced the fruit, it withers and can no longer produce more fruit—
so too, once karma has brought about its present fruit, it can no longer produce fruit in future lives.

Once food is digested, it can no longer be transformed into other food; likewise, the maturation (*vipāka*) of beings cannot be transformed, such that it must be experienced within realms like those of the gods.
Question: At the moment of initial birth, the body and mind are dull and inferior, incapable of giving rise to the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of afflictions through one's own power.

Since the body and mind are dull and inferior at this stage, how can one give rise to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and their attendant outbursts? Regarding the body and mind during this state:
The answer is as follows:
"Dull and inferior" refers to the four kinds of nutriment (*catur-āhāra*). When the World-Honored One had first attained the Way, he went to the Deer Park to deliver the five bhikṣus.

After crossing the Ganges, he encountered the non-Buddhist Pūrṇa. Seeing the Prince’s majestic and upright demeanor, Pūrṇa asked: "Gautama, it appears you have attained some supreme Dharma. The Buddha [replied].
The statement that "all things abide by means of nutriment" is spoken with the intention of refuting the non-Buddhist ascetics who practice self-starvation;
it distinguishes right awakening and right teaching from their false awakening and false teachings.

Regarding "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*): "edible" means that which is divided into portions and serves as sustenance. Once it has entered the stomach, it benefits the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
It is beneficial at two times: first, by alleviating hunger and thirst; second, once the eating is finished, it further benefits the sense faculties and the primary elements.
That which benefits neither the sense faculties nor the primary elements is edible but not food; yet it is called "food" based on its future function.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The essence consists only of the three objects. These three objects are comprised solely within the desire realm and all constitute the essence of substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The essence of substantial food comprises thirteen categories; by dividing the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), it becomes eleven. Question:
Although these two [types of touch] remove hunger and thirst, how can they be designated as the essence of food? Answer: These two are the most preeminent forms of food.
If these two were absent, there would be no need for food; because these two can nourish and benefit the sense faculties (*indriya*), they constitute the essence of food.

The six faculties apprehend the six objects: when the nose apprehends fragrance, it benefits the nose; when the eye sees form, it damages its own faculty—how much more so would it benefit the other faculties?
Therefore, visible form (*rūpa*) is not the essence of food. Sound is not mentioned as food because it lacks physical substance (*mūrta*).
Because they do not continue in succession, and because joy and pleasure arise when seeing visible forms, these are the three harmonious conditions.

Since form gives rise to the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), and that nutriment is subsumed within the nutriment of contact, why does the Sūtra praise the excellence of visible forms, odors, and tastes?

It is because visible form serves as the auxiliary condition for odor, taste, and tangibility. Furthermore, since the Sūtra cites the superiority of visible form to represent odor and the others, why does it not likewise praise tangibility?

Dharmatrāta replies: This is not a case of a bad tangible possessing a sublime fragrance and so forth; furthermore, since the tangible is the substance of nutriment, its status as such is established even without being explicitly stated.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), although there is visible matter, sound does not give rise to a mind of craving, and thus it is not called 'sublime form' and so forth.

Although there are great elements (*mahābhūta*) that can sustain and benefit the sense organs, these are not 'edible food' (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Even though they are not included within edible food, they are nonetheless obtained."

If it were as you say regarding food, then in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), only that which is swallowed or inhaled through the mouth and nose would qualify as "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); this would result in the fallacy of losing other defining characteristics.
However, in the desire realm, even a slight act of swallowing serves as the gateway, and by extension, all other such characteristics are designated as edible food.

This is like sunlight and so forth. In the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*), there is not even a fraction of swallowing to serve as a gateway; therefore, by extension, form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and joy (*prīti*) are established as edible food. [This is] the northern tradition.

Regarding "nutriments by tasting" (*āsvādya-āhāra*), it refers to fragrant objects that become tangible and are pleasing to the senses; it is not defined by the act of swallowing or chewing, but by its nature as a substantial nutriment (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

Furthermore, untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*) and all tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), although they provide temporary benefit to the sense-faculties and the body in the present, do not constitute "nutriment," because they do not project a future existence (*punarbhava*).

Regarding the statement, "There is the arising of a perishable self-substance and the birth of a perishable world," one commentator explains: "The 'perishable' refers to the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*);

the 'arising of a self-substance' refers to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*); and the 'perishable' [of the intermediate existence] refers to the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), which is the birth of the world. The term "intermediate existence" refutes the Mahāsāṃghikas' position that there is no intermediate existence;
"the birth of the world" refutes the eternalist non-Buddhist outsiders who claim that the five aggregates are permanent, whereas they actually arise from causes and are impermanent.

The delusions within the *bhava-avasthā* (existence-state) of "moistening" (*snigdha*) are called the "bond of arising" (*utpatti-saṃyojana*); the delusions within the *bhava-avasthā* of "moistening birth" (*janma-snigdha*) are called the "bond of birth" (*janma-saṃyojana*).

Regarding their abandonment, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of abandonment: first, the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through the acquisition of permanent antidotes; second, the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through the acquisition of permanent non-arising.
Within the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the term "abandonment" should be understood by reflecting upon these two types of abandonment.

Regarding the phrase "the first two benefit this life and so forth," this refers to the Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) speaking according to the Sautrāntika position concerning the seeds of consciousness and so on.
There are two ancient interpretations: one agrees with this [Sautrāntika] view, while the other represents the Sarvāstivāda position that "seed" has the meaning of "cause.
The verse states, "The first two benefit this life and so forth," which is said in terms of their predominance. Of these two interpretations, the former relies upon the Sūtras.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that all four nutriments (*āhāra*) sustain the present faculties (*indriya*) and primary elements (*mahābhūta*); furthermore, the two nutriments of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and contact (*sparśa-āhāra*) draw forth future existence.

Among these, the three internal nutriments—odor, flavor, and the tangible—sustain the three [faculties] beginning with touch, while collectively drawing forth the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) for future existence.

As for those that benefit the present, the nutriment of edible food is superior because it depends on external objects, whereas contact is superior because it depends on the perception of a preceding excellent object.

The fragrance and so forth that arise within the body produce the fragrance and so forth that constitute the food of sustenance; this is the benefit for the present life. As for the two foods of volition (*manasikāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they draw forth [the conditions] for the future, as explained in the commentary.
Regarding the benefit of the food of volition for the present: once, during a time of famine, there was a father who wished to travel to another country, carrying a sack...
He placed ashes in a hexagram-patterned cloth and hung it on the wall, claiming it was a bag of roasted flour. The two sons watched in terror for a long time without dying.
Later, someone arrived, took it down, opened it, and saw only ashes; their hope shattered, they died.

The *Saṃgītiparyāya* states that when great beings in the ocean come ashore to lay their eggs, they bury them in the sand and return to the sea; while the mother thinks of her offspring, the eggs do not spoil.
If the mother loses mindfulness, the egg is immediately destroyed; this should be understood as the child thinking of its mother at that time, whereby it is not destroyed.
That treatise should be applied by analogy here: even if the child thinks of its mother until reaching the stage of "touching" (sparśa), there is still the thought [of the mother];

yet due to the power of distinct karmic forces, consciousness is not destroyed, and one perceives excellent forms and so forth in the present. As for why there are four nutriments (*āhāra*), according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is said:

Because one remedies the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena, for what reason does one remedy the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena? All sentient beings have, since beginningless time, clung to the body as pure. The Buddha’s word says to them: "This body consists of thirty-six impure substances; because it is sustained by morsel food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it is impure. This is why morsel food is mentioned. Because they cling to it as being pleasant, contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*) is taught; because they follow after [craving], mental volition-food (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*) is taught; and because they grasp at perceptions, consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is taught. Thus, by means of these four foods, one remedies the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena. Therefore, it is said that the four foundations of mindfulness remedy the four perversions. Furthermore, the body is the basis for the other three; therefore, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is established first. Once the body is understood, one can then understand sensations, the mind, and phenomena. For this reason, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught in this sequence. Furthermore, the body is the vessel, while sensations, the mind, and phenomena are the contents. Just as one first observes the vessel and then the contents, so too does one first observe the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is coarse, while sensations, the mind, and phenomena are subtle. One first observes the coarse and then the subtle. Furthermore, the body is the support for all conditioned phenomena; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the primary object of attachment for sentient beings. Therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the root of birth and death. Therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the four great elements; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the five aggregates; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the six sense bases; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the seven consciousnesses; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the eightfold path; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the nine successive attainments; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the ten wholesome paths of action; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the eleven factors of enlightenment; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twelve links of dependent origination; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the thirteen types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the fourteen difficult-to-understand points; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the fifteen aspects of the truths; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the sixteen aspects of the four truths; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the seventeen types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the eighteen elements; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the nineteen types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty-one types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty-two faculties; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty-three types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty-four types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty-five types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena. Furthermore, the body is the locus of the twenty-six types of emptiness; therefore, one first observes the body and then the sensations, the mind, and phenomena.
