Because there is suffering and pleasure, it is said that the mind is grasped as permanent; because it is sustained by the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*), all activities and movements are mental volitions.
Because one grasps phenomena as a self, and since consciousness cognizes those phenomena as being entirely non-existent, I speak of the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
Among the four alternatives, one takes the fourth: the three nutriments beginning with contact (*sparśa*) that are untainted (*anāsrava*), and the subsequent contact and so forth.

Regarding the three categories, there is a difference between their breadth and narrowness: contact (*sparśa*) and the others encompass both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), and are thus broad; edible food (*kavalīkārāhāra*) does not encompass the latter and is therefore narrow.

Furthermore, while food encompasses all four types, it does not encompass the non-outflowing, and this can be understood by reflecting upon them through the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). One should understand that the four types of food are subsumed within the three categories by means of such reflection.

Regarding the phrase "there is birth, death, and so forth," the term "birth" (janman) also encompasses the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). According to the preceding text, the intermediate state is not called "arising" (*utpāda*), but it is indeed called "birth.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Since one who dies in the formless realm experiences the initial moment of mind of the intermediate state belonging to the desire or form realms, it follows that this [initial moment] constitutes the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire and form realms;
therefore, it is known that this too may be termed 'birth'."
Regarding one who, while having a body in the lower realm, gives rise to a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of a higher realm:

even if it were granted that such a person has a body in the higher realm when giving rise to an absorption of their own level, there would still be no death or birth, because the absorption provides benefit through its stabilizing influence. Furthermore, for rebirth to occur, it requires a defiled mind;

since an absorption of a higher realm is not defiled and arises through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), one does not undergo death or birth through it either. [Question: Does the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at the time of death extend [to the next life]?
Regarding how the three natures [are subsumed by] only two, and why one does not enter *nirvāṇa* with the non-conceptual mind:

because the death-moment of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) occurs through a wholesome preparatory mind that is free from defilement, one does not enter *nirvāṇa*. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks: "If innate wholesome states are inferior, why does one not enter *nirvāṇa*? It answers:
"Because there is a maturation (*vipāka*) that does not give rise to a wholesome mind. If that were so, then while abiding in the present maturation, one should likewise not enter *nirvāṇa*.

The case of *paryavasthāna* (obsessions) is not like this; because one realizes the fruit by means of the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) based on the present body, there is volition that does not weary of the present fruit, but only wearies of future fruits.

Consciousness has no physical form; it merely ceases simultaneously with vitality and warmth, just as when a small amount of water is placed upon a heated stone, it gradually diminishes and fades away until it suddenly vanishes entirely.
This severance of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) exists only among humans; it does not exist in the hells because [the hells] are characterized by constant suffering.

It occurs among humans in the three continents, as well as among animals (*tiryagyoni*) and hungry ghosts (*preta*), and even among the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) practitioners who are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). There is no separate entity [to this severance]; rather, it is simply the cutting of the limbs and joints of the body.
According to the *Nyāya*, it arises from speaking words that mock or pierce another person—whether true or false—which wound and cut the human heart, and by which [the victim] shall [suffer].
This refers to the suffering at the vital points (*marmaccheda*) that approaches [death].
The *Nyāya* states: "Once these five signs appear, death will occur within no more than five days. Even if such signs appear, even the World-Honored One cannot avert them.
Furthermore, not all sons of gods possess these signs, nor does every single son of a god possess all five."

Regarding the statement "one who possesses the signs will die," the mention of "five" here refers to the general total number. Furthermore, there are five minor signs that appear which do not necessarily mean one will die, as explained in the *Śāstra*.

As for "the state of certainty" (*niyāma*), it is because after the *duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*, one definitely attains *nirvāṇa*. [Question: What is the certainty of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)?
Question: How is it that one who has attained *nirvāṇa* does not receive this designation? Answer: (1) Because such a person might still revert to a state of wrong nature (*mithyātva-gotra*);

(2) because they have not yet abandoned the state of wrong nature; and (3) because the time [of their attainment] is not yet fixed. From the first moment of the stage of *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, one is destined to attain *nirvāṇa* within seven births. Question:

One who has attained the stages of Supreme Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) also attains *nirvāṇa*; for what reason are they designated as "wrong" (*mithyātva*)?
The reason for the brief answer is twofold: first, because time was short; second, because they had not yet abandoned their false nature.
● In the eleventh section of the main treatise, regarding the "small vessel":
this refers to a single set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), such as those with water or golden wheels, measuring twelve *lakṣas* and three thousand four hundred [yojanas] in diameter.

One hundred and fifty *yojanas* is the measure of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) upon which one set of four continents rests; an immeasurable number [of such] constitutes the support for a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the wind-circle serves as the support for a water-circle of one hundred *koṭis*.
One *koṭi* equals ten billion (*śata-koṭi*), and one hundred *koṭis* equals one hundred times ten billion. A great trichiliocosm consists of one hundred times one hundred [such units].
From this we know that the wind-wheel serves as the support for the great trichiliocosm: if there is a fire calamity, it is formed by wind and rain arising from below the second dhyāna;
if there is a water calamity, it is formed by wind and rain arising from below the third dhyāna; and if there is a wind calamity, it is formed by wind and rain arising from below the fourth dhyāna.
"Permitted" (許) means that which is commonly accepted by all schools; "raised" (擧) means to lift up.
Regarding the phrase "like one holding grain," the *Jiezhang* states: "The four sides are like the shape of a tray or a rafter."
Sumeru (妙高) is composed of four precious substances; it is called "Wondrous" because it excels all other peaks and "High" because it rises above them.

Regarding the eight preceding mountains, the *Śāstra* states that their summits are square, with each side being three times [the width of the mountain], and further states that there are four peaks at the four corners.
The ninth mountain is circular; according to the *Śāstra*, its circumference is like a wheel that encircles one world-system.

The first seven are called "internal" because Mount Sumeru (the Golden Mountain) is situated within the four continents; the eighth mountain is called "external" because it lies outside the four continents.

The interpretation that the "Elephant-Nose" is not the correct meaning is incorrect; here it is said that there is a deity with obstructions, a certain spirit-god who has the form of a human with a head [of an elephant].
Whatever superior phenomena one perceives are like the mountain peaks that serve as obstacles, resembling the heads of those deities.
As for the brilliant colors of the Jewel’s majestic power manifesting in space— the azure hue that the Sautrāntikas call the "single manifest color of space"—
this is in fact the color of the Jewel itself.
Regarding the "Treasury of the Seed-Store of All Jewels": water can act as the seed that produces them and serves as the storehouse from which they emerge.
Originally, upon the Golden Wheel, there was but one great ocean; later, struck by the winds of karma, it surged forth all at once as the nine great mountains.
Between each mountain is an ocean, wherein the water has been transformed into jewels.

Regarding the statement that the eighth ocean is divided into sweet and salty waters: it is said that its outer edge is an iron mountain, and because water has stagnated there for a long time, it is salty.
This explanation is irrational; rather, it is by the power of the wind that the sweet and salty waters of the eighth ocean are separated.

Altogether, the nine mountains and eight oceans total one million two hundred thousand, eight hundred and seventy-five *yojanas*, which is the same as previously stated regarding the golden [mountain].
The diameter of the second water wheel is twelve billion three hundred and forty-five *yojanas*, slightly less than the exact measure;
its magnitude is the same as the others.
Because there is no other basis (*anupadhiśeṣa*) and no other location, there is no other person for whom this concentration serves as a basis, as it is without remainder.

Regarding the location that serves as the basis for this meditative absorption, ancient masters have said: "Based on the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, it is proven that the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) is near the south and that the hells are below;
this proves that the Vajrāsana is near the north. Master Bao remarked: "This land measures two thousand [yojanas] on each of its three sides.
On the southern side, there are three and a half [yojanas] down to the Avīci hell, which already measures twenty thousand *yojana*s; furthermore, there are many other [hells]."
Many hells fill the subterranean regions so densely that they cannot be described as being near the south;

the current explanation states that just as a person and a ghost do not obstruct one another within the same dwelling, so too the Vajrāsana in the realm of the central heavens does not obstruct the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Regarding *rākṣasa*, the phonetic and semantic explanations state that it is sometimes called *āsurī* or *asura*, which is a general name for malevolent spirits;
it is also called *rakṣa*, which means "protector. If female, she is named *rakṣasī*. The older term "Rakṣa" (*羅剎*) is a corruption and abbreviation.
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 172, there are three explanations, two of which are as recorded in the commentary (*shu*).

The third [point] states that the eight intermediate continents (*antaradvīpa*) are alternative names for the four great continents (*mahādvīpa*). Each of these four continents has two alternative names;
the commentators (*vibhāṣā-ācārya*) adopt the first explanation, as all are inhabited by humans.

Regarding "length and breadth" (*āyāma-vistāra*): according to the common interpretation, the north-south direction is called length (*āyāma*) and the east-west direction is called breadth (*vistāra*). The *Guangya* (Broad and Elegant Lexicon) defines it as "long. This is the current explanation.
It should be understood that its length is vertical and its breadth is horizontal. The four mouths of the lake each measure forty *li* in circumference.

The eastern mouth is made of silver and resembles the head of an ox; the southern mouth is made of gold and resembles the head of an elephant; the western mouth is made of crystal (*sphatika*) and resembles the head of a lion;
and the northern mouth is made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and resembles the head of a horse.
In Sanskrit it is called *naraka*, which here means "place of suffering.
