Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [attainments], they are acquired at two prior times; adding to these the acquisition of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) that sustains birth in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as well as the unconditioned states of the four truths and the first eight categories of the afflictions of the lower realms, they are acquired at two times. The ninth category is acquired at one time.

As for the Pratyekabuddha, when he has exhausted the afflictions of the eight lower stages—whether in the ordinary stage (*pṛthagjana-avasthā*) where there is no place [to dwell] or where there is a place—and if it is in the *Anāgamya* stage...

Prior to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains at three moments the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states of the eight stages abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the seven stages above the First Dhyāna abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):

first, the acquisition of one contaminated (*sāsrava*) sustaining [attainment] that maintains birth; second, the acquisition of two uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sustaining [attainments]; and third, the acquisition of the attainment of the fruit.

If one enters the Path of Seeing from the intermediate state or the five [other] stages, one simultaneously acquires the unconditioned states of the desire realm abandoned by seeing and cultivation, as well as those of the seven stages above the First Dhyāna.
Regarding the acquisition of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the unconditioned:
one acquires the unconditioned of the four truths of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the first eight categories of the path of cultivation at two times;

one acquires the ninth category at one time—namely, excluding the single instance of acquisition upon taking birth. Question: As for a person who has "leaped over" to the third fruit and is practicing in the desire realm...
Is the unconditioned attainment (*asamskṛta-prāpti*) of the abandonment of the ninth grade [of afflictions] the essence (*svabhāva*) of the third fruit? No.

For the Buddha and the Pratyekabuddha, the unconditioned attainment of the abandonment of the six grades through cultivation is difficult to answer based on this same principle; since it is not repeatedly confirmed, it cannot constitute the essence of the second or third fruits.

However, for the Pratyekabuddha, it does constitute the essence of his fruit. The Buddha is not like this; he allows it to be the essence of the fruit because of his mastery (*vaśitva*), just as in the case of attaining the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*). If...

If it were not so, there would be no unconditioned fruit-essence. Since the fruit of awakening consists of untainted dharmas, when the Dharma-King first ascends the stage of awakening, the myriad virtues come to court him.

Furthermore, the fundamental stage is not of the desire realm; the path of the heavy seal does not take the unconditioned of the four truths of the desire realm as its third fruit-essence, nor can the unconditioned of the nine grades of the path of cultivation constitute the third fruit.

The essence of the fruits and so forth is explained according to this principle. Question: Since both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas have exhausted the afflictions of the lower eight stages through the paths of seeing and meditation, for what reason do Pratyekabuddhas—ranging from the first dhyāna up to the "base of nothingness"—repeatedly seal their attainment with the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), whereas Bodhisattvas do not arise [in such a manner]?
Answer: Because Buddhas possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), they directly sever the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) following the path of seeing.

Regarding the Pratyekabuddha, according to the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise Following Reasoning), fascicle 126: upon arising from the first dhyāna, the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) possesses sufficient momentum through repetition to be able to sever the possession (*prāpti*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

If this is so, since the Khadga-viṣāṇakalpa (Rhinoceros-like) Pratyekabuddha and the Buddha do not sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) pertaining to the stage of seeing (*darśana-heya*), they are identical to those of sharp faculties;

why then do they repeatedly give rise to the four types of Dharma-knowledge-forbearance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*)? Answer: It is because, like those who follow the gradual sequence (*ānupūrvika*), they give rise to the [path of] seeing.

The Path must necessarily involve the contemplation of all four truths (*catuḥsatya*) in order to sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), because it arises for the first time and the Path is difficult to cultivate.
However, the Path that severs the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can sever them upon contemplating even a single truth, as it does not arise for the first time.

Although the rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddhas and Buddhas do not sever the delusions of views pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) [at this stage], they do so because they have already previously generated the untainted path of vision (*anāsrava-darśanamārga*). By generating the four *dharmajñānakṣāntis* as a preliminary means, they induce the four subsequent cognitions (*anvayajñāna*).
It is the wisdom of patience (*jñāna-kṣānti*).
Its essence is the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that brings about universal knowledge; what was formerly called the "nine knowledges of permanent abandonment" refers to this.

Wisdom is the "knowledge of universal knowledge" (*parijñā-jñāna*), while permanent abandonment is "abandonment through universal knowledge" (*parijñā-prahāṇa*). Wisdom is that which realizes the abandonment, and abandonment is that which is realized. What is realized is termed the "fruit of universal knowledge" (*parijñā-phala*); it is taken as such.

Question: Regarding the name "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*): while it is appropriate to apply this name to the wisdom (*jñāna*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), how can the eight forbearances (*kṣānti*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) be called complete knowledge?
Answer: These [forbearances] are also designated by the name "wisdom" because they are the retinue (*parivāra*) of wisdom; just as when a minister acts, it is also said that the king acts.

Furthermore, if one speaks of what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), one obtains six fruits; if one speaks of the path of seeing itself, there are five fruits, with the sixth being the fruit of the path of cultivation.

Question: Since the three fetters beginning with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) are abandoned at the first fruit (srotāpattiphala), how is it that the fifth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)—the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*)—is only attained at the third fruit (anāgāmiphala)?
Answer: There is no fault in this, as it is stated according to the point at which the five lower fetters are entirely exhausted that the thorough knowledge is attained.

Furthermore, the essence of this thorough knowledge is taken to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state manifested by the abandonment of the three fetters beginning with the view of a self; thus, it is referred to as the "five lower fetters."

The meaning of the "exhaustive knowledge" (*parijñā*) regarding the exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*) is likewise not lost. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains that for the person who proceeds through the five stages of the lower-tier fetters (*pañca-aṅga-hīna-bhāgīya*), there is the abandonment of two [fetters] by one who transcends them;
for the person who abandons the view of a self in existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there are three. These two cases are explained together.

If the craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*) is exhausted, it refers exclusively to the exhaustion of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the realm of form. The explanation of "exhaustive knowledge" regarding all fetters follows the explanation of the five factors conducive to the lower realm (*pañca-aṅga-hīna-bhāgīya*).
The afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the two upper realms are treated identically and thus established together as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

Regarding the six [thorough knowledges] that are the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*): a question arises—just as in the case of the third person who transcends [the stages], at the sixteenth moment of mind, one does not take the lower thorough knowledge of the path of the two upper realms because the *Saṃyukta Āgama* compiles them into five "thorough knowledges of the factors conducive to falling back" (*pañca-hīna-bhāga-parijñā*). Therefore, the tenth... [is established].

At the moment of the sixth mind, one attains the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). This full knowledge is precisely the fruit of the patience (*kṣānti*) of the fifteenth mind;
when combined with the fruits of the preceding patiences, there are six. Thus, it is said that the fruit of patience consists of six attainments.

In response to this, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 63, states that the five lower fetters are admitted to be the fruit of patience. As for the statement that "six are attained," this refers to... [the attainment of the fruit of] the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*).

Regarding those who attain the fruits through the gradual sequence, it is said that if one attains them by means of both the gradual and the leap-over methods, they simultaneously obtain seven kinds [of fruits].
For example, abandoning five and obtaining one constitutes the leap-over attainment of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvara-bhāgīya*).
Regarding the "fruits of the remaining three knowledges": it is accepted that dharma-knowledge may obtain three [results], anvaya-knowledge obtains two, and conventional knowledge obtains two;
what is now called the "fruit of knowledge" refers to the three types of knowledge taken collectively.
Regarding "all [results] of the *anāgamya*": since the path of seeing exists in the six stages beginning with *anāgamya*,

and because there are nine grades (*navaprakāra*) of untainted paths (*anāsravamārga*) as well as tainted paths (*sāsravamārga*) within the nine stages of *anāgamya* that sever the afflictions of the desire realm, one attains the results of the nine universal knowledges (*parijñā*).

According to the orthodox doctrine of the Sarvāstivāda, one who enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) first exhausts all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and does not further abandon the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing or cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, since this is fundamentally not a path for abandoning the desire realm, how can it be said that it separately induces the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

Now, the four types of patience regarding the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) arise as the preparatory stage (*upāyabhūmi*) for the four types of subsequent knowledge-patience (*anvayajñānakṣānti*). This intermediate stage is [the path of seeing].
These are also the five fruits.

Regarding the "nine of the noble ones," this refers to the fact that all nine stages possess uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths; this is explained in terms of one who enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the *anāgamya* stage.

For a Bodhisattva, while in the causal state, relying on the fourth dhyāna at the stage of the path of seeing, they accomplish two fruits of the path of seeing pertaining to the higher realms through the abandonment of what is to be eliminated by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the sixteenth mind is accomplished in the middle, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) destroys the first two and establishes one; because there are five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya), there is no realization of the fruit of enlightenment.
When the stage of the fruit is accomplished, it is called "one," meaning that all fetters are exhausted. For the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha], it is according to the previous case.

Regarding the Bodhisattva, it is said that upon entering the path of seeing (darśanamārga) from the fourth dhyāna, they rely on the previously mentioned "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) state to enter the path of seeing; while in the position of the path of seeing, the five [factors] are accomplished.

Regarding the five fruits of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*): if one enters the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) from the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*), one achieves only the two pervasive knowledges (*parijñā*) of the higher realms as the fruit of the path of vision;

this continues until the sixteenth moment of mind. At that time, when entering the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one abandons the previous two and establishes them as the five pervasive knowledges of the lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya-parijñā*).

Then, through the arising of one hundred and twenty-six moments of mind, one successively seals the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and attains the pervasive knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya-parijñā*).
Knowledge of the fruit is the complete knowledge that all fetters have been exhausted. Among the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: (1) those proceeding toward the first fruit obtain six;
(2) those in the first fruit, as well as those proceeding toward the second and third fruits, likewise obtain six; (3) those in the third fruit obtain one;
(4) those proceeding toward the second fruit obtain two; and (5) if one transcends the third fruit and enters the path of seeing from the stage of *anāgamya*, they obtain five.

Regarding the fruits: there is one [fruit] for the fundamental [attainment], and two for those entering the path of seeing toward the second fruit; there are six for those who leap over toward the second fruit. Question:
For a person who leaps over to the third fruit, once they reach the stage of *duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of suffering), the three conditions are fully present;

why is "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) not established at that point? Answer: This is explained according to the sequential [attainment]; it is only when reaching that specific stage that [the designation] is established. For one who leaps over, the desire [realm] has not yet been attained.

Regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the lower untainted (*anāsrava*) states within the realm (*dhātu*): if one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the fundamental dhyānas, one does not acquire the three [factors] to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question: How is it that the three conditions for the path of seeing establish full knowledge (*parijñā*), while four conditions establish it for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

Answer: The path of seeing has only the defiled as its object, whereas the path of cultivation applies to both the defiled and the non-defiled. Furthermore, the upper unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) serves as their common substance (*tulyajātīya*). It is the path of cultivation that is capable of taking the afflictions as its object.

Because the characteristic of the afflictions not yet being exhausted has not yet manifested, "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) is not established; only when one reaches the subsequent transcendence of the realms and the characteristic becomes manifest is thorough knowledge established.

Regarding the dual causes for transcending realms: as in the case of the abandonment of the defilements of the path of cultivation, the abandonment of the afflictions of the first, second, and third dhyānas [constitutes such a cause].

At the time of exhaustion, both causes are necessarily not yet attained; the same applies to transcending the realm and the formless realm (*ārūpya*). Only when two conditions are present does one gather universal knowledge (*parijñā*) and attain the fruit.
Regarding the fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the relative presence of these two conditions—attaining the fruit and transcending the realm—the first fruit constitutes the first alternative:
attaining the fruit but not transcending the realm. The first and second fruits constitute the second alternative: transcending the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

The third fruit and the fourth fruit constitute the third and fourth phrases; the fourfold analysis regarding the attainment of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) without attaining the fruit can be understood according to the preceding pattern.
An *anāgāmin* (non-returner) born in the fourth dhyāna accomplishes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), as does one born in the formless realm who has transcended craving for form (*rūparāga*).

Because of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of exhaustion, one knows the arising of the first thorough knowledge; because of the thorough knowledge of the arising, one knows the path of the seal of the arising.

Furthermore, there is the abandonment of one and the attainment of one, which is the Buddha’s rhinoceros-horn-like [path]: the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the attainment of the total destruction of all fetters is one thorough knowledge.

This section explains that the attainment of thorough knowledge is accompanied by abandonment; therein, there are two meanings: if one advances to a superior path and abandons the inferior, it is called "abandonment."
It is not that the essence [of the defilement] is abandoned. If one regresses and loses what is superior to acquire what is inferior, then both the name and the essence are abandoned.

One view holds that "arising" refers to regression; another view holds that it refers to reaching the phase of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*). According to this latter view, one is said to regress only when the arising of a defilement reaches the present.
Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya:
A Draft of the Essential Meaning, Part II, composed by the Śramaṇa Huīhuī of Xīmíng Monastery in Jìngzhào.
Treatise Text, Chapter Twenty-two: The Chapter on the Noble Ones (Āryapudgala).
The commentary on this chapter is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the analysis of the text.
Regarding "Worthy Harmony" (*xianhe*): "harmony" refers to harmony in practice. Regarding "Noble Correctness" (*shengzheng*): "correctness" refers to the principle of *nirvāṇa*;

because the Noble Ones have attained certainty regarding this correctness, the text says they possess many talents through their conduct, which is called "worthiness. The *Guiyuan zhucóng* states that there is no [further explanation].

In this context, those who have not yet attained realization are not termed "sages" (*ārya*); according to the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are called "worthies" (*bhadra*), while those on the stages and above are called "sages.
Thus, there are five stages of cultivation consisting of the three worthies and the ten sages. This treatise [distinguishes] seven sages and eight sages:

the seven preparatory means (*upāya*) constitute the seven worthies, and the four candidates (*pratipannaka*) and four fruits (*phala*) constitute the eight sages. There are likewise five stages of cultivation; the first three preparatory means constitute the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

The four stages of application are as follows: the stage of application (*prayoga-mārga*) is the stage of preparatory practice; the stage of penetration (*prativedha-mārga*) is the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is the path of meditation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); and the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-mārga*) is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

Regarding the verse’s mention of the "abandonment of afflictions" (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) factors, which are abandoned together with the afflictions; however, [the verse] speaks of their abandonment.
That which is attained necessarily through the power of the Path (*mārga-bala*) is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states:

"If a single moment of mind (*citta*) can suddenly sever the nine grades [of afflictions] and is thus untainted (*anāsrava*), then the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) should also be untainted when it severs the five categories—such as the lower-lower, upper-middle, and upper-upper grades—in a single moment. Answer: The five categories are severed together because they are simultaneously loathed.

If it were easy [to abandon them] by discerning and severing the nine grades at once, that would be difficult. Question: Since the two types of cessation (non-analytical and analytical) are not emptiness, why are they not included within the Four Noble Truths?
Answer: If a phenomenon is a fruit of suffering, a cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, or an antidote to suffering, it is established as a Truth (*satya*).

Because the two cessations do not belong to these four categories, they are not included in the Four Truths. Furthermore, because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, they are not included in the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not subsumed under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*); because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is not subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

There is another explanation, as already described in the previous fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā*: "Regarding the Four Truths, if one relies on the actual substance (*dravya*) of their nature, there are three, because suffering, origination, and the path are each a single entity;
if one relies on cause and effect, there are five, because the five categories (*pañcavastuka*) possess both cause and effect; if one relies on clear realization (*abhisamaya*), [there are four]."

Question: There are eight truths because there are four truths each for the higher and lower realms. Answer: Based on cause and effect, the Truth of the Path is established as one by being combined with the departure from suffering.

Question: If that is so, since Suffering and Origin lead to the same destination, why are they not combined and established as one? Answer: Because they are observed through distinct aspects (*ākāra*). Question:

If that is so, why are the aspects of the Truth of the Path not observed distinctly? Answer: Because one has faith based on the Truths; it is like the case where there is no [distinction] regarding the Truths in the case of wrong view.

Since accumulation (*samudaya*) is without past [existence], one does not slander the present fruit; therefore, regarding the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Accumulation, one observes their aspects distinctly.
As for the Truth of the Path, because slandering the cause is equivalent to slandering the fruit, one observes the aspects of the Truth of the Path with the same conviction as this. Question:

Since the Four Truths are observed by both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), why are they called "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*) only for the noble ones? Answer: Because the noble ones know suffering and so forth as they truly are, they are called Noble Truths; ordinary beings do not.
If one perceives suffering as pleasure, it cannot be called an "ordinary truth" (*pṛthagjana-satya*). If that is so, why not define an ordinary truth by way of its being a perversion? Answer:

That which is known through the vision of the noble ones (*ārya*) is non-perverted and is thus termed a "noble truth" (*ārya-satya*). That which is perceived by ordinary people is not known to be perverted, and therefore it is not termed an "ordinary truth.

It is like the claim of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): if seeing even a single eyeless person in the world is already suffering, how much more so is it within *nirvāṇa*, where all six sense faculties [are absent]?

Without cause, one contemplates [the lower realms] as suffering; furthermore, in the six modes of practice, one first contemplates the desire realm as suffering and so forth, and contemplates the first dhyāna as tranquility and so forth.

However, if one relies on the second dhyāna, one then contemplates the first dhyāna as suffering and so forth; since these aspects of contemplation are not fixed, they are not called the "truths of ordinary beings.
Because a noble one has attained noble wisdom and does not regress after that single attainment, the objects of their contemplation follow accordingly.
The wisdom capable of such observation is also called the "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*); because ordinary persons subsequently observe incorrectly, it is not called a Noble Truth. Question:

Since all four truths are observed through four aspects (*ākāra*), why are the four aspects of observing suffering designated as the "Truth of Suffering" and so forth, rather than the "Truth of Emptiness" and so forth?

One should apply this same principle to the other three truths. Answer: The names are established based on their unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇa*). For example, suffering is unique [in its specific nature].

Because the three types of suffering are established upon all contaminated (*sāsrava*) resultant phenomena, the other three [aspects] are not fixed. Impermanence (*anitya*) is common to the truths of suffering, origin, and the path; emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*) are common to all four truths.

The name "origin" (*samudaya*) applies exclusively to that which can summon the fruit of suffering. If the term "cause" (*hetu*) is taken as a condition (*pratyaya*), it extends to the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*);

however, the name "cessation" (*nirodha*) is restricted to the truth of cessation alone. "Tranquility" (*śānta*) applies to contaminated meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) as well as the uncontaminated path, while "sublime" (*praṇīta*) refers to the latter.
The paths that lead to the Truths of Cessation and the Path are designated as "paths" (*mārga*) because they specifically manifest the route toward *nirvāṇa*.

Just as the practice that penetrates worldly principles is called "penetrating" (*prativedha*), and the practice that leads out of existence and penetrates the Truth of Cessation is likewise so called, neither of these are established under the name of "Truths" (*satya*).

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the Truths of Cessation and the Path are exclusively termed "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*) because they are exclusively truths; whereas Suffering and Origination are termed "Worldly Truths" (*loka-satya*) because they are observed by both ordinary beings and Noble Ones. (5)
Regarding the suffering within sensation (*vedanā*), how is it that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)?

If there were no place for pleasure (*sukha*) other than what merely resembles the aspect of suffering, then suffering would not exist as a distinct entity. For the practitioner, among the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of cessation (*anityatā-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is preeminent and subsumes the other three.

Regarding this, a dissenting teacher of the Vaibhāṣika school explains that while pleasure is slight, suffering is abundant; however, the correct position is as follows: *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, specifically concerning the nature of suffering and the interpretation of the four characteristics.*

Regarding the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), it is accepted that all are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), even though there exists actual pleasure. According to the Sautrāntikas, pleasure is also suffering for three reasons.

Regarding the Sautrāntika view that the four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): first, craving for present existence (*bhavābhinandana-tṛṣṇā*), which is attachment to present fruits;

second, craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*), which is attachment to future fruits; third, craving accompanied by delight (*nandī-sahagata-tṛṣṇā*), which operates toward objects already obtained; and fourth, [craving for non-existence].

Regarding the statement that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises toward objects not yet obtained according to one's various inclinations and attachments: the first two conditions arise within one’s own body, while the latter two conditions arise with respect to external objects.

The Sarvāstivādins explain in general that craving is taught as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) from the perspective of its predominance. Question: How do the Four Noble Truths and the Two Truths subsume one another? Answer:
The two subsume the four, but the four do not exhaustively subsume the two. Regarding the two subsuming the four: the truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*) [are included].

Destruction is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); the true meaning is subsumed under ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The Path is like a boat or raft—it may be abandoned [conventionally], yet its reality is ultimate.
Cessation is ultimate; both types of cessation are also subsumed under the ultimate. These two cessations are not included within the Four Truths;
they encompass both the conventional and the ultimate, as well as both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). Objects such as a jar or water are called conventional.
Because they can be destroyed, they are called "worldly" (*loka*). They are manifest in the context of worldly sentiment, and thus are called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*), such as a jar or water.

When these have not yet been broken or analyzed, they are considered "truths" (*satya*) from the perspective of worldly sentiment because they exist as real entities. According to the Sautrāntika masters, when untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and other such cognitions apprehend phenomena without error, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*);
other forms of wisdom that apprehend phenomena by first viewing them as pleasant and subsequently viewing them as suffering, and so forth, are [conventional].

Regarding conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) in the Mahāyāna, there are four pairs: first, the true and the conventional; second, the provisional and the real; third, principle and phenomena; fourth, the shallow and the deep; fifth, the expression and the referent.

First, regarding the single [category] of the conventional and the ultimate: 1. The "army," "forest," and so forth are purely conventional; 2. The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are both; 3. The Four Noble Truths are both; 4. The two kinds of emptiness and suchness (*tathatā*) are both; 5.

The single true dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*) is purely ultimate. In the intermediate cases, when viewed from the perspective of what precedes them, they are ultimate; when viewed from the perspective of what follows them, they are conventional. This is extensive.

As it is described: one who wishes to enter the noble stage first contemplates the virtues of *nirvāṇa* and the faults of *saṃsāra*, draws near to virtuous friends, and gives rise to morality, concentration, and wisdom.

Regarding the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one contemplates the Dharma like a beginner learning to swim; one constantly clings to the water, let alone clinging to the text while contemplating the meaning.

Regarding the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), it is like one who has practiced before and can temporarily let go of the wood, let alone temporarily letting go of the text while contemplating the meaning. Regarding the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)... [it is like... as if...

Those who have practiced for a long time are able to abandon the wood forever; how much more so can they completely abandon the words? Contemplating the meaning relies on the wisdom acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha-prajñā*) and the wholesome states acquired at birth;

the wisdoms arising from hearing the teachings—namely, the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and so forth, as well as the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayī-prajñā*)—arise solely from application (*prayoga*). The wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), however, pertains to all three types of attainment.
The first two, which are easily accomplished, consist of physical and mental seclusion (*kāya-viveka* and *citta-viveka*).

Regarding contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that once one has obtained robes and other requisites—whether many or few, coarse or fine—one does not further long for them; this is called contentment (formerly translated as "knowing sufficiency").
Not extensively seeking robes and other items, whether in quantity or quality, is called having few desires (*alpecchatā*). Question: In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no...
Question: Since there is no desire for clothing, food, and so forth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how can the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) exist there?

Answer: In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no object of resentment; thus, the wholesome root of non-ill will (*avyāpāda*) can exist. Although there is no clothing, food, and the like, what prevents the existence of the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*) and its function of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*)?

Furthermore, in the form realm, there are paths that serve as antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the four types of craving, and in the formless realm, there is the path of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa*). Therefore, these noble lineages can exist in those realms.
Furthermore, regarding the two paths of progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) and advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*), one does not covet robes and so forth for the sake of the body, nor does one covet them at all.

With robes and such as conditions, one is able to give rise to the seeds of the various noble ones (*ārya*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (181) states: "One delights in the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of abandonment and delights in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of cultivation.
Moreover, the former is the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the latter is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks: "Is the fourth [dhyāna] also..."
Question: Why are non-aversion (*adveṣa*) and so forth not taken as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) for the antidotes to afflictions such as aversion? Answer: In principle, it should indeed be so;
however, because the first three [antidotes] have non-greed (*alobha*) as their nature, the fourth likewise has non-greed as its nature, just like the preceding three.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 181, states: "Question: Since contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) both have non-greed as their nature, how is it that..."

It is sufficient to say that contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), whereas fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) is not. The answer is: contentment is established as a noble lineage because it is difficult to be free from greed regarding what is present;
fewness of desires is not so established because it is easy to be free from greed regarding robes and such that have not yet been obtained in the future. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

contentment is established because it does not involve seeking, whereas fewness of desires is not established because it involves further seeking. Moreover, since non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also possess fewness of desires, [the latter] would be confused with them; therefore, it is not [established].
Question: How is it that clothing and other requisites, when free from craving, possess the nature of being untainted (*anāsrava*)? Answer: The Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is untainted;
since clothing and other requisites are produced by taking non-craving as their condition, they too are untainted in accordance with the Noble Path they have induced.

Question: Why is medicine not mentioned as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*)? Answer: Because one does not give rise to craving for medicine, and furthermore, it is only after a patient has taken medicine that they eat [other food].
Not all people eat [these things], and because they are subsumed within the previous three categories, some are included among food, such as those suffering from indigestion eating kudzu powder;
some are included among bedding, such as those suffering from cold wearing a wooden board as bedding; and some are included among clothing, such as wrapping one's abdomen with tree bark.

Broadly speaking, there are eighty-four thousand types; specifically, there are the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastuka-vipaśyanā*), wherein those with excessive greed contemplate impurity.

Excessive anger, compassion, attachment to the eighteen *dhātus*, ignorance regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, and improper reflection on breath-counting meditation—these are the two types of "evil.
This is explained according to the method of proximate counteraction (*pratyupakṣa-dvāra*), wherein the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) remedies greed;

at a distance, it universally remedies afflictions such as anger. All other cases should be understood accordingly. If one were to apply specific remedies, there are four doors of counteraction; here, we rely upon [the former].

Because it treats all [objects] universally, it distinguishes the bone-joints (*asthi-saṃdhāna*). "Offering service" (*pūjā*) refers to bending, turning, bowing, and raising—meaning one offers service to others by means of one's own body.

There is a tradition held by some that this means others offer service to oneself; however, that the arising of greed regarding the subtle touch of the excellent forms and colors of others is not a correct contemplation (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), because one practices the meditation on the chain of bones (*asthi-śṛṅkhalā*) by settling the mind upon one's own body and so forth. Thus, we know that the four types of greed are categorized according to the self.

Regarding the arising [of the perception] upon the body, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "This person of dull faculties first contemplates external objects, such as the sounds of others, and only afterwards contemplates the internal body.
One of sharp faculties, however, first contemplates their own body, taking the skin as the outer boundary and the thirty-six internal constituents and so forth as the object.

The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) does not sever the afflictions because its objective condition (*ālambana*) is limited; it is like the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), which function in a similar manner.

One abandons afflictions by taking a specific stage (*bhūmi*) as the object. Furthermore, there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*): first, that of specific characteristics; second, that of common characteristics; and third, that of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

Among these, it is through the mental attention of common characteristics that one abandons afflictions. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 31, the Master of the Critical Evaluation (*viniścaya*) maintains that its essence is non-attachment (*alobha*).

It simultaneously encompasses the four aggregates or five aggregates, takes the form-aggregate of the desire realm as its object, and consists of the cultivation of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), rather than taking form itself as its name-object.
Question: These characters are of a virtuous nature; why are they called "impure" in terms of their mode of activity (*ākāra*)?

Furthermore, if this contemplation universally takes as its object [the realm of desire], how can it be said to be universal when Aniruddha did not contemplate the heavens as impure, and Śāriputra did not contemplate the Buddha as impure?

Answer: Those who surpass Aniruddha are able to contemplate the heavens as impure, and the Buddha was likewise able to do so. Thus, it is called "universal" because it encompasses the form-realm (*rūpadhātu*) of the desire realm.

The Buddha stated that it is impure; the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says that when first arising, it occurs among humans, and later, when cultivated to completion, it may arise even in the heavens and manifest there.
One tradition holds that both its initial arising and its final state occur only among humans. This treatise agrees with the former statement.

This [mental application] associated with resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) takes only its own temporal period as its object. Just as the five consciousnesses take objects without generating [supernormal] penetration, it does not universally take the three periods of time as its object. The *Vibhāṣā* states:

This is not acquired by birth, but is acquired through application (*prayoga*) and attained through detachment (*vairāgya*). Having attained detachment from the defilements of a lower stage, one subsequently acquires the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) of the higher stage only through application.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is acquired through application; for a Pratyekabuddha, it is acquired through intermediate application;

and for a Śrāvaka, it is acquired through either intermediate or superior application. As for the abandonment of the "near-attainment" (*sāmantaka*), this refers solely to the abandonment of sensation (*vedanā*), specifically the suffering of the Desire Realm.
Sorrow, joy, and pleasure arise respectively in the first two dhyānas; joy arises in the third dhyāna, and pleasure can give rise to vitarka and vicāra.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states that Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas can initiate these on their own, whereas Śrāvakas initiate them only upon instruction. Counting both the entering and exiting [of the meditative states] together, they total ten.

Regarding the mind following the breath: as the breath moves from the heart, it passes through the waist, thighs, calves, and down to the tips of the toes, extending for a fathom or whatever distance it reaches.

Since the breath is comprised within one part of the body, and the body is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the breath is thus subsumed under the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*) among those four.

It is only upon reaching the fifth stage, when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are complete, that there is breath. Breath functions in dependence upon the mind; where there is no mind, there is no breath.

If there were breath [in the absence of mind], then one whose body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has entered the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) should also have breath.

Furthermore, for one whose body resides in the desire realm or the first three dhyānas and enters the fourth dhyāna, because the entry into meditative absorption lacks the coarse mind that draws forth the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), [breath would not exist].
Question: Throughout the body there are no open pores. How is it that in the fourth dhyāna there is external wind, yet there is no inhalation or exhalation?
Answer: Although there is external wind in the fourth [dhyāna], because that [level] relies upon a body that does not accommodate it, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Upon entering the fourth contaminated dhyāna, one draws forth those firm and dense primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which pervade the entire body to produce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); thus it can be said that there are no hairs."

Question: When one enters that untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*), the unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the place of birth is neither solid nor dense;

how then can there be no opening of pores? Answer: Although the unmanifest form produced by the untainted [state] is comprised within the four great elements of the place of birth, it is extremely subtle and resembles them;
therefore, there is no fault. Question: Since there are no [pores] when one is born in the fourth dhyāna...
Regarding how speech is produced when the pores open: it is because they move that sound can also be emitted, just as a mechanism produces sound when opened.

As for the claim that there is a "roar" of hair upon the throat, some say this occurs during speech; others say that at the moment of speaking, the roar of hair momentarily opens and breaks [the obstruction].
Regarding the latter two views, if one has attained a body free from the roar of hair, how could speech be produced? It is simply by opening [the channels] that it occurs.
*Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā-gāthā-ṭīkā-artha-saṃgraha*, Part 5, Lower Section.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Huīhuī of Ximing Monastery in Jīngzhào.

● Treatise, Chapter Twenty-three: Particular Characteristics (Svalakṣaṇa) has two aspects: first, particular characteristics; second, common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) within particular characteristics. The arising of one cognition for each of the ten bases is called a cognition of particular characteristics;

the arising of one cognition [encompassing them all] is called a cognition of common characteristics. This extends even to the contemplation of each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) of form, which is itself a particular characteristic.

The same applies to blue and so forth, as well as to their mutual perception and so on; how then can one respond regarding the non-informative (*avijñapti*)? This teaching refers to obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and does not speak of the non-informative.
Its distinction from the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) within the five preliminary concentrations (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-vinodana*) is threefold:

first, they differ in essence—the former is non-greed (*alobha*), while this is wisdom (*prajñā*); second, they differ in their antidotes—the former counteracts greed, while this counteracts the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*); third, they differ in their modes of activity (*ākāra*).

Regarding the four objects of focus, they differ from the previous [case of the body] in that while the former concerns only form (*rūpa*), these pertain to both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*).
Among the four foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—the two categories of body and phenomena may not exist simultaneously with the mindfulness itself;

this is how the Vaibhāṣikas explain it, taking wisdom (*prajñā*) as the effect and mindfulness (*smṛti*) as the cause. The Master [Vasubandhu], however, takes wisdom as the cause and mindfulness as the effect.
This is the causal relationship of the stages (*avasthā*). Regarding the four factors (*dharma*), there are four propositions when each is taken as a distinct object;

this is called "non-mixed" observation. When two factors are combined as objects, there are three propositions; when three factors are combined as objects, there are two propositions; and when all four factors are combined as objects, there is one proposition—this is "mixed" observation.

In the fourfold cultivation of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), one observes each Truth (*satya*) until it is matured, at which point one changes the mode of observation. Each of the three stages—Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*)—possesses [these modes].

The three grades arise in successive order. If one has not yet seen the six paths of cultivation and severs the afflictions of the desire realm, then the wisdom of reflection induces the wisdom of cultivation.

If one has previously severed the afflictions of the desire realm, then the wisdom of cultivation induces "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and the subsequent stages. In the Mahāyāna, these stages of Heat and so forth are named "Luminous Virtue" (*prabhākari*) and "Increased Luminosity" (*arcismati*);

they correspond respectively to the "Preparatory" (*anuloma*) and "Immediate" (*ānantarya*) concentrations. In the stage of Heat, one contemplates the emptiness of the grasped object; in the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), it is...

Regarding the emptiness of the grasped, which accords with the emptiness of the grasper, there are three grades in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*): at the level of lower patience, one seals the emptiness of the grasped;
at the level of middle patience, one seals the emptiness of the grasper; and at the level of upper patience, one doubly seals both forms of emptiness.

"Like the crown of a person's head" means that among the body’s parts, the crown is the highest, most prominent, and the most excellent among the moving [faculties]; it is like a mountain peak because it stands at the point of advancing or retreating.

"Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to faith, for one faithfully accepts the Four Noble Truths. Although there is faith in the two preceding stages, because of the possibility of regression, this stage is uniquely named "Patience" due to its non-regression.
The "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is even more excellent than this, yet it is not called "Patience," because it belongs to the middle or upper [levels of the path].
Since the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) does not yet possess the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) or the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), how much less so the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?

Regarding the distinction between "selflessness" (*anātman*) and "not-self" (*anātmiya*): "selflessness" refers to the absence of feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates within form (*rūpa*); "not-self" refers to form itself not being the self or belonging to the self.
Because these sixteen aspects are mutually exclusive, they cannot arise simultaneously; rather, one practices each aspect individually while cultivating the others.

Regarding the statement that "the aspects (ākāra) are all acquired through cultivation and do not diminish when the eight truths are being taken as objects," it refers to the fact that even those aspects diminished under the eight truths arise as "previously acquired" (pūrvaprāpta).
As for the correspondence between the four aspects of the desire-realm suffering (duḥkha) and their respective names in sequential order, this was the view of the master Guṇaprabha.
In the Sanskrit language, he is called Guṇaprabha; he was a person from the country of Mathurā in Central India.

He was a learned sage of the West who composed over a hundred treatises in his own land. Like those who have entered the path of vision through the contemplation of impermanence, he [attained] the eightfold realization regarding the truth of suffering as non-self in the desire realm and the higher realms, the truth of origin as inferior, the truth of cessation as inferior, and the truth of the path as inferior, leading to liberation.

Because they are modes of activity (*ākāra*), they are designated as "provisional" (*nīyānika*) and "corresponding" (*pratirūpa*). They are bound to the first cycle: [the contemplation of] suffering, the origin, cessation, and the noble path;

[the contemplation of] the lower realm, emptiness, arising, and passing away; and [the contemplation of] the subtle and the path—these are the eight modes of activity. The second cycle consists of the reduction of the following eight modes of activity: [the contemplation of] suffering, the origin, cessation, and the noble path;

[the contemplation of] the lower realm, emptiness, arising, and passing away; and [the contemplation of] the subtle and the path. The third cycle consists of the reduction of the remaining eight modes of activity.
If the aspects (*ākāra*) are not reduced, then three cycles are reduced; as for the remaining eight aspects that enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this follows what was stated previously.
These two preceding explanations both interpret the *Mahāvibhāṣā* text: sixteen and twelve, eight and four aspects.

The sixteen aspects are explained in reference to the time when the path has not yet been reduced; the twelve are explained in reference to the time when the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) has been reduced. Guṇaprabha [explains] according to the second...
One cycle omits eight aspects; the explanation of the remainder follows this principle. Master Guāng takes the latter explanation, while Master Bǎo takes the former.
[The author] refutes Master Déguāng, who says that according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, one observes the seven points of excellence (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*):

observing form as suffering, form as the origin of suffering, form as the cessation of suffering, form as the path leading to cessation, form as gratification, form as a calamity, and form as renunciation. Since [this is already established], it is not mentioned again.

Because one contemplates the Path (*mārga*), one knows that from the subsequent stage onward, one eliminates the three aspects (*ākāra*) below the Path and does not contemplate them when taking the Truth of the Path as an object.

Furthermore, for those in whom the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) increases, how is it that they retain the aspect of impermanence (*anitya*) upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the other aspects—such as dispassion (*virāga*) and emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*)—are eliminated simultaneously with the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) under the Truth of Suffering? Question: Why is the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) called "supreme"?

Is it supreme in its entirety, or is it supreme in part? If it were supreme in its entirety, how could it surpass conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), since it is merely an attendant of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?

If it were supreme in part, then the first three stages—Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth—are also supreme in part; thus, they too should be called "Supreme Worldly Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*). Answer:

This dharma is supreme in its entirety among all contaminated (*sāsrava*) states, for it is capable of opening the gateway to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), whereas conventional knowledge lacks this capacity. Therefore, it alone is not [merely] so-called.
The "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is also conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), for it is only by means of this Supreme Mundane Dharma that [supramundane knowledge] can arise.

Question: The present Supreme Mundane Dharma is able to induce the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) and is thus called "superior. However, the future [Supreme Mundane Dharma] lacks the power to induce the Noble Path;

should it not therefore be considered the "Supreme"? Answer: That which accords with what has already arisen in the future is also termed the "Supreme Mundane Dharma. Question: [Regarding] those that arise simultaneously...

Question: Since the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of matter do not function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), should they not likewise not be called "supreme" (*agradharma*)?

Answer: Because they share the same fruit—namely, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—they may also be designated as "supreme. Question: How does the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) act as a strong equal-and-immediate condition for the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)?
Answer: Because it possesses the four virtues, because it belongs to the same category (*nikāya*), and because it is identical to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
1) Because they are of the highest grade (*uttama-prakāra*); 2) because they are produced from two immeasurable wholesome dharmas; 3) because their duration is equal to sixty *kalpas*;

and 4) because their nature and characteristics are identical—since their nature is identical, they take wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential characteristic, just as the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) takes the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha-ākāra*), so too does the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

Furthermore, this is because it extensively cultivates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) for the sake of this "dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*).
Question: How can the fruits of śrāmaṇya (śrāmaṇyaphala) be taken as their own essence (*svabhāva*), whereas the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) cannot? Answer:

The fruits of śrāmaṇya are established as an essence based on the state of accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*). These four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are not established as an essence based on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), because their sequence is not fixed.
This is unlike the [attainment of] birth, etc., or the morality associated with meditative concentration (*samādhisamvara*), which do have fixed sequences.

If [the fruit] were to constitute the essence of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth because they share the same result, then since the factors superior to Heat and the others would always remain in the body after [attaining the fruit], Heat and the others should arise constantly.
Once the fruit has been attained, how could the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) still be established?
The three paths are called "definitive discernment" (*nirvedha*). These four [stages] are the causes that accord with them, while the three paths are the results that they accord with;

because they accord with definitive discernment, they are explained as *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds, and thus "conducive to definitive discernment" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) refers to the stages (*bhāga*).

Because the inhabitants of Uttarakuru and the form-realm heavens possess superior physical bases and feel aversion toward their own realms, they do not have these stages; therefore, they exist only among humans and devas—making nine types in total.
Because abiding in this body possesses two meanings, one is able to give rise to the roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat).

Regarding the fourth root of goodness, when it first arises for those born in the heavens, this refers to having cultivated the first three [roots] while among humans, then passing away to be reborn in the heavens, whereupon one again gives rise to *uṣmagata* and so forth, eventually giving rise to the *laukikāgradharma* (the supreme mundane dharma). It is not possible for the first three [roots] to arise for the first time within the six heavens.

Because the superior basis (āśraya) possesses a mind of revulsion toward its own realm, the four roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) can all first arise among human beings, as they fulfill both conditions.

Regarding women, two [roots] can be attained; because during the stages of the first three roots of goodness there is ample time for the transformation of the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti), as in the case of a woman attaining the female roots of goodness.
The male roots of goodness are acquired and perfected within the body and are also manifest; the female roots of goodness are acquired but not perfected within the body, nor are they manifest.
Regarding the male body, two cases apply as explained above for the fourth [category]. As for the female, two cases apply:

because the female realm can be transformed into a superior body, the male has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female body at the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and above; therefore, the male does not [attain it].
Regarding the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) of women and men: both obtain two [roots] just as one obtains the Prātimokṣa vows, each being capable of arising separately.

As for "losing the stage" (*bhūmi-hāni*) and "abandoning" (*tyāga*): if, based on the first dhyāna, one generates the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, and then dies to be reborn in the second dhyāna, this is called "losing the stage.

However, if one is reborn in the first dhyāna, it is not called "losing the stage"; therefore, one does not abandon the Heat and the other stages. These four are contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*).

Fulfilling karma (*pūrṇakarma*) cannot act as a projecting cause (*ākṣepaka*), because it involves aversion toward existence (*bhava*). Furthermore, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) to support those roots of virtue such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*);

therefore, they relinquish them at the end of life. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that those who give rise to "Heat" and the other stages based on the fundamental dhyāna grounds (*maulabhūmi*) are those who, having previously exhausted their afflictions during the stage of an ordinary being, subsequently give rise to "Heat" and so forth; this is because in the fundamental grounds, calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are balanced.
Regarding the statement that one attains entry into the noble state (*ārya*) in the present life and will certainly reach *nirvāṇa*— as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 6—

one who has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and subsequently gives rise to the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages in the preparatory (*anāgamya*) or intermediate (*dhyānāntara*) concentrations does so because their serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) were previously unbalanced and unstable. For those who enter the noble sequence and attain the fruits of the path,
they necessarily rely upon the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) to enter the path of seeing.

Having relinquished [the precepts], to obtain them again is not the same as what was previously relinquished; it is like the Pratimokṣa vows, where obtaining them again after having relinquished them is not the same as what was previously relinquished.
Regarding those who have understood the stages, that is, for those who understand the sequence of the five stages of cultivation, one explains the cultivation of the *uṣmagata* (heat) stage next.
The cultivation of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) and the arising of "patience" (*kṣānti*) from the summit follow this same principle.
Regarding those born from eggs or moisture, because they encounter much delusion, once they have attained the state of an Arya, they do not undergo rebirth;

however, it is also permitted that before attaining the state of an Arya, they may still undergo such rebirth, as in the case of Śaila and others. Furthermore, regarding the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), it is certain that they lead to Nirvana.

What is the distinction between *uṣmagata* (Heat) and the subsequent stages? The answer is that the former is subsumed under "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), while the latter is subsumed under "definitive discernment" (*nirvedha*).

The former is subsumed under "wholesome states of distraction" (*vikṣiptakuśala*), while the latter is subsumed under "wholesome states of meditative concentration" (*samāhitakuśala*). The former seven stages of the aids to penetration (*saptāṅga-prayoga*) do not include the latter, which is instead subsumed under "preparatory application" (*prayoga*).

The latter cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), whereas the former does not possess these sixteen aspects; this wisdom constitutes their essence. These distinctions between the former and the latter as distracted wholesome states comprise five points in total.
1. They will certainly attain nirvāṇa; 2. they do not sever the roots of goodness; 3. they do not commit the heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); 4. they do not follow the evil destinies (*durgati*);

5. they do not fall back from the stage of *ūṣmagata*. The first four apply to the stage of *mūrdhan*; the first two apply to the stage of *kṣānti*; and those at the stage of *laukikāgradharma* possess all five.

This is because the Unconscious Ones (*asaṃjñisattva*), the Great Brahmās (who are a locus of false views), the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, and those with the bodies of the *andha* and *jaḍa* lack the sharp faculties and the afflictions required for the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

Regarding the "eighth existence" and so forth: according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts, this refers to one who has acquired the karma for one birth in a single location among the sixteen heavens of the form realm.
Having experienced one birth in that location, they will not experience a second; regarding that second birth, they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the karma for an eighth birth in the desire realm and the karma for a second birth in the form realm are obstructed upon attaining the superior grade of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
First, while acting as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in the present, it draws forth the arising of the "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

At the stage of the "Supreme Worldly Dharmas" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*). If this is so, then an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would be a noble one (*ārya*), because at the time when the Supreme Worldly Dharmas are present, there is the attainment of the path of seeing.
Answer: It is only when the patience regarding the Dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is in the state of its characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) that [the attainment] exists.

If one has attained [the stages] while still in the body but has not yet completed them, one is not called a noble one (*ārya*). Among the Śrāvakas, those at the lower level; among the Pratyekabuddhas, those at the middle level; and among the Buddhas, those at the upper level.

It is permitted for one who has completed the cultivation of Śrāvaka-patience (*kṣānti*) to transform into a *vargacārin* Pratyekabuddha, but it is not permitted to transform into a Buddha, Bodhisattva, or one who proceeds toward evil destinies due to the cultivation of causes.
Regarding the *vargacārin* Pratyekabuddhas, it is permitted that they may transform into Buddhas from the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, just as with the Śrāvakas.

Regarding "one sitting," this further explains why the Buddha and the rhinoceros-horn-like [pratyekabuddha] do not regress from the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Some say it is because they cultivate [the path] starting from the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

As for the similarities and differences in the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) among the three vehicles: the causes of the first two vehicles consist of (1) shared revulsion and (2) the cause of seeking the great meaning of tranquility (*śama*).

Furthermore, there are differences: first, regarding the duration of practice and the speed of realizing the fruit—the Śrāvaka requires three births and sixty *kalpas*, the Pratyekabuddha four births and one hundred *kalpas*, and the Buddha three incalculable *kalpas*.

Second, regarding the thickness of merit and the quality of the body—the Śrāvaka is without marks (*animitta*), while the Pratyekabuddha may possess thirty-one marks, etc., and the Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks. Third...
1. The sharpness or dullness of the faculties and the depth or shallowness of entry into the Dharma correspond to the simile of the three animals crossing a river. 2.

The thickness or thinness of the four types of compassion and the differences in their departure and abiding correspond to the simile of the three animals being surrounded. 3. Regarding the five matters, the benefits for body and speech differ;

the Pratyekabuddha’s bodily karma consists of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), whereas the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva employ both bodily and vocal karma in transformation. 4. Regarding the attainment of the Path, it concerns the time of attainment.
Regarding the attainment of awakening: Śrāvakas depend on both time and instruction; Pratyekabuddhas depend on time but not on instruction; Buddhas are likewise [independent of both].

Regarding the abandonment of obstacles and the timing of the realization of the end of birth and death (*saṃsāra*): there is a difference in the objects of observation compared to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Śrāvakas abandon one obstacle, namely a portion of *bhavasaṃsāra*; Bodhisattvas abandon both obstacles. Śrāvakas realize the fruit within the four postures while observing the Four Noble Truths; Pratyekabuddhas observe the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

Based on the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the ten thousand practices, both [the first and last] fruits are attained while seated; eight [fruits] depend on the path and the body meeting a Buddha; they differ according to the stage [of attainment]:

the Pratyekabuddha attains the fruit through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), while the Śrāvaka attains the first and last fruits through the untainted path and the intermediate two fruits through a path that is both tainted and untainted (*sāsrava-anāsrava-mārga*);

the Buddha attains them solely through this [untainted] path. Regarding the physical basis, the Pratyekabuddha attains it in all three continents, whereas the Śrāvaka attains it only with a body in this continent (Jambudvīpa).

Those who attain the first two fruits throughout the three realms rely on the *anāgamya* stage; those who realize the third fruit may rely on up to the sixth stage; and those who realize the fourth fruit may rely on all nine stages.
As for the *vargacārin* pratyekabuddhas, they rely on all nine stages. When realizing the state of a *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* pratyekabuddha or a Buddha, they rely on the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding the *vargacārin*, they are common to both śrāvakas and [pratyekabuddhas]; as for the *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* and the Buddha, they are not common to śrāvakas. Furthermore, regarding the *vargacārin*, there are those who see the Buddha and those who do not see the Buddha; the *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* and the Buddha do not see [the Buddha].

The Buddha’s nine applications of mind differ in their extent; the rhinoceros-horn-like [pratyekabuddha] has thirty-four moments of mind; the group-practicing pratyekabuddha has one hundred and sixty moments of mind;
and the śrāvaka who lacks awakening has eighteen moments of mind. Regarding the first fruit (srotāpanna), there are sixteen moments of mindfulness;

for the middle two fruits, there is one path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Liberation is the fruition; as it accords with the cause, it is called "conformable liberation" (*anuloma-vimukti*).

Regarding the *mokṣabhāgīya* (factors conducive to liberation), according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that both men and women may cultivate and attain them whether they encounter a Buddha or not.

If one attains them in three lifetimes—as previously explained regarding the arising of the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) from the root—how can it be said that one enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*) in the present life?

There are three cases where one attains [the roots of merit] in two lifetimes. To answer: if one gives rise to *ūṣmagata* and so forth in the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) in this life, it is because one must have previously given rise to *ūṣmagata* and so forth in the preparatory stage (*sāmantakabhūmi*) in a prior life; therefore, it is said that they are attained in three lifetimes. Question:

Between those who attain them in three lifetimes over sixty kalpas and those who attain them in four lifetimes over one hundred kalpas, which are dull-witted and which are sharp-witted? Answer: Both categories include both the dull-witted and the sharp-witted; the difference lies only in the duration of time.

This is due to the superiority or inferiority of the mind of renunciation; thus, there are times when [the duration] is long or short. If three lifetimes are required, this is for those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*); at that time, it is longest, whereas for those of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*), it should be longer. Question: Regarding the Pratyekabuddha who first abandons the afflictions of the eight lower stages up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and having exhausted them, attains the fruit in the second lifetime by entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the fourth dhyāna—how can one reconcile this with the treatise stating that it takes four lifetimes? Answer: [The treatise refers to the case of] one who, having previously abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna, and then, in the second lifetime, abandons the remaining afflictions of the higher realms and enters the path of seeing based on the fourth dhyāna. Alternatively, it may refer to a case where one has already abandoned the afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and, in the third lifetime, abandons the afflictions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and attains the fruit. Or, it may refer to one who, having previously abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, and then, in the second lifetime, abandons the afflictions of the higher realms and enters the path of seeing based on the fourth dhyāna; this is what is meant by "four lifetimes. In the "Chapter on Previous Lives," one account states that *pratyekabuddhas* are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while another account states they are those who have attained the first three fruits [of the path].
According to the preceding text, since even those who have attained "Patience" (*kṣānti*) are not subject to regression, how much less so those who have attained the first three fruits?

Furthermore, the general statement that the fruit of a *śrāvaka* or a *pratyekabuddha* is attained through a total of three or four lifetimes cannot be definitively assigned [to specific stages]. Question 6.
Regarding the question of what kalpa-measure is taken when referring to ten or a hundred kalpas: according to the standard, for a Bodhisattva, one takes three incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;

for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), one likewise takes the number of *kalpas* ending in the *kalpa* of destruction by fire (*tejaḥ-saṃvarta-kalpa*). This amounts to sixty *kalpas* and so forth. If one were to take the *kalpas* of increase and decrease (*vivarta-saṃvarta-kalpa*), it would be as follows:

suppose there is a person today who plants the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); subsequently, during the ninth *kalpa* within the period of formation and emptiness (*vivarta-śūnya-kalpa*) following the *kalpa* of destruction, [he attains realization].
For sixty kalpas, there were no sentient beings in the three continents or the six heavens; where could they have attained the fruits [of the path]?
Based on this, one should understand that the number of fire-disaster kalpas (kalpas of destruction by fire) amounts to sixty kalpas and so forth.
Regarding the mention of the subsequent "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), this refers to the subsequent knowledge (*jñāna*) being the outflow fruit of the patience (*kṣānti*).

By mentioning patience first and then knowledge, and subsequently mentioning knowledge first and then patience, the former mentions the fruit of knowledge to reveal that patience is its cause, which is untainted (*anāsrava*). This distinguishes it from the patience within the seven stages of preparation (*saptaprayoga*).

The term "patience" refers to faith; having previously, since beginningless time, clung to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as self and what belongs to the self (*ātman-ātmīya*), one now attains [this state].

Untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) knows the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as being without self or what belongs to a self; the conviction that there is only the principle of suffering is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).

Because the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) is situated below, is coarse, is the fruit of suffering, and is a distracted stage (*vyavakīrṇa-bhūmi*), one first contemplates it. One subsequently contemplates the sufferings of the two upper realms together, because they are equal in being stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*).

Regarding this, the third volume of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents three explanations. The first states: "The Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) [arises] in the [Desire Realm]..."
In future lives, one can eliminate the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*); in the present, the attainment that severs delusions is like a lamp dispelling darkness;

and in the present, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) destroys darkness and burns the wick. Because its power obstructs that nature of an ordinary being from arising, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that three dharmas in the future possess functional efficacy:

first, light; second, the characteristic of arising; and third, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). Some say this refers to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukika-agra-dharma*).

The ability to abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), although it is itself contaminated (*sāsrava*), is like riding and controlling a tamed elephant; alternatively, it may be abandoned by both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation].

Just as the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) perishes simultaneously with the birth of the nature of an ordinary person during the Path of Non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), so too does the Forbearance regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) arise simultaneously with the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the nature of an ordinary person during the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). This treatise explains it in this same way. This refers to the Path of Non-interruption.

Although it coexists with the acquisition of defilements (*kleśaprāpti*), the acquisition of defilements lacks the power to draw forth a subsequent acquisition of defilements to the state of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).

When the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is in the state of arising, it is not obstructed by the acquisition of defilements belonging to its own category; this is called "correct liberation" (*samyag-vimukti*). Upon reaching the present moment, it is called "already liberated" (*vimukta*).
Regarding the Mahāsāṃghikas' view that one contemplates all four truths simultaneously when seeing a single truth—such as when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)—this...
