Knowing the cause of suffering is called the abandonment of the origin (*samudaya-satya*); realizing the cessation of suffering is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and cultivating the path for the cessation of suffering is the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*).
Thus, under the truth of suffering, all four tasks are present; for each of the other three truths, there is only one task—namely, abandonment, realization, and cultivation. The critique states:
"If one sees the four truths at the very moment of seeing suffering, then one should see them simultaneously and be designated as having attained the first fruit [of stream-entry] and so forth."
Since this is not permitted, we know it is incorrect.

For example, for one who has cultivated the vision [of the truths], the sixteenth moment of mind is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Just as in that case, because one subsequently cultivates the path after having already seen the truths (*satya*), it is subsumed under the path of cultivation.
The meaning of the objection is as follows: The "Path-type Patience" (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) of the fifteenth moment is the principle of the Truth of the Path;

it is only upon reaching the sixteenth moment that one truly perceives the "Path-type Knowledge" (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*). Since the sixteenth moment perceives even the fifteenth moment—which was previously unperceived—how can the sixteenth moment be categorized as belonging to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)?
In response, it is said: with respect to the Truths, the sixteenth moment is indeed the "Known" (*ājñāta*) regarding the eight [factors].

The principle of the truths is not established by the fifteenth mind-moment; because it has not yet been fully known, it is subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and furthermore, because it is subsumed under the resultant path (*phala-mārga*), it is like the other paths of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). If this were so, one should experience retrogression just as in the other paths of cultivation. Answer:

Because one possesses the unconditioned attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*) that sustains the path of seeing, there is no retrogression. If this were so, then one who abides in the possession of the unconditioned attainment that sustains the path of seeing should also be seen [to retrogress].

The Sautrāntika master [Saṃghabhadra] replies that there is a great fault in this: if the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth were all subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), how could they all be considered acquisitions of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-prāpti*)?
Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntikas, the sixteenth moment of mind is subsumed under the path of seeing; their inference (*anumāna*) is as follows:

because it is subsumed under wisdom (*jñāna*), it is like the other [moments] of the path of cultivation consisting of the seven knowledges (*sapta-jñāna*). The Vaibhāṣikas argue that these are causes for the path of cultivation, saying: because they are subsumed under the resultant path (*phalamārga*), they are like the others.

This refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It is difficult to designate the latter three candidates (*pratipannaka*) as such, because the first six persons have not yet eliminated those bound by all fetters; the next three persons have not yet eliminated the six grades [of afflictions];
and the final sixty-four persons have not yet eliminated the ninth grade of affliction in the desire realm. One person [the Arhat] has eliminated it.

Regarding the statement that those in the latter seven stages are not "possessors of all fetters" (sakalabandhana): one who has abandoned the defilements of a lower stage is precisely a "possessor of all fetters" of the higher stage.

Among the root afflictions, there are inferior, medium, and superior grades, which are designated as the three categories; inferior greed directed toward a medium object is termed "lower-part" (avarabhāgīya).
The establishment of the nine grades is based on the distinctions arising from the three types of objects—superior, intermediate, and inferior.

When inferior greed arises directed toward a superior object, it is designated as the lowest-of-the-low grade; when inferior greed arises directed toward an intermediate object, it is designated as the middle-of-the-low grade;

and when inferior greed arises directed toward an inferior object, it is designated as the highest-of-the-low grade. As for greed of the middle grade, when it arises toward a superior object, it is designated as the lowest-of-the-middle grade. If...

Among these, when arising with respect to a medium object, it is called the medium-medium grade; when arising with respect to an inferior object, it is called the medium-superior grade. When superior greed arises with respect to a superior object, it is called the lower-inferior grade;
when arising with respect to a medium object, it is called the middle-inferior grade; and when arising with respect to an inferior object, it is called the upper-superior grade.
Having abandoned the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), one realizes that there are nine grades of cultivated delusions (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm;

because these collectively moisten seven births, when considering the maximum number of lives, one undergoes seven births. However, those who attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa* (Arhatship) after only one or two births will be explained in a later section.

Upon reaching the seventh birth, when all cultivated delusions of the three realms have been completely abandoned, one immediately attains the fruit of *aśaikṣa*. Question: Does a *parinirvāyin-anāgāmin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa after passing through all states) undergo ten more births?

Question: How is it that regarding the six births, it is stated only that one attains the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*) within seven births? Answer: According to the treatise below, a noble one (*ārya*) must necessarily undergo birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
they do not go to take birth in other realms. Furthermore, the preceding text mentions "the eighth existence" (*aṣṭama-bhava*) and so forth;

this collectively refers to those who, having taken one or two births in a single location of the form or formless realms, will not undergo an eighth existence. Thus, these belong to the category of "seven births," specifically referring to a single location in the form realm.
One who has exhausted the karma of a single lifetime is an *anāgāmin* (non-returner);

therefore, it is known that one who is bound to seven more births cannot take rebirth in the two higher realms, and those who take rebirth in the two higher realms cannot take rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). These two classes are distinct:

having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one who exhausts the afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation attains the third fruit (*arhat*) and is born in the first dhyāna and so forth; this constitutes sixteen births.
This is by way of analogy.
For instance, as for the "seven-step snake," its venomous power does not extend beyond seven steps; likewise, the power of the four great elements does not diminish after seven steps.
As for the malaria that recurs on the fourth day, it is certain to manifest every other day.

Regarding the phrase "because one does not produce karma leading to decline and falling": a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) does not create karma for the three miserable realms (*apāya*).
If they had previously possessed determinate karma for the three miserable realms, they would not even attain the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), let alone attain the first fruit.

Question: In the twenty-fourth verse of the root treatise, it is stated that the abandonment of three or four categories of defilements subsumes three or two births. Why, then, are three and two births mentioned separately? Answer:

Just as among those in the first fruit (srotāpanna), although sixteen classes of birth are abandoned, there are still those who undergo many births, such as the "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner. Thus, even when three or four categories are abandoned, one may still experience multiple births; therefore, the specific mention of three and two births is made to distinguish these cases.
One who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life after one birth abandons three or four categories of defilements; because [the timing] is not fixed, three or two births are mentioned separately.

If one in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) abandons six categories of defilements and enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga), they will not give rise to the repeated application of the path and shall not attain the untainted (anāsrava).
One who lacks the three conditions for the faculties is called a candidate for the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin-patipanna), but not a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* maintains that upon severing each of the nine grades of afflictions of the realm of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), one attains emergence from meditative absorption; this is because the first path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) does not attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of a third birth.

Furthermore, the third [grade] cannot attain the fourth [fruit]. If it were admitted that upon severing the fifth grade one should immediately attain the sixth, [it would contradict the established sequence].
This is because they give rise to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This commentary explains that the nine grades [of defilements] moisten seven births;

this specific allocation of the number of grades is the interpretation of Master Daoping. According to Master Baoliang, however, it is not yet the case that the ninth grade is severed, as they collectively moisten seven births.
Thus, from the highest-of-the-high grade having the power to moisten seven births, down to the lowest-of-the-low grade having the power to moisten seven births. If...

When the previous category [of fetters] is severed, the subsequent category alone moistens seven births; even those who do not complete seven births are still subsumed within the category of "seven births.

If that is so, then those who do not complete seven births would be subsumed under the category of "seven births," and those who do not complete three births would likewise be subsumed under the category of "three births" (kulaṃkula).

Answer: The category of "seven births" does not require the presence of all conditions; whether they are fulfilled or unfulfilled, all are subsumed within the category of "seven births. However, the category of "three births" (kulaṃkula) must possess three specific conditions.
It must be that one possesses three or two births to be included among the *kulaṃkula* (those who go from family to family). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"After attaining the state of an ārya, one never creates projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), though it is admitted that one may create completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 53, presents two views: one view is the same as above—that one does not create projecting karma;

the other view admits that one may create it, as in the case of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens. Since it is asked what karma produces birth there, we know that one must create the former [projecting karma].

The Master [Sthiramati] explains: Since these are the requisites for both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentrations, one does not even create karma conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
how much less could one attain the Path of Seeing? How then could there be the creation of karma? Even the "seven births" of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) involve past karma and afflictions.

When a Noble One (*ārya*) abandons afflictions through the tainted path, they achieve partial detachment from defilement; it is permitted that at the end of life, they are sustained by untainted concentration. This applies to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as well.

There is no principle of death while remaining separated from defilement, because the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) is not firm; thus, one regresses immediately upon emerging from meditative absorption.

If a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) makes a vow to enter absorption and sever the six grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they emerge only after having done so, thereby attaining non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding those six grades.
If they were to emerge prematurely, they would only attain [the cessation] of the sixth grade at the stage of the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Question: When one gives rise to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding this [sixth category], since the five must necessarily be abandoned when the sixth is abandoned, why is it that at the time of abandoning the fifth grade, one does not simultaneously give rise to non-analytical cessation regarding the six?
Answer: At the time of abandoning the five, one necessarily abandons the six, because there is the possibility of falling back from the second fruit;

therefore, one has not yet attained non-analytical cessation regarding the six. According to the Commentary (*Śāstra*), when one abandons the uppermost grade of the intermediate [category], that is the fifth grade.

If one abandons the upper two grades [of defilements] in each family, one becomes a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family). If one abandons five grades, one becomes a *ekajātipratibaddha* (one bound to one more birth).
Why is there no such thing as a *kulaṃkula* who abandons six grades? Answer: Because the middle and upper grades are designated as three grades, yet they are identical in being both upper and middle;

therefore, they must necessarily be abandoned together as six grades. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are seven types of gods and seven types of humans, down to one type of god and so forth, who experience seven [rebirths].

Regarding birth, it is based on being born among humans and attaining the Way while among humans, then entering *parinirvāṇa* there; this explains the previous text’s “four sevens” or twenty-eight births, which this treatise shares with the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Regarding the heavens, three [births] and for humans, two; and for the heavens, three and for humans, two—this explains the severing of the three grades of desire in three births, known as the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*).
Regarding the heavens, two and for humans, one; and for the heavens, one—this explains the severing of the four grades [of desire] in two births.
"House-to-house" (*kula-kula*) here refers to the differences in the locations where one attains the fruits and enters *parinirvāṇa*. "Perfect stillness" (*yuanji*) is *nirvāṇa*.

Those who have attained the three fruits and four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) attain *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*, but do not yet attain the other two types of *nirvāṇa*. Upon reaching the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they realize the eighty-nine categories of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as the essence of the two types of *nirvāṇa*.

While the body and wisdom remain manifest, there is the *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); when the body and wisdom cease, there is the *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

This demonstrates that one attains the first fruit without remainder; having realized it, one then abandons three grades [of defilements] and undergoes three more births, or abandons four grades and undergoes two more births.
The previous treatise’s statement of "seven births" refers to the maximum number; if speaking of the minimum, one attains the fruit of Arhatship in the present life.
One should reflect according to reason upon the intermediate variations in number. Previously, while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one had abandoned three or four grades.

Furthermore, those who have abandoned seven or eight grades of afflictions and enter the path of seeing, up until the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), are not designated as "one who goes from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*) or "one with one interval" (*ekavicika*),
because they lack the necessary faculties.
As for those who go once to the heavens and return once to the human realm, this refers to those who, among humans, have attained the second fruit and possess the three lower [faculties].

The defilements of this stage jointly moisten [the seeds] for one lifetime each among humans and devas; having gone to the heavens to undergo one lifetime, they return to the human realm and enter nirvana.
This is explained according to the principle that having attained the fruit in the heavens, they return to the human realm.

In the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one who has abandoned the nine grades of afflictions but lacks the roots and conditions [for the path] is not called a "One-Interval" (*ekavīcika*). Furthermore, if one has attained *srotāpanna* or *anāgāmin*, and lacks the [remaining] births and numbers [of rebirths], they are likewise not called a "One-Interval.

Regarding the phrase "transcending the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the ninth grade of affliction": the ninth grade is the outflow-result of the preceding eight grades; it is by abandoning this that one transcends it.

The exhaustion of the afflictions of this ninth category is called "transcending. Question: Why is it that there is no *antarāparinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state) for one dying in the desire realm and receiving a *gandharva* (intermediate existence) in the form realm, nor for one dying in the first dhyāna and being reborn in the second dhyāna, and so forth? Answer:

Because the mind of revulsion toward the suffering of the womb-birth in the desire realm is superior, there is an *antarāparinirvāyin* within the intermediate existence of the form realm; however, this is not the case for the form realm [itself] or for those above it.
Because they are contradictory, there is no *antarāparinirvāyin* among the [other] two fruits. Why is it that these two fruits do not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: The intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) is weak; the unwholesome afflictions of the desire realm are difficult to sever, and the noble path (*āryamārga*) does not exist in its own level.

Since one cannot even transcend the desire realm while in the state of abiding [in the womb], how much less so while in the intermediate state? The preceding text cited that the intermediate state is incapable of severing [the afflictions].
Unwholesome afflictions arise according to the stage (*bhūmi*) in which they are produced; the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) of that stage arises, while that of other stages does not.
According to the Sautrāntikas, those who previously lacked practice but subsequently engage in it possess a path of rapid accumulation that does not depend on effort;

this explains why "non-practice" was mentioned first. Because there is no path of rapid progress [for them], and because practice involving effort constitutes "practice," "practice" is mentioned later.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Regarding 'with effort' (*sābhisamskāra*) and 'without effort' (*anabhisamskāra*), both are taught in the sūtras according to their sequence.

Because the state 'with effort' is more venerable, it is taught first, and 'without effort' is taught later. Furthermore, both "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) with effort and without effort are explained in reference to *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), not in reference to *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). This is because in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one lacks mastery over the relinquishing of life.
This is because the necessary conditions are fulfilled.

Furthermore, regarding the term "flowing" (*srotas*), there are two meanings for its movement: first, the movement toward the fruits of the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the bliss of wisdom (*prajñā*, resulting in rebirth in the realms of form and formlessness);

second, the distinction between those who fall back from the three higher concentrations and are born in the Brahmakāyika heaven—such as those who achieve the "complete leaping-over" (*aśaikṣa-samāpatti*) and the other three types—and those who fall back from the two higher concentrations.

Regarding those born in the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābhā*) who fall away and are reborn in the fourth dhyāna, those born in the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubhā*), and those born in the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhrakāḥ*), all are able to perform the three types of leaping, such as the "complete leaper" (*atyantapluta*). Regarding this, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (174) states:

one view holds that they cannot, because the three types of leaping—such as the complete leaper—are established based on sixteen heavens, and the higher levels are incomplete; another view holds that they can perform the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*).

It is said that all three types are attained. Question: Regarding the attainment of birth in the realm of infinite space within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) while practicing "leap-over" (*atyantābhinirhāra*) and the other two methods, can one also attain the three types?

Answer: One may indeed attain all three types. Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may possess upward movement, they are not called "upward-streamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) because they return to lower births.

Although the three types of persons, such as those who "leap over" (*pluta*), attain *nirvāṇa* in the lower stages, this does not preclude the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) from being their ultimate destinations.
Furthermore, regarding the karma for leaping over and the three types of karma for subsequent rebirth, these are explained according to the principle of determinate (*niyata*) karma;

in reality, they also create indeterminate (*aniyata*) karma. Question: If a noble one (*ārya*) of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) creates [karma] for the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), [how is this so?]

When one’s life ends through karma, one is immediately reborn; this is called "birth-karma. How can it be called "subsequent"? In response, it is explained that while this refers to birth-karma, in reality one also creates birth-karma during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

This statement regarding the creation of karma concerns the creation of karma during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not the creation of karma after having attained the state of an Arya.

Regarding the division of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) into three types based solely on their afflictions (*kleśa*) and faculties (*indriya*): the division into three categories of afflictions consists of the lower-lower, the lower-middle, and the lower-upper;

the division into three categories of faculties consists of the upper-upper, the upper-middle, and the upper-lower. Thus, by way of these afflictions and faculties, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are established as three types.
The three grades of defilements for those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth are: medium-low, medium-medium, and medium-high. The three divisions by way of faculties are:
high-medium, medium-medium, and low-medium. Thus, through the distinctions of defilements and faculties, the attainment of parinirvāṇa upon rebirth is divided into three types.

The upward-streaming [attainment] is divided into three types. Those distinguished by the three grades of afflictions, faculties, and karma correspond respectively to the three types: the "complete leaper" (*skanda-gāmin*) and so forth.
Those distinguished by the three grades of faculties—lower-lower, lower-middle, and lower-upper—are, in turn, the lower-lower, lower-middle, and lower-upper [types].
The division of karma into three grades refers to the variation in the number of rebirths in the "complete leap" (*pluta*) and other modes of birth.
This is explained in the commentary on the lower section regarding the "complete leap" karma. Because they perform only wholesome deeds, they are called "paths of the virtuous" (*satpuruṣagati*).

Regarding the first two fruits [of stream-enterer and once-returner], although they have wives and households, those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), despite performing only wholesome deeds, are not "paths of the virtuous" because they lack further progression toward higher goals. Furthermore, the preceding...

The two fruits [of Once-returner and Non-returner] involve rebirth either higher or lower; however, these seven [types of Non-returner] are established as such only because they proceed solely toward higher rebirth.
Furthermore, the term "one-interval" (*ekavicika*) is not applied to those among humans who have one more birth remaining, as their upward or downward movement is not fixed.

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (115) asks: "Why is the 'Upstreamer' (*ūrdhvasrotas*) not established separately? It answers: "Because the two types of 'intermediate birth' (*antarāparinirvāyin*) are designated by the name 'one-birth' (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*)."

Because their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is difficult to discern, the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is divided; because they undergo many births, it is easy to discern them, whereas [the others] are not.

Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is brief and thus easy to establish, while the Upstreamer undergoes many births and is difficult to establish; therefore, they are combined into one. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further states: Question:

What are the five ways in which the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) excels? Answer: First, excellence of stage (*bhūmi*); second, excellence of realm (*dhātu*); third, excellence of the destruction and cessation of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); fourth, excellence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Question: Since those who have overcome the five afflictions to a slight degree also exist, why is the "destiny of a noble person" (*satpuruṣagati*) not established for them? Answer: It is not established because they are not coarse or manifest, and thus difficult to discern.
Furthermore, do such distinctions not exist? Regarding these two preceding gates, there are five [reasons] concerning birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, regarding this distinction: does this text—concerning noble ones (*ārya*) who take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—not describe the same distinctions of seven or nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) as exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
It states they do not go to other realms, but it does not say they do not [go to] their own realm;

for it is permitted that within their own realm they may undergo many births over a long period of time, which constitutes the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*). One who was formerly an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and then undergoes births.
Attaining the names of the two fruits (*phala*) and so forth within the body of an Ārya is called the "excellent basis" (*viśeṣāśraya*).

First, there is one untainted (*anāsrava*) and one tainted (*sāsrava*), resembling the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*); subsequently, there is one untainted [moment], resembling the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The first moment of mind severs and enters the second; the second moment of mind severs and enters the third, which is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) free from hindrances.

The concentration of mindfulness has the five aggregates as its substance; it functions as an obstruction to concentration. The first two moments of mind and the obstruction to concentration perish simultaneously, while the subsequent single moment of untainted (*anāsrava*) mind is like closing a door.
Question: Does the attainment of the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*) result from past karma serving as a supporting condition, or is it produced by newly created karma?

If it relies on past karma, it would be inconsistent to say that the preceding and succeeding untainted moments support the intermediate tainted (*sāsrava*) state. If, on the other hand, [it were produced by new karma]...
Question: Since [the inhabitants of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens] are already noble ones (*ārya*), how could they further create karma for future existence? Answer:

Because they utilize both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) as their resources, the karma that brings about rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens is actually the karma of the fourth dhyāna previously acquired since beginningless time, which is now being utilized.

As cited earlier from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two explanations regarding this; the present commentary states that "the power of the uncontaminated perfumes and cultivates the contaminated" is an admission that such karma is indeed created.
This commentary states that the six moments of mind further give rise to three more moments of mind to constitute the "six moments of mind" and so forth; this is the position of the first master.
The second master asserts that they further arise separately as six moments of mind, up to fifteen moments of mind and so forth.

Furthermore, within the five grades [of the Path of Cultivation], both those who emerge from meditative absorption and those who do not are included. Moreover, the six grades of mind do not necessarily arise in immediate succession. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says: "For..."
The karma that definitely results in rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens is called "definite" (*niyata-karman*); it does not depend on meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If one asks whether karma depends on concentration, the answer is: both are produced by the power of these two. Question: When cultivating the three lower dhyānas, how many grades of mind are there? Answer:

One school asserts there are three—namely, inferior, middling, and superior. According to this explanation, there are also five grades of mind. If there are five grades of mind, then [the following] should apply...
Regarding the answer that there are five grades of fruits: although there are no five grades of fruits [in the formless realm], there are five grades of fruit-roots.
If there were five grades of fruits, then there would be Pure Abode heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*) within the lower three dhyānas.

The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is mindless and closely resembles *nirvāṇa*. Because one realizes this attainment by means of the body, it is called "realization through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] explains that when one emerges from this attainment, the conscious body is tranquil; therefore, one refers back to that attainment as being "extremely similar to *nirvāṇa*.

The Buddha told the householder Anāthapiṇḍada that fields of merit and so forth are established upon the basis of the three trainings (*śikṣā*), which are untainted (*anāsrava*). As for the attainment of cessation, it is established upon these same untainted dharmas of the three trainings.
Question: Since it is not an untainted (anāsrava) dharma, why does the body-witness (kāyasākṣin) not enter [nirvāṇa]? Answer:
Because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) possess bodily liberation, whereas for those still in training (śaikṣa), the body is not liberation; thus, it is not established [for them].

Regarding "because the cause does not exist": "cause" refers to the causal basis for the noble ones; after emerging from meditative absorption, the dharma subsequently attained (prsthalabdha-jñāna) resides within the body, and is thus also called "bodily realization" (kāyapratisaṃvit).
By the power of the ninth path of immediate succession (anantarya-mārga), one is able to sever the afflictions of the three realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation;
since these have already been severed previously, the ninth grade is not severed—just as when the great light appears, all minor darknesses are extinguished. Question: Is this not so?

If it is argued that since the delusions regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the Path of Seeing must therefore be the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), the answer is given:
because the nine grades are abandoned collectively, the path that abandons the most inferior of the inferior delusions is not the Diamond-like Samādhi.

However, the Diamond-like Samādhi exists in all nine stages—the Preliminary (*anāgamya*), the Intermediate (*dhyānāntara*), the four Dhyānas, and the three Formless Absorptions (*ārūpya*)—because in all these stages there is the abandonment of the delusions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Daowen asked: "Should one who is dull and has not yet attained the sharp state of *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) be called a *śaikṣa* (one in training), because they will further train toward sharpness?

The answer is: No, because such a person has not yet attained a distinct fruit or specific spiritual qualities (*guṇa*). Furthermore, the three—precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—constitute the essence of what is to be learned (*śikṣā*). Since these have not been fully mastered, one is not yet a *śaikṣa*.

The cause is named "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*), and the fruit is named "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*). According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one is called "worthy" because one should eternally destroy the thieves of the afflictions, because one should eternally sever the cycle of birth and death with its limited segments (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*), and because one should receive extensive offerings from gods and humans. Question:

Why are two fruits established for those who cultivate the path while still possessing defilements in the desire realm, whereas only one fruit is established for those who cultivate the path while possessing defilements in the form and formless realms? Answer: Because of the desire realm... [text ends]
Because delusions of an unwholesome nature are difficult to sever, difficult to destroy, and difficult to transcend, two fruits are established for them;
the form and formless realms are contrary to the above.

As for establishing one fruit for the severance of delusions of view and three fruits for the severance of delusions of cultivation: because delusions of view are easily abandoned, one fruit is established.
Regarding the abandonment of the afflictions of the fruit-stage (*phala-kleśa*) and those of the higher realms, three types of attainment (*prāpti*) are established.

Since the noble ones (*ārya*) abandon the afflictions of the eight stages through distinct attainments—both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—only ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess the principle of a single contaminated attainment.

Furthermore, the abandonment of the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) stage occurs solely through a single uncontaminated attainment. This is because...

The path of the outflows does not abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation at the Peak of Existence; this is called "not being accomplished by what was done" because, although the afflictions of the eight lower stages abandoned through the path of seeing have been severed, the path of seeing does not abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation—this is what is meant by "not being accomplished by what was done."
In the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the noble one of sharp faculties first attains two knowledges prior to the arising of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).

First, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) arises because of his previous vow that afflictions (*kleśa*) would be exhausted; subsequently, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arises. Following these, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is acquired.

This treatise omits this for brevity. According to the *Nyāya*, however, for those of dull faculties, the knowledge of exhaustion takes a long time, whereas for those of sharp faculties, the knowledge of non-arising [arises quickly].
It arises in the second moment following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) over a long period.

It is now called the "fourth fruit" and designated as a *śramaṇa* because it takes the name of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) in its entirety; this is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) referring to both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Although the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) can indeed sever the afflictions of the eight stages below the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [it does not fully qualify as such].
Because they are not completely severed, there remain various faults that are inconsistent with the nature of a śramaṇa.

Upon reaching the stage of the subsequent fruit, one gives rise to a single type of acquisition (*prāpti*) which acquires the preceding unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is not the case that there is a single collective acquisition for all unconditioned phenomena, as each unconditioned phenomenon has its own distinct acquisition.
Because the five causes for refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcara*) are complete, this is also called "attaining the fruit" and "attaining the benefit of the fruit."

The latter three fruits all possess five causes: they consist of the dharmas and subsequently attained wisdoms that obtain the first eight knowledges (*jñāna*) and sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), or they are termed "obtained" because they have already been named as such.
The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is called the nature of a śramaṇa; it draws forth the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its superior attainment and realizes the unconditioned as its fruit.
The *Nyāyapravēśa-śāstra* states: "Because the first three fruits transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the latter fruit transcends the upper realms."
It is established as such because it is supreme; "True Brahmā" refers to the first dhyāna, while "Provisional Brahmā King" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
Because this path is turned over to the bodies of others and crushes the thieves of affliction, it is called the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

According to tradition, this refers to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) because it subdues what has not yet been subdued, and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) because it suppresses what has already been subdued. This interpretation must necessarily conform to the principles of the treatises.

The wheel exists only on the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). To explain: because it subdues what has not yet been subdued, it refers to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*); because it suppresses what has already been subdued, it refers to the seven knowledges (*jñāna*).

Since both are situated within the Path of Seeing, it is only at the initial attainment of the Way and at the time of *nirvāṇa* that the earth and space deities proclaim the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
This is because these mark the beginning and the end; it is not turned at other times. In the interim, it is merely called "teaching the Dharma" (*dharmadeśanā*).

Furthermore, World-Honored One, regarding the term "turner," this is spoken in reference to the person who turns [the wheel]. In reality, it is the five persons who constitute the Wheel of Dharma. Question:
Why is it not called "the severing of suffering" but rather called "the knowing of suffering"? Answer: Generally, one who severs suffering merely severs the causes of accumulation (*samudaya*);
thus, subsequent fruits of suffering do not arise. It is not that this body can be severed, for the body itself is suffering. Question: Under each of the Four Truths, there are... [text ends]

Regarding the four aspects (*ākāra*): why is it said only that one "knows suffering" and so forth, rather than "knows emptiness" and so forth? The answer is that such a formulation is logically appropriate.

Among the four types of suffering, the term "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is designated as its unique characteristic. Once one knows it to be suffering, one simultaneously knows it to be empty and so forth.
The Sautrāntika school defines the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) as the vocal sound of the teaching that conveys the three paths; for by hearing this teaching, others attain awakening to the path.
Therefore, circling the Four Truths three times constitutes the twelve aspects (*ākāra*). Question: Since this is the actual turning [of the wheel], why was it previously called "already turned"?
Answer: It was already reached at the beginning of the turning; the term "already" does not mean that the turning is finished. The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"Because this serves as the entrance to the Eightfold Noble Path, it is not the essence of the Dharma-wheel."
● Treatise, Chapter Twenty-five:
On the Stream-enterer having seven births, the *kulaṃkula*, and the *anāgāmin*; based on the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*), there are 107,739 persons;
the fourth fruit also has distinctions such as the timely and the untimely—these two interpretations.
Liberation (*vimukti*) takes as its essence the resolute liberation (*adhimokṣa-vimukti*) associated with the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).

Regarding the distinction between the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) and the resultant stage (*phala-avasthā*), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* offers another explanation: one is called "liberated at a specific time" (*samaya-vimukta*) because the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is inferior;

the other is called "not liberated at a specific time" (*asamaya-vimukta*) because the path of cultivation is superior, such as that attained by a Buddha after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). Furthermore, these two names— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.*
There are two names for the single liberation of mind: first, liberation through detachment from craving; second, liberation through wisdom, which is detachment from ignorance.
Regarding the six types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the first five were previously explained according to their arising, while the last was named later.
This was done for the convenience of composing the verse, as it was more practical to name the last one first and then explain its arising later.
Regarding the two stages of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), those of the "nature of falling back" (*parihāṇadharman*) exist first because they are both inferior.

The Sarvāstivādins state that there was an Arhat named Ghaṭīkāra who, due to his dull faculties, fell back six times; fearing that he might again take his own life with a blade on the seventh occasion, it is known that he did indeed fall back.
The four schools, such as the Mahāsāṃghikas, maintain that the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) can be lost because it is initially attained in a state of inferiority.

In this school as well, the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) is initially attained without falling away because it is an initial attainment; there is no basis for falling away from what has been newly acquired.

By extension, the two intermediate fruits attained through "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*) are also initially attained without falling away. This applies to both dull and sharp faculties regarding the first fruit and the leap-over of the two intermediate realms, as they are not subject to falling away due to being initial attainments.
As for the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they arise conditioned by non-entities (*avastuka*); "entity" (*vastu*) refers to their essential nature.

It is also like grasping at suffering as "self"; within that suffering, there is no substantial entity of a self. Both types of feeling—those that are pleasant and those that are neutral—are conditions that lack a [substantial] object.
When practicing the path, greed and other afflictions arise toward objects; these two types of objects can be observed. One may observe them as being either attractive or repulsive, and so forth.
Since these characteristics are not absent therein, it is known that they are like form and so forth, which can be seen, heard, and so on;

furthermore, it is understood that the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) arise through deliberation, while the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise suddenly and may regress. The Sautrāntika school asserts that the first and last fruits realized by the Noble Path do not regress, whereas the intermediate fruits may regress.

Furthermore, they maintain that what is realized through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) does not regress, while what is realized through the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) is admitted to be subject to regression.

Fifth, regarding "not prior to the fruit": this excludes the two paths whose natures are identical yet whose attainments differ; it allows for the possibility of falling away from the mind-states [of the dhyānas].
As for the four dhyāna-concentrations, the Buddha stated that he taught the Unshakable (akopya) state of Arhatship to be such that there is no basis for falling away from it.
Since this is an unshakable dharma, how could one fall away from the concentration? If one falls away from the fruit, it does not mean one loses one's life.

In the end, one retreats from the middle [stage] and is permitted to pass away. The *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states that the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its essence;

entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*) from this stage allows for regression. The mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) has non-delusion (*amoha*) as its essence when entering the state of a noble one, and there is no regression; since non-delusion is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), it is so designated.

Furthermore, among the three [meditations], two are said to allow for regression because they possess conditions for regression, whereas the six classes of desire-realm devas, such as the gods (*deva*), do not regress, as they lack such conditions.

Furthermore, due to the conditions for retrogression, a mind associated with the concentration of the stage conducive to retrogression (*hāna-bhāgīya*) undergoes retrogression; however, a mind associated with the concentration of the stage conducive to stability (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) does not retrogress.

Moreover, one who delights in concentration may retrogress, whereas one who delights in wisdom does not. If one is entirely free from desire, both wholesome and neutral minds are capable of giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*);

if one is only partially free from desire, afflictions arise through minds of all three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*). If that is so, [what of] those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? They have already...

How can there be a state of regression (*hāna-bhāgīya*) regarding the abandonment of defilements? Answer: Within the concentration conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*), there is a small portion that is conducive to regression.

Regression by nature (*prakṛti-hāna*) means not giving rise to defilements; regression of the fruit (*phala-hāna*) means first giving rise to defilements and subsequently regressing from the fruit. [The term] *p'u* (with the second tone, or alternatively *pǐ* and *dòu*) refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) in an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*).
This path of preparation is both previously obtained and not yet obtained. The paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are exclusively not yet obtained.

The preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*)—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—as well as the liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*), are exclusively without outflows;
the same applies to those cultivated in the future. In the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), there is one each for the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
The ninth liberation path is both with and without outflows, because it cultivates the merits of all stages (*bhūmi*).

Question: Regarding the nine grades of ignorance—unobscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta)—arising from the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) on the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*), which obstruct the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*):

are they severed by the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) that induce [the attainment]? Question: When the transformation of reflection (*cintā*) and so forth results in the attainment of protection (*rakṣā*), why does it not result in the attainment of sharp faculties?

Answer: Because the many grades of ignorance have not yet been entirely eliminated, it does not constitute the attainment of sharp faculties; rather, it is simply the transformation of those inferior natures that is designated by the name "attainment of sharp faculties."
The transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) does not mean abandoning inferior faculties and separately attaining superior ones.

For the first two fruits, the stage upon which they rely is necessarily the same as the stage for the transformation of faculties; for the third fruit, it relies on six stages. For the first two fruits, the stage for the transformation of faculties and the stage for the attainment of the fruit must be identical;
for the latter two fruits, they may be either the same or different.

Regarding the possibility of abandoning the path of the fruit (*phalamārga*): because one seeks the path of the fruit while in the state [of the path], when the faculties are transformed (*indriyasaṃcāra*), one abandons the fruit and attains the fruit;

while abiding in the path directed toward [the fruit] (*pratipannaka*), when the faculties are transformed, one abandons the path directed toward [the fruit] as well as the fruit. What is obtained consists solely of the fruit and solely of the path seeking the fruit; therefore, the term "possibility" (*saṃbhava*) is employed.

For example, the preparatory path (*prayogamārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for the transformation of the faculties regarding the third fruit are all subsumed under the path of the third fruit. If one abides in the... [text truncated].

The preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and superior-result (*viśeṣa*) paths of the four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*), as well as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), are all subsumed under the third fruit-path;

since the ninth path of liberation for the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is also subsumed under the third fruit-path, those in training (*śaikṣa*) rely upon six stages (*bhūmi*). Question:

Since the path of liberation has already reached the fruit of nirvāṇa and the path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) has already transcended it, how can they be called "paths"? Answer: Because they are similar to the preparatory path.

Because they are of a similar nature, or because everything from the beginning to the end is the Path (*mārga*), or because they lead toward the remainderless nirvāṇa (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), it is called the "Path.

The meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is the eighth liberation (*vimokṣa*), and thus it is called "liberation. It is explained that the term "bliss" (*sukha*) refers to proceeding effortlessly and spontaneously;

proceeding with hardship is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*). That which is not the Path is called suffering. The "easy path" (*sukhā pratipat*) is exclusively the untainted (*anāsrava*) path; it is not said to exist [otherwise].

The path of outflows (*āsrava-mārga*) has the five aggregates as its essence in the form realm and the four aggregates as its essence in the formless realm. "Slow" and "quick" are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds based on the person;
"common" and "distinct" are *tatpuruṣa* compounds based on the dharma. If referring to the dharma itself as the cause, they are *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds. Awakening has three meanings:

self-awakening (*svabodha*), awakening others (*parabodha*), and the perfection of the practice of awakening (*bodhicaryā-sampad*). These respectively exclude ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and lesser bodhisattvas, [referring instead to] the ultimate and the non-arising.
"Wisdom" refers to the Bodhisattva.

The "thirty-seven factors" (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) have the meaning of "parts"; they are the means by which one can approach the stage of a Bodhisattva. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents three explanations:
one states that these are identical; another explains that by dividing ethical discipline (*śīla*) into two, there are eleven factors, with right livelihood being subsumed under the first two.

The twelve *ānulomika-śikṣāpada* are explained as the three *vibhāṣās*; furthermore, the establishment and abolition [of categories] based on the seventy-five dharmas is omitted here as it is overly prolix.

Regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), they do not speak of them as "kings of the mind" because the king of the mind takes its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, whereas the factors of enlightenment take common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as their objects; moreover, as for "enlightenment" (*bodhi*)...

These mental factors (caitta) cannot assist the mind-king (cittarāja); furthermore, joy (prīti) is established while pleasure (sukha) and equanimity (upekṣā) are not, because the aspects of the investigation category (vitarka-vicāra) are sharp and intense, whereas pleasure and equanimity are stagnant. Therefore, they are not established [in that context].

Regarding the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*): for those evil states already arisen, one cultivates restraint to abandon their further acquisition; for those evil states not yet arisen, one cultivates abandonment to prevent their acquisition.

The character "abandon" (*prahāṇa*) here refers precisely to the Path. For those wholesome states already arisen, one cultivates protection to maintain them; for those wholesome states not yet arisen, one cultivates practice to bring them forth.
Because these four types all involve the cultivation of abandoning evil and so forth while cultivating the arising of wholesome states, they are all termed "abandonment."
Question: Once wholesome states have already arisen, how can one cause even a single category or a single moment of them to further increase? Answer:

The Sūtra explains that what is called "increase" refers to the stage of progress (*viśeṣabhāga*), rather than the stage of maintenance (*sthityanukūlabhāga*). Question: In the desire realm, there is evil, so it is possible for all four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) to be present.

However, in the two upper realms, there is no evil; how then can they possess the four right efforts? Answer: Although those realms lack unwholesome dharmas, they do possess those specific virtues; furthermore, [the four right efforts] exist there because...

Because there is a path capable of counteracting that which is to be countered, the formless realm possesses both the distant antidote (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) and the supporting antidote (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*).

If this is so, how can those in training (*śaikṣa*) who possess defilements have all four [bases of power], while those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who are free from defilements also have four? The answer is the same as what was stated regarding the two realms above.

The four—desire, effort, and so forth—are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and serve as the bases (*pāda*) for supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Other masters say that supernormal power itself is [the basis].

These four—concentration, desire, and so forth—are called "bases of spiritual power" (*ṛddhipāda*) because they take concentration as their basis; this is a case of naming the result after its cause. Question:

Why are the five faculties (*indriya*), such as faith and the rest, first described as "faculties" and later described as "powers" (*bala*)? Answer: That which is inferior is a faculty, while that which is superior is a power.

That which is susceptible to being bent is a faculty, while that which cannot be bent is a power. There is a distinction between superiority and inferiority. The distinction is that that which can produce [a result] is called a faculty, while that which... [is called a power].
The abandonment [of defilements] is called "power" (*bala*); being unshakable is the "faculty" (*indriya*), and being unsubdued is "power.

Regarding the sequence of the five faculties and the five powers: first, one gives rise to faith in the cause and the fruit; next, for the sake of the fruit, one practices the cause through diligence (*vīrya*).
Because of diligence, mindfulness (*smṛti*) abides in its object; sustained by the power of mindfulness, the mind then attains concentration (*samādhi*).
Because the mind is concentrated, one is able to know things as they truly are; therefore, faith and the other [faculties] follow this sequential order.

Regarding the three factors such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), their nature as auxiliary companions extends throughout all preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*). What is now stated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so forth is spoken of in terms of their predominance.

According to the Vaibhāṣikas, the foundations of mindfulness are cited as the beginning and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) as the end. These factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) exist within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The path that severs the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is proximate to the Bodhisattva’s assistance toward excellence.
Regarding the "all" in the first dhyāna, this refers to the commonality across preceding and succeeding stages; there are thirty-seven factors in total.

However, within a single moment of thought, they are not all present simultaneously, as the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and so forth certainly do not coexist at once, though others may potentially coexist.
Regarding the transformation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*): from the foundations of mindfulness up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is called "transformation.

The realization and vision of the principle of the Four Truths through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is called "realization" while in meditative observation. Giving rise to pure faith by taking the Three Jewels and the precepts as objects during observation is called "pure faith.
Furthermore, being unable to be destroyed by the Māras of devas, Māras of Brahmā, and so forth after emerging from concentration is called "purity."
Regarding the phrase "toward the Buddha and so forth," the locative case (the seventh sound) is used here because this object is personally realized within.

It does not mean that there is impure wisdom regarding the existence of outflows (*āsrava*) or that it cannot be called pure when conditioned by afflictions; rather, it refers exclusively to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that takes as its objects the Three Jewels, the Dharma, and the precepts.

The eight types of persons—the four candidates for the fruits and the four who have attained them—consist of the five untainted conditioned aggregates (*skandha*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); these constitute the essence of the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

The fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) and so forth are all subsumed within the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). When one realizes the Truth of the Path, one acquires the "attainment prior to the dharma" (*dharmapūrvaka-prāpti*).

As for those on the paths of the Bodhisattva and the Pratyekabuddha: a Bodhisattva is exclusively a learner (*śaikṣa*), and in the ten directions there is only a single person [of this type]; a Pratyekabuddha takes [the path] alone.

The *Khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like) practitioners are the same as the *śrāvakas*. This fourfold sequence is explained according to the order of the states following emergence from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*), not according to the order of their actual realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Regarding the precepts received by the noble ones (*ārya*), they are received with faith as their essence; within all fifteen moments of mind, there is the designation of "precept" (*śīla*). All.

At that time, there were four categories of the Dharma-treasure: teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. Teaching and principle apply to all four truths; practice pertains only to the truth of the path;

and the fruit applies to both the truths of cessation and the path. Although the first three fruits may also be attained by laypeople, here we take the harmony of principle to define the Sangha, rather than taking the harmony of receiving [the precepts].
Right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and liberation (*vimukti*) arise simultaneously; when right knowledge is absent, perfect liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) is also absent.

Regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions (*kleśa*), this obstructs the liberation of the mind. While the acquisition of afflictions in the present obstructs [liberation], those in the two time periods (past and future) obstruct the future mind and wisdom.

When speaking in terms of the predominant factor, it is said that afflictions act as obstructions; however, in reality, both the acquisitions of the two higher realms (*dhyāna* and *ārūpya*) and determinate karma (*niyata-karma*) are capable of acting as obstructions.

Regarding why only the liberation of the mind (*citta-vimukti*) is mentioned with respect to the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and not that of mental factors (*caitasika*), it is because mental factors follow the primary mind (*citta-rāja*).
Although those in training (*śaikṣa*) also partially attain liberation from the hindrances, this is not mentioned because they differ from the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

The attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation by one beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitutes bodily liberation, not mental liberation; this is the first case. The attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation by one in training (śaikṣa) is the second case.
The attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation by one beyond training is the third case. The fourth case can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the teaching that the three realms are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): this is spoken according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) based on a single characteristic. It is said that "severing craving is called detachment" and so forth;
while each contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharma is attained as a distinct entity at the moment it is severed, in terms of their ultimate meaning they are not separate entities.

Disenchantment (*nirveda*) is broad because it encompasses both the abandoned and the unabandoned; its being restricted solely to the objects of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) is narrow. Detachment (*virāga*) is broad because it encompasses all four truths;

its being restricted solely to the abandoned is narrow. Detachment is universal, whereas disenchantment is specific; this is what is meant by "disenchantment-detachment" as a term for the universal and the specific. Wisdom (*prajñā*) itself is not disenchantment; rather, it is called "disenchantment" when it is associated with disenchantment.
● Treatise Root Text, Chapter Twenty-Six: Part One of the Seventh Chapter, "Discrimination of Knowledge.
The commentary on the text is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the detailed analysis of the text.

Wisdom (*prajñā*), vision (*darśana*), and patience (*kṣānti*) share the same essence but differ in their specific meanings. That which performs definitive discernment is called wisdom; that which discriminates is termed insight (*mati*);

and that which investigates is termed vision. Patience can indeed be considered faith; however, when one speaks of "noble wisdom-patience" (*ārya-prajñā-kṣānti*) among the four types of preparatory patience, this refers to the noble wisdom-patience itself.
It denotes the state where the afflictions to be abandoned by oneself have been severed or not yet severed, and where what was previously unknown or unaccomplished has reached definitive discernment.

Regarding the other two: apart from the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the eight patiences (*kṣānti*), the remaining eight knowledges and so forth are both patiences and views, as well as wisdoms.

The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses cannot be called "view" because it lacks investigation and deliberation; "right view" refers specifically to the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

First, regarding the abandonment of afflictions through the six practices during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), although one has already decisively severed them upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the stage of the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), this is because they are abandoned by the flow of that patience.

Furthermore, when an ordinary person abandons afflictions within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), the wisdom therein is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and not "patience" (*kṣānti*), because there is the possibility of subsequent regression.

As for the patience of endurance (*kṣānti-kṣānti*), its essence is non-aversion (*adveṣa*); as for the distinct patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*), its essence is diligence (*vīrya*).
The "patience of individual investigation of phenomena" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-dharma-kṣānti*) is precisely this "patience of the subsequent knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*). Question:

If patience cannot be called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) when it coexists with doubt (*vicikitsā*), then it should likewise not be called "vision" (*darśana*) when it coexists with ignorance (*avidyā*). Answer:

Patience is not called "knowledge" when it coexists with doubt because doubt is either severed or not yet severed; however, when it coexists with ignorance, it is called "vision" because it clearly illuminates the Four Truths and the attainment of the Four Truths.
This is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Because it is only at a later time that it is able to take all four truths as its object, it is said to "pervade" the six knowledges (*jñāna*). This addresses an external objection:

[the opponent] argues that since it takes suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) as its objects but does not take cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as its objects, its essence should not pervade the six knowledges.

Regarding the distinction in how contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdom apprehend their objects: contaminated wisdom functions with lack of clarity and in a distorted manner, whereas uncontaminated wisdom functions with clarity and without distortion.
Question: Since conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has observed suffering since beginningless time, why is it not called "knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: Because it may subsequently observe [that same object] as being pleasant and so forth, it is not called "knowledge of suffering."
The supramundane knowledge of others' minds does not know mundane minds because it takes mundane phenomena as its object through conceptualization and does not discern them individually;
furthermore, it does not take superior levels as its objects.
The mundane knowledge of others' minds knows fifteen mental states and mental factors, namely those belonging to the desire realm.

The four dhyānas each possess three levels of mind—lower, middle, and upper—and since the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) within these four dhyānas is common to all twelve, the lower paracittajñāna of the first dhyāna knows the lower-grade mind of the first dhyāna as well as the three minds of the desire realm;

the middle paracittajñāna of the first dhyāna additionally knows the lower and middle minds of the first dhyāna along with the three minds of the desire realm; and the upper paracittajñāna of the first dhyāna is able to know [the remaining grades].

The six minds and two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) should be understood accordingly. If uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas do not possess degrees of superiority or inferiority based on their level (*bhūmi*), but rather based on the hierarchy of their faculties (*indriya*), then a mind of lower grade belonging to the second dhyāna cannot know a mind of middle grade belonging to the first dhyāna.

As for the uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), that which knows and that which is known each consist of twelve types; there are three for each of the four dhyānas, just as in the case of the lower [minds] of the second dhyāna.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) belonging to the mental level of its own stage or the first dhyāna knows the two grades of mind—middling and inferior—of the second dhyāna.

The knowledge of others' minds belonging to the superior grade of the second dhyāna knows the three grades of mind—inferior, middling, and superior—of its own stage, the lower stages, and the first dhyāna.
Because there is no single person who achieves all three grades through uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds, it knows only its own stage and the lower stages.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that pertains to the three categories of mind with outflows (*sāsrava*), since a single person may possess all three categories, it is capable of knowing six types of mind. Question:

If there are four dhyānas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) belongs to the first dhyāna, how many types of mind does the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the first dhyāna know? Answer:

According to one explanation in the *Vibhāṣā*, it knows all four, because they are all subsumed under the desire realm. According to another explanation, it knows only one, namely, it knows only the transformative mind of the first dhyāna.

Regarding the above, although the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) may transform objects of the desire realm, it does not know them because they are superior [to its own level]. Question:
Among the three grades of mind in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), which stage’s knowledge of others’ minds knows them? Answer:

The *Vibhāṣā* mostly says that the knowledge of others’ minds can know all three grades of the first dhyāna, because they are subsumed under the same stage. However, the knowledge of others’ minds does not know the past or future, nor insentient matter.

Because the objects of the two knowledges—the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*anvayajñāna*)—are distinct, they do not cognize one another, just as two people facing away from each other—one looking at the heavens and the other looking at the ground—do not see each other’s faces. Although the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path within the desire realm cognize the two higher realms, this is not because they can cognize them in their entirety.
According to one account in the *Nyāyānusāra*, the rhinoceros-horn-like [pratyekabuddha] knows the four foundations of mindfulness.
The first, second, eighth, and fourteenth moments of mind constitute the correct knowledge; the three minds [the third, seventh, and ninth] are not correct knowledge.
Regarding the Śrāvakas, they know two moments of mind; among the fifteen moments of mind, whichever two moments they know, they are described as being the same as the *vargacārin* Pratyekabuddhas.

This treatise states that the *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like) Pratyekabuddha knows three moments of mind. As for those who do not know further, one tradition holds that there are two types of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the two types of knowledge concerning mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), it is said that one has already completed the first; thus, the first two moments of mind are known.

Through five moments of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one achieves the knowledge of the eighth moment and beyond, though its power is weak, and it is only through seven or eight moments that it is fully established.

One tradition states that the dharma-knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) share the same object as the contaminated (*sāsrava*), whereas the preparatory application for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is easily accomplished. Furthermore, the dharma-knowledges of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) share the same object as the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The five applications of mindfulness do not constitute [independent] practice, just as when a monkey offered honey to Kāśyapa and Kāśyapa exhorted the Buddha to know the path;
nor was it that Ānanda could know for himself that he was to be the attendant. It was through the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*) that he was made to know.

After emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the statement "I have known suffering" and so forth indicates that within the absorption one only attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while the distinct statement "I have known" refers to the post-meditative state.
Regarding the statement "I no longer know suffering," this indicates that within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), two types of knowledge are simultaneously attained.

Although those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) obtain these distinct benefits, it is said "I no longer know" specifically to indicate that those of sharp faculties do not [repeatedly] attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) while in concentration. By stating "I have already known suffering;
I no longer know it," it is indicated that both types of knowledge are attained while one remains in contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the statement that "conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) comprises one whole and a small portion of another": whenever it is said that something "comprises one whole," this refers exclusively to the inclusion of its own self-substance;
all subsequent instances of "comprising one whole" should be explained according to this principle.

As for conventional knowledge comprising a small portion of another, it includes contaminated (sāsrava) knowledge of others' minds, but does not include uncontaminated (anāsrava) knowledge of others' minds.
Within the substance of the four knowledges (*jñāna*), they are termed "partial" (*pradeśa*) in contrast to the other three knowledges.

Regarding the statement that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) subsume seven partial portions: these four knowledges (the knowledge of suffering and so forth) are subsumed by both the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge.
The knowledge of phenomena subsumes the phenomenal portion, but does not subsume the subsequent portion; the subsequent knowledge subsumes the subsequent portion.
The term "partial" (*prādeśika*) refers to those categories that do not encompass all phenomena.

The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have six knowledges as their essence. Within the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), it encompasses both the partial aspect of phenomena and the partial aspect of the four truths;
however, it does not encompass the partial aspect of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Regarding that which encompasses the mental states of others (*paracittajñāna*), this knowledge has four knowledges as its essence: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) encompasses the aspect of phenomena, and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) encompasses the aspect of subsequent realization.

As for the four partial aspects of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, these two knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge—pervade the knowledges of all four truths. Regarding suffering:
The knowledge that encompasses the limit of suffering (*duḥkha-anta*) is analogous to this;

the same applies to the knowledge that encompasses the origin and cessation [of suffering]. As for the knowledge that encompasses exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), these two types of knowledge have six knowledges as their essence:

the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) subsumes the limit of suffering among the six knowledges, while the knowledge of origin and cessation subsume the limits of origin and cessation among the six knowledges, as well as the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) among the six knowledges.

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) each comprise a portion of the four truths; that is, the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation each include a portion of suffering, origin, and cessation within the categories of phenomena and subsequent knowledge.

Regarding the statement that the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) comprises five portions: this knowledge of the path includes both the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge, as these two knowledges pervade all four truths.

The dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna*) that take the path-truth as their object do not include the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge that take the other three truths as their objects.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are subsumed within these two knowledges;

they have six knowledges as their essence, specifically the path-knowledge among the six knowledges, as well as the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge that take the path-truth as their object. Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that takes the path-truth as its object is subsumed within four knowledges as its essence.
This is the wisdom of the Middle Way.
