Wisdom serves as the antidote for numerous phenomena. Wisdom can remedy doubt, yet doubt cannot have non-wisdom as its essence;
wisdom can remedy fear, yet fear cannot have non-wisdom as its essence. Can wisdom then have fearlessness as its essence?

When the Buddha preached the Dharma, he did not instruct sentient beings [to maintain mindfulness]; thus, there would be no three applications of mindfulness (*triṣu smṛtyupasthāneṣu*). This is what the World-Honored One taught.

The Dharma should not fail its recipients. Answer: When the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, he intends for people to understand it. If a person does not understand, it is because those among the gods who could have understood do not understand;
thus, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) possess three types of gods who attain understanding. Therefore, there is no failure of the Dharma to suit the capacities of the recipients.

Although the great śrāvakas possess the three foundations of mindfulness, [the Buddha’s] is distinct for two reasons: first, because it is not merely the severing of habits; second, because it is extraordinary.
For this specific reason, [the name] "Brahman" is not established; in Sanskrit it is *Gautama*, which is one lineage among the Kṣatriyas. The old translation "Qiutan" (瞿曇) is a corruption.
It was heard long ago that in the past, a member of the Kṣatriya caste was stripped of his throne by bandits. When his father died, his son became a *ṛṣi* (seer) who nurtured the lineage.
Later, the court astrologer reported: "A star belonging to the Kṣatriyas has appeared; Your Majesty, instruct the people to seize it."
Having caused his body to ring out as a sign for others, the rishi arrived later; not seeing the boy, he observed the site and knew at once that the child was no longer alive.
He called out from afar to the boy, urging him to rise, manifesting the worldly sentiment of a rishi.

He conjured a dense cloud to provide concealment and let a fine rain fall to soothe the suffering of hunger. Then he manifested a woman to stir the boy's faculties; through this condition, the boy [was moved].

The seer who had discharged his semen wrapped it in cow dung and placed it within a sugarcane grove. When touched by the rays of the sun, the mass opened and a small boy was born, whose appearance was exceptionally wondrous.
Later, he grew up to become a king; for this reason, he was known as the Solar Lineage (Sūryavaṃśa), the Cow-Dung Lineage (Gomaya-vaṃśa), and the Earth-Lineage (Bhūmi-vaṃśa).
Among the Brahmins, there was one of the Kāśyapa clan, a man of uniform stature and a height of one thousand *zhī* (chi), who maintained the True Dharma.
It lasts for a thousand years or seven days.

When afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, one attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); when the meditative hindrances (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*) are severed, one attains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Ultimate severance refers to the non-retrogression of the aforementioned two. Regarding their shared qualities, they are identical in name and substance, yet differ in their functions and degrees of excellence.
In Sanskrit this is called *araṇā-vihāra*, which here is translated as "the practice of non-affliction" (*wu-jing xing*).

This means that one who has attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) understands that the cycle of birth and death in the past arises due to the afflictions (*kleśa*) produced within one's own and others' bodies.

Since even the arising of afflictions within my own body—which is already free from afflictions—can still engender birth and death, how much more so would it be for the arising of afflictions within the bodies of others? Thus, [one practices] with the intention of not allowing [afflictions] to arise even in oneself on the morrow.
Regarding the practice of alms-gathering and so forth, one first makes a vow: "May the sentient beings in that place not give rise to any afflictions toward my person tomorrow.

Then, entering a superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one proceeds to those places by the power of that concentration so that the afflictions do not arise. Purity is threefold: first, purity of the aggregates;
second, purity of speech; and third, purity of afflictions—this refers to the purification of the afflictions that delude one regarding phenomena.

Question: What is the difference between the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*)? Furthermore, what is the difference between the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)—which knows the present—and the knowledge resulting from resolve that knows the present?
Answer: The knowledge of past lives cognizes the five contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) of the past within the realms of desire and form; its mental object is indistinct.

The knowledge resulting from resolve cognizes the five contaminated and four uncontaminated aggregates across the three realms; its mental objects are distinct and clearly discerned. As for the knowledge of others' minds, it [cognizes] the present. Thus is the distinction.

Knowledge of others' bodies in the present perceives only their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and is not clear; the Knowledge of Aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), however, clearly perceives both the specific and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of one's own and others' bodies.

Regarding the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), such as those of phenomena (*dharma*) and language (*nirukti*): these are the objects and the knowledge; being unimpeded regarding the objects is "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*), and this unimpedement is itself "analytical knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*).

This is precisely wisdom; it is called "name" (*nāman*) because it summons the excellence of phenomena (*dharma*), and thus the verse mentions it. When complete, name, phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*) constitute the three.

If this is so, since names and so forth are themselves the referents (*artha*), why are they not called "referents"? The answer is: that which is excellently expressed is the "referent," whereas names and so forth do not qualify as referents because they take multiple phenomena as their objects of cognition.

Regarding the two grounds for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) and the five grounds for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): the two grounds for language refer to the realm of sound (*śabda*), while the five grounds for phenomena—encompassing the three higher dhyānas—are established based on the existence of wisdom that takes names and so forth as its objects.

Regarding the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the *Vibhāṣā* presents four positions: two are evaluative texts stating it follows speech and thus belongs to two grounds; one states it follows the body and thus belongs to all five grounds.

Regarding the five bodies, the former [opinion] is accepted; as for the latter two opinions, one states they belong to the desire and form realms (*kāma-dhātu* and *rūpa-dhātu*), while another states they pertain to all three realms.

Regarding the former opinion, the *Śāstra* cites two interpretations: the first is from the *Dharmasena-assembly*, and the second is the subsequent evaluation. This subsequent evaluation is identical to the former one; it is not the case that a single treatise contains two distinct evaluations.
The meaning of the text is that [the vocal karma] does not extend to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), as vocal karma exists only in the two [lower] stages. Thus, the grounds are equal.

Likewise, the names and so forth follow speech in two stages; if following the body, they exist in five stages. Now, taking the sense of being the object-condition (*ālambana*) and distinguishing it as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), it pervades nine stages.
All four are obtained through preparatory application (*prayoga*), because they take the practice of the Buddha’s words as their preparatory object-condition and essential nature.

They differ from the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*) regarding the stages, while otherwise they are the same as the absence of strife. The "ultimate concentration" (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) is the cause; it is the cause.

The concentration induces these six [knowledges], and these six are its fruits. These six—such as the "pure" (*anāsrava*) and so forth—rely upon the fourth dhyāna to constitute the six limits (*ṣaḍ-koṭi*).
These six concentrations are of the same category (*nikāya-sabhāga*); for example, a single verse consists of four lines, and thus the verse is of the category of lines.

The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which takes words as its object, is produced by relying on the fourth dhyāna; however, the substance of the words themselves is comprised within the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Regarding the nine grades: one recitation constitutes the lowest-of-the-low, two recitations the lower-middle, and so on, up to nine recitations for the highest-of-the-high.

Sixth, to explain the names: "spiritual" (*shen*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while "object" (*jing*) refers to the four or two sensory objects of those being transformed; "penetration" (*tong*) refers to realized wisdom.

The three dharmas establish their names based on the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This power is able to give rise to the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and its transformed objects; thus, it is called "knowledge that realizes the object. Regarding the knowledge of others' minds:
the other's mind is the object, the supernormal power is the realizing knowledge, and the name is established based on the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). Regarding the knowledge of past lives:

the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the past are the object, the recollection is the mental factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) associated with the mind, and the supernormal power is the knowledge itself. If one speaks of *nirvāṇa* as the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), then the exhaustion of outflows [is the realization].

That which is the realized attainment (*abhijñā*) is identical to the realizing wisdom (*jñāna*). When these arise within a body that has exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), they are designated by names derived from their basis and their realizing wisdom.

The first five superknowledges are common to both ordinary persons and noble ones; because the sixth is attained only by noble ones, it is categorized as a "virtue common to ordinary persons" based on the majority. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called 'superknowledge' (*abhijñā*) because it clearly manifests the initial emergence from obstructions and is unimpeded; it is called 'excellent progress' (*viśeṣa-mārga*)."
The Path also exists [in this regard]. Having first observed the ten stages of this life in the preliminary abiding, one then observes the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
The initial moment of this observation is called the completion of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), because the intermediate existence is subsumed within this present life.

Question: Regarding the objects of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), since one has not yet attained rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, how can one remember them? Answer: There are two ways of remembering:
first, through seeing; second, through hearing. One remembers the Śuddhāvāsa heavens by means of hearing.

Regarding the application of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): the supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhiviṣaya*) has the nature of volition; the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) has the nature of volition and matter;

and the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) has the nature of volition and sound. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), these functions do not exist, and thus there are no five supernormal powers there. Question:

If the supernormal power of the divine eye perceives matter, how does the supernormal power of the divine eye—which is the clear knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*)—come to know the mental states [of others] and so forth? Answer: It is because the supernormal power of the divine eye can induce a distinct excellence.

The knowledge that arises is able to discern the distinctions of mental states and so forth; when combined with the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), it is established under the name "the clear knowledge of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna-vidyā*).
This is a designation based on its fruit. If the knowledge of death and rebirth itself is called the supernormal power of the divine eye, then it is a designation based on its cause.
Question: Since the supernormal power of the divine eye is the knowledge of death and rebirth, how does the divine eye know the present [beings] through the knowledge of death and rebirth?

The knowledge that knows the future is explained in terms of its retinue; the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) takes the future as its object by way of its retinue, or the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) takes the future as its object.
Regarding the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), it is virtuous (*kuśala*), whereas the divine eye is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This indeterminacy refers to the nature of the faculty (*indriya*) and the nature of the supernormal power itself; "virtuous" is stated here with reference to its retinue. Question: Is the wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses called a supernormal power (*abhijñā*)? Answer: It is the divine eye.
Question: How does the divine ear (divya-śrotra) arise from the four dhyānas? Answer: It is said that it arises from the four dhyānas with respect to the sense faculties of the eye and the ear.

Question: Why are three of the six supernormal powers (abhijñā) established as "clear knowledges" (vidyā)? Answer: Because the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna) takes the past as its object, the knowledge of death and rebirth (cyutyupapādajñāna) takes the future as its object, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) rejoices in nirvāṇa;
thus, these three possess superior function and are therefore established as clear knowledges. Furthermore, the clear knowledge of the wisdom of past lives leads to emptiness (śūnyatā).

The clear knowledge of the certainty of death and rebirth induces the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) induces the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); therefore, these three are established as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*), for their realization is itself clarity.

It is possible that these are truly so; they are distinct in taking the ten knowledges as their essence. Conventional [knowledge] is with outflows (*sāsrava*), while the supernormal power of knowing others' minds is also with outflows.
Regarding the statement "the remaining eight knowledges are all untainted (anāsrava)," it is said that they are "capable" because they are all untainted.

"Showing the Path" means showing, that is, manifesting the true teaching; "guiding" means leading others to enter the True Dharma; "manifesting supernormal powers" (ṛddhi-prātihārya) means causing them to resolve their minds [toward awakening];

"reading the minds" (ādeśanā-prātihārya) means causing them to believe by revealing their thoughts regarding good and evil deeds; and "liberating the mind" (anuśāsanī-prātihārya) means causing them all to resolve their minds [toward awakening].
The instruction of the mind and the teaching of the Dharma are called "guidance" (*nidarśana*).
*Khaṇḍalī*—the True Meaning (*Tattva*) says there is a goddess named Khaṇḍalī, and it is named after her;

alternatively, it may be the name of a country, as this [work] originated from that country. *Ilini* is the name of the treatise; *Lukhinga* refers to a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) who composed a treatise.
This spell is named after its place of origin.
When practicing the three types of mental power (*manomaya-ṛddhi*), the Buddha’s mastery over bodily movement and resolve—these three constitute transformation of substance (*dravya-nirmāṇa*).

For example, when Aśvajit ascended to the higher realms, he transformed the two objects of form and touch to serve as the basis for his body and its enclosure; likewise, when Brahmā descended to the desire realm, he transformed [his appearance].
The four objects (*viṣaya*) serve as the basis for the earth and the cage of this body; it is only within the lower realms that one can perceive them. Question:

Regarding the statement that "one arrives as soon as the intention is raised," if—as stated in the preceding text—one traverses a single atom (*paramāṇu*) is called a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), how can one arrive so immediately from such a great distance?
Answer: The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "It is like the sun extending its rays, which can reach [the destination] instantaneously. Were it otherwise, there would be an interruption in between."
When the practice of the meaning is not yet perfected, as soon as the mind is raised, a great body appears and reaches that place, like the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and others.

This mastery of transporting the body (*kāyavikrānti-vaśitā*) and the resolve (*adhimukti*) applies to both the two vehicles and ordinary beings. These eight transformations are explained as being of the nature of the four external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).

Regarding the question of whether one can manifest a body in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) while remaining in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or manifest scents and tastes [in the desire realm] while remaining in the form realm: [the answer is that it is possible]. Furthermore, while remaining in the desire realm, one may manifest a body in the form realm.

Question: How many atoms (*paramāṇu*) are there in a transformation (*nirmāṇa*)? Answer: The *Vibhāṣā* states that a being of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) can manifest transformations of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), including fragrance and taste.
If one were to say that such transformations do not possess fragrance and taste, it would entail the fault of [denying] their accomplishment. Answer: There is no fault of non-accomplishment;

although they are manifested, they are not accomplished because they do not combine with the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), just like external objects such as clothing. According to one interpretation, the preceding text’s statement that "the substance itself is manifested" applies here as well.
This explains that those of the Hīnayāna alone are unable to transform others into animals and so forth.
Regarding the transformation of transformative acts, is the transforming mind that performs the act of transforming the objects of transformation itself the supernormal power (abhijñā), or is it not?

Regarding the statement that the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) arises from the supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhi-vidhi-abhijñā*): this explains that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which emerges from obstacles, constitutes the essence of the supernormal power.

The transformative mind arises from the supernormal power of the basis and takes it as its fruit. While the object to be transformed is distant from being the fruit of the transformative mind, it is proximate to the supernormal power as its fruit.

If one speaks of "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*), it is wisdom (*prajñā*); if one speaks of "the basis" (*ṛddhi*), it is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If one speaks of "power" (*śakti*), it is...
The fruit-mind that is unobstructed is called "pervasive" (*abhijñā*); that is, it is the fruit of both wisdom and concentration. This "pervasive" [mind] is the pervasive-fruit mind. Question:
Between the transformation-mind produced in the desire realm based on the second dhyāna and the transformation-mind produced based on the first dhyāna, which is superior and which is inferior?

Answer: If judged by way of the level (*bhūmi*), the transformation-mind of the first dhyāna is superior and the transformation-mind of the desire realm is inferior, even though [the latter] relies upon the second dhyāna.

Because the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if one considers it in terms of its basis (*āśraya*), the transformation mind of the desire realm is superior, as it relies upon the second dhyāna.
Since the transformation mind itself does not transform sound, there is a separate "mind that initiates speech" (*vāk-pravartaka-citta*).

When the mind that initiates speech arises from the second dhyāna, the initial mind of the first dhyāna remains in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and it is precisely this [initial] mind of the first dhyāna that can initiate the transformation mind of the first dhyāna to produce speech. This applies to both those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
In the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), speech and other functions cannot be inconsistent or sequential unless one has attained mastery.

Kāśyapa’s Mahāyāna statement regarding "entering the extinction-concentration" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and this treatise’s statement that "after death, one reaches the presence of Maitreya and manifests eighteen transformations" are both due to the power of his original vows.

If a transformed person (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*) consumes food or drink, it is digested within the body of the transformer; if they employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they may consume even metal or stone as sustenance.
"Equal" refers to their being either absorbed within the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) or placed elsewhere.
"Attained through cultivation" means that their substance consists of the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) of the four fundamental dhyāna stages;

by entering those meditative absorptions, one induces this pure matter, and based upon these two faculties, one is able to give rise to the two consciousnesses and perceive distant forms, sounds, and so forth.

The fleshly eye sees what is near but not what is far; the divine eye sees both the distant and the near. The fleshly eye possesses both the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*);
the divine eye is exclusively homogeneous. The fleshly eye sees what is in front but not what is behind, nor does it see to the left or right;
the divine eye sees all that is in front, behind, to the left, and to the right. The fleshly eye sees within obstructions but not outside them; the divine eye sees both inside and outside.
The fleshly eye sees what is coarse but not what is subtle; the divine eye sees both. The fleshly eye sees by day but not by night;
the divine eye sees both by day and by night. The fleshly eye sees light but not darkness; the divine eye sees both light and darkness.

The fleshly eye possesses obscurations and defects, whereas the divine eye has none of these. The divine eyes of those such as the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm are those obtained through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*).

If the eye is acquired through cultivation, then "heaven" (deva) is the eye; if it is the eye obtained by birth, such as that of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and so forth, which resembles the divine eye, then it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive compound).
The same applies to the three types of explanations for the ear.
● Treatise Root Text, Chapter Twenty-Eight: Analysis of Meditative Concentration (Samādhivibhāga), Part One of Eight.
This commentary on the chapter is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the analysis of the text.

In Sanskrit it is called *dhyāna*, which here is translated as "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). Regarding its purpose: concentration is the condition for the arising of wisdom. Following this, there is the section on concentration;

the various types of knowledge have already been explained, and the meritorious qualities accomplished through those distinctions of knowledge are now summarized. This concludes the ten powers and so forth mentioned previously.

The subsequent text requires that the mind and mental factors be unified, not scattered across multiple objects; this is termed "one-pointedness" (*ekāgratā*), and this one-pointedness is [concentration].

Regarding meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Sautrāntika school asserts that it is provisionally established upon the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). They refute the position that, apart from the mind-king, there exist separate entities for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) by arguing:
"If feeling and the others are able to experience [objects], then why should there not be separate entities for feeling and so forth apart from the mind?

If absorption is able to cause the mind to be one-pointed, what prevents there being a separate entity for absorption apart from the mind? This applies even prior to entering the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), where the preceding moments of mind...

If seeds of mind and mental factors were formed upon the perfumed matter, then when one is born in the formless realm and cultivates meditative concentration, how could the seeds of matter be formed upon the perfumed mind and mental factors?
Furthermore, in the desire and form realms, both matter and mind are capable of maintaining seeds.

[The opponent] names the three natures of mind differently and claims they maintain their own [seeds]. To refute this: when one enters an unwholesome state of mind, what kind of mind maintains the seeds of wholesome matter?
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that all dharmas, upon reaching the present moment, possess the power to grasp their subsequent effects;
this refers to the final moment of form at the time of death in the desire and form realms, which grasps the last effect of form in the formless realm.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "This emptiness exists simultaneously with form; one gives rise to the conceptualization of resolve and contemplates that emptiness."
Although the essence of space coexists with form, it is only when the perception of form is absent that space becomes manifest.

In the stage of the fundamental attainment (*maulasaṃāpatti*), which is fully endowed with conditions, one contemplates the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) through the preparatory stage (*prayogamārga*) and establishes the name "formless" (*ārūpya*). Having grown weary of the external space previously [contemplated], one gives rise to the perception of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣasaṃjñā*) and considers everything from the internal six bodies of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*) up to all things as being merely consciousness. Furthermore, the fundamental attainment also takes the five aggregates as its object of emptiness.

Since the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of consciousness are manifold, coarse, and agitated, while the mental aspects of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) abide in tranquility, it is named the "Sphere of Nothingness.

Question: For what reason are the four formless states called "spheres" (*āyatana*)? Answer: They are the places where beings are born; furthermore, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to them as being *nirvāṇa*.
Now, in order to refute that [view], they are established as places of birth. The *Nyāyabindu* (or *Prayogalakṣaṇa*) says: "Concentration and..."

The nature of the five aggregates associated with craving, which serve as the basis for relishing and its accompaniments, is what is meant here. As for why other afflictions associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are not called "relishing" (*āsvādana*):
it is because this craving, being focused on a single object, causes the concentration to acquire the name "relishing," whereas other afflictions are distracted and thus cannot be so named.

Furthermore, from a preceding moment of pure concentration, a subsequent moment of craving arises; within that preceding moment of pure concentration, there exists a factor conducive to retrogression.

The concentration of equipoise (*samāpatti-samādhi*) and a portion of the concentration conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-anuloma*) are capable of producing subsequent moments of relishing concentration (*āsvādana-samādhi*).

Other pure concentrations (*śuddhaka-samādhi*) do not produce relishing concentration. According to the Vaibhāṣika school, concentration is both the substance (*dravya*) and the factor (*aṅga*); the remaining four [factors] are auxiliaries to concentration and possess the factors, while that which depends upon them is not concentration itself.
"Factor" (*aṅga*) signifies the sense of accomplishment; the five factors manifest the first dhyāna, and so on up to the four factors [of the fourth dhyāna].
This clarifies the fourth dhyāna and so forth; or it has the sense of "conformity," meaning each conforms to the meditative absorption (samādhi) of its respective level;

or it has the sense of "assistance," meaning the five factors assist the initial arising and so on. Regarding the four propositions: there are factors of the first dhyāna that are not factors of the second dhyāna, such as vitarka and vicāra;

there are factors of the second dhyāna that are not factors of the first dhyāna, such as internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda); and there are factors of the first dhyāna [that are also factors of the second].

The fourth phrase regarding the factors of joy and bliss in the two concentrations can be understood accordingly. Question: Just as one enters the sphere of infinite space by leaping over the third concentration, the sphere of infinite space should likewise possess its own factors.
Answer: For a beginner practicing concentration, it is necessary to possess the factors in order to give rise to the subsequent state;
however, once mastery is achieved, it is easy and does not require the factors or the like to arise.

"Lightness" (*laghu*) means lightness and agility; "ease" (*praśrabdhi*) means fitness, which acts as a cause of gratification for the associated mind. In the first two [dhyānas], when one is in meditative absorption, there is no pleasure (*sukha*) belonging to the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

Among the seventy-five dharmas, the feelings (*vedanā*) of all four stages (*bhūmi*) are established as factors (*aṅga*). Within the explanation of the five factors, the names of the feelings of the four stages are clarified;

this is their specific distinction, though here they are discussed according to the five types of feeling (*pañca-vedanā*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 80, treats this in terms of the seventy-five dharmas.
To avoid making the text overly prolix, I shall not describe the Sautrāntika position here. According to them, the second dhyāna is distinguished from the first by the absence of vitarka and vicāra;

it possesses internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) and samādhi, which are merely specific states of mind and have no separate ontological substance. It is difficult to sever and difficult to destroy, being a mundane path that is hard to transcend, serving as the path of liberation.
It may also be "separated from within": having first separated from the defilements of desire and attained the savoring of the first dhyāna, one realizes the emptiness of that concentration;
subsequently, upon attaining the second dhyāna, because the first dhyāna—like the desire realm—is also understood as something to be abandoned through faith, there is "inner purity."

Regarding "separation from external uniform flow": in the first dhyāna, there are three consciousnesses that take external objects as their conditions; in the second dhyāna, one is separated from these, which is why it is called "separation from external uniform flow.

Consequently, there is "internal clarity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda). The Sthavira school asserts that the joy (*prīti*) of the first two dhyānas is not the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*), because the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) in the third dhyāna is entirely the feeling of joy.

Regarding the phrase "because it arises without being separated from afflictions": since this meditative concentration arises in association with afflictions, it is said to arise without being separated from them.

Upon entering the fourth dhyāna, one is able to illuminate all things; it is tranquil and free from calamity, moving like a lamp in a sealed room that illuminates all things while its flame remains unmoving.

However, those bound to that stage do not give rise to a mind of a lower stage by means of the three consciousnesses or vitarka and vicāra; nor does one give rise to it by means of an indeterminate nature.

The Master of the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Dharmatrāta, maintains that maturation does not allow for arising in another stage, and that the skillful [consciousness] does not penetrate the higher stages.

The *Pratisamvid-phala* (Result of Penetration) arises only through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As for these three consciousnesses—the functional, the deportment, and the indeterminate—Master Guǎng maintained that they arise from the body.

Regarding the consciousnesses of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the two consciousnesses of ear and eye pertain to deportment and also to the result-of-retribution (*vipākaja*); discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are also [pertinent to] deportment.
Master Bao states: "The four types of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) do not exhaustively encompass matter, nor do they exhaustively encompass mind.

Since deportment is indeterminate by its own nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) and lacks sound, how could the auditory consciousness be of that deportment? Therefore, we know it is indeterminate by its own nature."

Immediately following the untainted (anāsrava) state of the first dhyāna, there arise the pure (śuddha) and untainted states of the first, second, and third dhyānas respectively. From the pure state, a defiled dhyāna may arise;

this refers to the arising of a defiled state from a pure state that is of the "receding" (hāna-bhāgīya) variety. That which arises from a defiled state is either of the "abiding" (sthiti-bhāgīya) variety or of the "arising" (utpatti-bhāgīya) variety that leads toward defilement.
As for the arising of the impure (aśubha), it refers to the mind of regression from meditative concentration.

Regarding the statement that "the pure [attainment] arises from the taste [of meditative absorption]," some say it arises from the *anuloma-sthitibhāgīya* (conducive to maintenance), while others say it arises from the *viśeṣabhāgīya* (conducive to progress);

there is no commentary [on this]. Regarding the statement that "the pure [attainment] arises from all [levels]," both the wholesome and the non-obscured-neutral are termed "pure," whereas the unwholesome and the obscured are termed "defiled.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Because the fundamental wholesome [attainments] of the formless realm are extremely tranquil, there is no *prāntakoṭika-jñāna* (limit-of-extremity knowledge) therein."

Because it is stated that there are paths belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānapakṣa*) which take as their objects the lower contaminated (*sāsrava*) unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena,

and because it is further stated that one "transcends" the characteristics of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) while no such transcending is mentioned for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), we know that in the form realm there are paths of the category of dharma-knowledge taking lower phenomena as objects. As for the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
they possess the aspect of non-self (*anātmanākāra*) and take only the four higher empty spheres as their objects, not the lower realms.
Although the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [path] performs the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), it does not sever the defilements of its own stage;

this is because the contaminated path has not yet attained clarity and sharpness, just as a lion-king obtained by a Tathāgata cannot harm wild beasts. Furthermore, the eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) have not yet abandoned the defilements of the lower stages and have not yet attained a mind associated with joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*).
Among the seven upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), there are no untainted (*anāsrava*) paths because they do not involve revulsion toward the afflictions of their own level.

As for why the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna does possess untainted paths: it is because it serves as an antidote to both its own level and to the lower realms, which are characterized by calamities and afflictions.
Regarding the flavorless concentration (*asvādanā-samādhi*), its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is the path of detachment; at the time of detachment, the flavorless concentration does not arise.

That which is not the path of detachment is nevertheless a derivative of the path of detachment. According to another explanation, even when the fundamental [dhyāna] has not yet been attained, it is also categorized as the flavoring of the form realm.

Question: Why is the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna called "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*), while the others are not? Answer: The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 78, states:
To distinguish it from the other preparatory stages, this initial preparatory stage is not induced by the [actual] dhyāna;

furthermore, because one does not relish (*āsvādana*) it, it receives the name "not-yet-arrived. The other preparatory stages are induced by the lower dhyānas and, because one relishes them, they do not receive this name.
This refers to the meaning that while the fundamental virtues have not yet manifested, one possesses the three meditative absorptions (dhyānas), such as *sāsvāda* (with relish) and so forth;

because it is a distinct place of birth (*upapatti-sthāna*), it is termed "intermediate" (*dhyānāntara*). It is designated as "intermediate" in relation to the stage above which there is applied and sustained thought (*savitaraka-savicāra*) and the stage below which there is no applied or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*).

In Sanskrit, this is called *samādhi*, which here is translated as "equipoise" (*samāhita*). It pervades all three moral natures (*tridhātu*) and both concentrated and distracted stages, and exists only where there is mind (*citta*).

This refers to the equality of the essential nature of concentration (*samādhi*) and its ability to maintain the mind; thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound meaning "the maintenance that maintains.

Alternatively, "equality" refers to the equality of the preceding mind that induces concentration, which then induces the arising of the maintenance of that concentration; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound meaning "the maintenance that is itself concentration and equality.

In Sanskrit, this is called *samāpatti*, which here means "equilibrium" (*ting-zhi*). It encompasses both wholesome and defiled states, is exclusively meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and occurs only when the mind is present.

"Mindless equipoise" (*acittaka-samāpatti*) refers to that which is induced; it is so named because the mind prior to this concentration induces one into the state of concentration, and it is designated as such by taking the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) as the primary term.
"Specific concentration" (*viśeṣa-samādhi*) is named by taking the activity (*karman*) as the primary term. In Sanskrit, it is called *samāhita*, which here means "equipoise.

It refers exclusively to concentration and the presence of mind. "Equipoise" (*samāpatti*) is concentration; "inducing" (*āpatti*) refers to inducing from concentration the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth; "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) refers to concentration.

The preceding mind, being equanimous, leads [the mind] to the state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. The latter [term], "meditative absorption," is exclusively of a wholesome nature.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there is a fourfold classification regarding the thirteen types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*): 1. There are meditative absorptions that are not meditative concentrations; these refer to the two mindless absorptions (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), which possess meditative concentration but lack meditative absorption because they are dissociated from a discursive mind. 2. There are meditative concentrations that are not meditative absorptions; these refer to the meditative concentration associated with a non-concentrated mind. 3. There are those that are both meditative concentrations and meditative absorptions; these refer to the mindless absorptions. 4. There are those that are neither meditative concentrations nor meditative absorptions; these refer to all other states of mind. Regarding the third category, it refers to the mindless absorptions (*citta-viprayukta-samāpatti*). In the case of the first category, it refers to the two mindless absorptions, which are meditative absorptions but not meditative concentrations because they are dissociated from a discursive mind. The third category refers to the mindless absorptions. As for the fourth, it refers to all other mental states. (Note: The provided source text contains some ambiguity regarding the specific application of the "fourfold classification" (*catuṣkoṭi-vyavasthāna*). The translation above follows the standard Abhidharma interpretation of the relationship between *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, aligning the categories with the logical possibilities of their coexistence or exclusion.)

The fourth line can be understood as follows: because one attains emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the aggregates (*skandha*) are not the self; thus, the self within the aggregates is refuted. Since there is neither "I" nor "mine" within the aggregates, the aggregates themselves are empty;
thus, the self apart from the aggregates is refuted. Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), being with outflows (*sāsrava*), are to be abandoned.

Although the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it too is to be abandoned like a raft. Therefore, the intention that takes emptiness as its object is the antidote to the notions of "I" and "mine. This is the joyful aspiration.
Realizing *nirvāṇa* is the intentionality of signlessness (*animitta*). Joy and equanimity toward conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are the intentionality of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Although emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-self (*anātman*) are conditioned, they are not called "wishless" because, being similar to *nirvāṇa*, one does not abandon them. The contaminated (*sāsrava*) emptiness takes all phenomena as its object;
the distinct uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) emptiness takes non-self and *nirvāṇa* as its objects. This is called liberation (*vimukti*). These three are able to grant...

As an entry point, one first uses the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) to empty the five aggregates and afflictions; since the signs of emptiness are manifold, they accord with the arising of wearying detachment (*vidūṣaṇa*).

One then contemplates through the three types of concentration, such as the contaminated emptiness (*sāsrava-śūnyatā*), thinking that even the previously attained signs of emptiness can be abandoned and not grasped.

This non-grasping of the previous signs—such as "I" and so forth—and the taking up of emptiness itself is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*); it is the emptiness of emptiness, whereby one perceives the five aggregates.

Because one does not give rise to craving or attachment toward emptiness, and because one perceives the five aggregates as selfless and does not give rise to aversion or abandonment, yet fails to reach the characteristic of emptiness itself, one grasps at the characteristic of emptiness.

Furthermore, through the meditative concentration associated with impermanence and wishlessness, one contemplates the preceding noble path as impermanent and gives rise to aversion and abandonment; this is [the stage of] "repeated" cultivation.

The signless (animitta) consists merely in observing the noble path associated with the signless as the characteristic of tranquility (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), which is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Previously, the noble path observed analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as being signless; now, when this signless state is present before the mind, it too may be abandoned through weariness.

One then gives rise to a contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*) and observes the previously mentioned noble path associated with the signless as being signless; because it is designated again as "signless," it is not analytical cessation.

The name "to be abandoned" (praheya) refers to something distinct from the untainted (anāsrava). Because one who has already given rise to delight toward the untainted cannot give rise to revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*), the three higher meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—the Sphere of Infinite Space and so forth—are not established as untainted *samādhi*.

Furthermore, one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) delights in the Noble Path and is unable to feel revulsion or renunciation toward it; thus, they cannot produce the three higher [attainments] such as the Sphere of Infinite Space.

Regarding the seven upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), they do not exist because they lack superior qualities; this is distinguished from the Sphere of Infinite Space which possesses them. As for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is excluded because it lacks such excellence.
Regarding their inclusion within the realms (*dhātu*): those that arise subsequent to the Path of the Unsurpassed (*anāgamya*) are included within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Those that arise subsequent to the Path of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) proceed toward the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [attainments] such as the "repeated emptiness" (*punar-śūnyatā*) and so forth—these three—because these two stages lack the Noble Path.

As for the remaining nine stages, the Noble Path arises subsequent to the Noble Path of its own respective stage. All of these are instances where, after having arisen through wisdom (*jñāna*), become free from defilement (*vairāgya*), and followed by skillful means (*upāya*), one further [engages in practice].

The preparatory application (*prayoga*) manifests [only] for the Buddha; for others, it manifests through aspiration. It is subsumed under the "gratitude and virtue" (*anugraha-guṇa*) of the desire realm and the "cultivated wisdom" (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) of the two upper realms.

These three types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) arise after the four knowledges (*jñāna*) of dharma, subsequent, suffering, and cessation. If they belong to the desire realm, they do not arise after the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);

if they belong to the two upper realms, they do not arise after the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*). The emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*) [absorptions] do not [arise after the aforementioned knowledges].
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is followed by the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*), but it does not arise following the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
It is said that one dwells in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*), rather than dwelling in happiness in a future life, because future happiness is not necessarily produced;
for either one may subsequently fall away, or one may enter *nirvāṇa*. Present happiness is certain, whereas the present itself serves as the basis for what follows. Thus it is established.
It is said that what serves as the basis for the present must necessarily have a future happiness as its supported state.

Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), two are cultivated: the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) because one observes birth and death, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) because one attains *nirvāṇa*; therefore, these two are specifically mentioned as being cultivated.
● Treatise Root, Chapter Twenty-nine: Analysis of the Absorptions (Samāpatti-vibhaṅga), Part 8-2.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 81. There are two explanations: first, that they serve as remedies for immeasurable afflictions;

second, that they are the vast playgrounds where the various noble ones (ārya) sport extensively. The desire to kill sentient beings is called "hatred" (dveṣa); the desire to harm sentient beings is called... [text fragment].
To be harmed by attachment to sense objects and never cultivate wholesome qualities is called "lack of contentment" (*anabhirati*).

To give rise to a defiled attachment toward the objects of exquisite desire without satiety is called "greed" (*lobha*). Question: What is the difference between the meditation on impurity (*aśubhā-bhāvanā*), which remedies greed, and this equanimity (*upekṣā*)?

Answer: There are two types of greed: first, greed for material objects (*rūpa-viṣaya*); second, greed for sexual desire (*maithuna*). The meditation on impurity remedies the former, while equanimity remedies the latter. Thus explains the Master of the Treatise.

The meditation on impurity (*aśubha*) remedies sexual desire; renunciation (*tyāga*) remedies attachment to friends and kin; compassion (*karuṇā*) remedies hatred—that is, it has non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its essence.

The previous statement that it does not remedy harmfulness was made from the perspective of describing it as a natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the true [state] and as a secondary remedy. Compassion and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) both have non-hatred as their essence;

the distinction between the two perceptions is that non-hatred remedies the killing of sentient beings by functioning with the aspect of joyful engagement, whereas non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) functions with the aspect of wishing them no harm.

The distinction between these two is that while one functions as the antidote to harm, the other functions with an affective aspect. The Master [Vasubandhu] states that non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) constitutes the essence of compassion (*karuṇā*).

Regarding what was previously stated concerning non-aversion (*adveṣa*), non-harming resembles non-aversion; thus, it is designated by the name "non-aversion. In the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are two views:

one holds that its essence is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), while the other holds that its essence is mental gladness (*cittasyābhipramoda*). The commentators do not offer a critique here, and this treatise agrees with the former view.
After explaining this, [the opponent] says: Since the meanings of "joy" (*muditā*) and "delight" (*prīti*) are entirely distinct, how can delight be the essence of joy?

The verse states that equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the antidote to greed; this is based on its primary antidote. The prose commentary, however, states that it also counteracts anger; this is said according to its secondary function.
As for the statement that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can counteract anger, it refers to counteracting the anger that is induced by anger; equanimity counteracts the anger that is induced by greed.

Question: Hatred (*dveṣa*) is distinct from these two. Since equanimity (*upekṣā*), having non-attachment (*alobha*) as its essence, can counteract hatred induced by attachment, and loving-kindness (*maitrī*), having non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its essence, should counteract attachment induced by hatred;
why is this so? Answer: Equanimity abandons both the beloved and the unloved, and thus it can simultaneously counteract both hatred and attachment.

Loving-kindness can counteract hatred because it prevents the subsequent arising of hatred; however, it does not counteract attachment, for it bestows happiness upon those very beings toward whom one feels attachment. Question: Regarding loving-kindness...
If bestowing happiness is itself compassion (*karuṇā*) that uproots suffering, why must compassion and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) be established as two distinct types? Answer:

Although there may be the act of bestowing happiness, suffering has not yet been uprooted; and although there may be the uprooting of suffering, happiness has not yet been bestowed. Therefore, they are explained separately.

Even when performing such practices as bestowing happiness, if the recipient does not obtain happiness because their mental disposition (*āśaya*) is not free from error, it is not the true [compassion] of the Mahāyāna.
Joy (*muditā*) is like transforming the great earth into gold and silver, or gathering the waters of the ocean into butter and curd.

First, that which is neither suffering nor joy refers to the manifestation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Second, regarding those who possess suffering—namely, those in the three evil realms and a small portion of the human realm—to extract them from suffering is compassion (*karuṇā*).

Third, if there are those who possess joy, to assist in their rejoicing is sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Initially, delusion increases in accordance [with these states], and thus one must depart from it.

The aspect of delusion (*moha*) is followed by suffering, the aspect of aversion (*dveṣa*) is followed by pleasure, and the aspect of attachment (*rāga*) is followed by desire; because it aims to cause one to be free from all evils, it is called the "immeasurable equanimity" (*upekṣā-apramāṇa*). Question:
In the lower three dhyānas, there is the movement of joy and pleasure, while in the [first] three stages, compassion (*karuṇā*) arises as the movement of dejection (*daurmanasya*).

How, then, can compassion be associated with the lower three dhyānas? Answer: It is like the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) state, which has the aspect of disenchantment (*nirveda*). Just as the uncontaminated path functions through the aspect of disenchantment despite being associated with the lower dhyānas, so too compassion, though characterized by dejection, can be associated with the lower three dhyānas.

Regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) in the three lower dhyānas, it is a transformation characterized by joy; once this has been attained, compassion (*karuṇā*) functions in the same way.
For those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) are thin, they are suddenly able to regard superior enemies and superior kin with equality, bestowing happiness upon them and extracting their suffering.
For those whose afflictions are increased, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) likewise bestows happiness and extracts suffering, each divided into three grades. All sentient beings are thus categorized.

The seven grades of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) all consist of bestowing supreme happiness upon those who are dear, and so on, up to the seventh stage, where one bestows supreme equanimity (*upekṣā*) equally upon enemies and those who are dear.

Specifically, regarding equanimity: first one practices it toward those who are neutral; next toward the three grades of enemies; then toward the three grades of dear ones—first the inferior, then the middling, and finally the superior.
The sequence of these four refers to the fact that for one who practices through joy (*prītisukha*), it arises first according to their inclination.
Even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) can give rise to these four; because they realize them within a body free from heavy afflictions, they are said to have "witnessed with the body" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Because they abide having attained this meditative absorption, they are said to be "dwelling in its possession" (*samanvāgata*).

"Abandoning and turning one's back" is the meaning of liberation (*vimokṣa*). The fundamental states and access concentrations of the first two dhyānas, as well as the intermediate state, all involve turning one's back on the mind of desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The third liberation involves the mind of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). The next four liberations involve the minds of desire for the lower stages.
The eighth liberation involves the mind regarding all objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Regarding those who possess craving for visible forms and shapes in the first dhyāna, this is induced by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Although the first and second liberations (*vimokṣa*) exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are not established there because they are overwhelmed and intermingled with their own afflictions.

Although the third and fourth dhyānas possess the antidotes to the cravings of the first two liberations, they are not established [there] because [the objects] are too distant. Furthermore, the second dhyāna lacks visual consciousness.

Because greed arises toward the forms of the desire realm, the third dhyāna is not established as a liberation (*vimokṣa*). Furthermore, because pleasure (*sukha*) still functions within the third dhyāna, it is not established as a liberation.
Liberation is the cause and the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are the fruit. The first two liberations apprehend the signs of impurity;

the third apprehends purity through its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and cannot observe it specifically. This [third sphere of mastery] can observe it specifically by taking it as its object.
One body is called "having few objects," while many bodies are called "having many objects"; this refers to mastery over the objects.

Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and liberation, it is as explained [in the *Abhidharma*]. This refers to mastery over the degree of transformation when grasping objects within the objective field;

because one does not give rise to afflictions therein, it is called "restraining the mind" and "the excellence of the mind. As for the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), they cannot be divided into the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative matter (*bhautika*).
Regarding the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the distinct contemplations of both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) pervade all locations.
When the world undergoes destruction, it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that one must first abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of a lower level before one can be born in a higher realm;
there is no case where one attains birth in a higher stage without having severed the afflictions of the lower stages.

Because of the teaching, there is realization; first comes the teaching, then realization. In the True Dharma (*saddharma*), there are both teaching and realization, as well as the precepts. In the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), there is no realization.
In the final period, there are neither realization nor the precepts—there is only the teaching of the Dharma. One tradition holds that both teaching and realization exist for two thousand years;

another tradition holds that the teaching of the Dharma persists beyond two thousand years. This treatise accords with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 22: "If my disciples uphold and expound [this Dharma]..."
The instruction for those abiding in practice is the realization of the abiding of the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "this treatise relies upon [the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*]," this refers back to the previous point that it subsumes that [work] as its ultimate meaning and relies upon it.

The passage beginning with "Master Bao Fa-shi, the Great Eye of the World, has long since closed" constitutes the section on circulation (*pariṇāmanā*), following the established outline of the chapter.
The text and the initial outline state that the final three lines of verse constitute the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) section;
this is an error in the outline of this commentary. This is the end of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-artha-saṃgraha*.
